faq.q: Is digital arrest a real legal procedure in India?
faq.a: No. It is not a term in any Indian statute and not a power any agency holds. An arrest under the Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita is a physical act, with the grounds communicated to the person and production before a magistrate within twenty-four hours. None of that is possible over a video call. Any call telling you that you are under digital arrest is a fraud, without exception.
faq.t: "Digital arrest": the scam that keeps you on camera until the money moves

faq.q: Can the police or a court ever contact me online at all?
faq.a: Yes. Section 63 of the BNSS allows a summons to be served in electronic form, and courts increasingly work over video. But a summons asks you to appear at a stated place and time before a named court or officer. It never demands money, never asks you to stay on camera, and never tells you to keep it secret from your family.
faq.t: "Digital arrest": the scam that keeps you on camera until the money moves

faq.q: The number on my screen looked like a real police station. Does that mean anything?
faq.a: No. Caller ID is display data, not proof of origin, and it can be made to show almost anything. Treat a familiar-looking number as neutral information. The only way to verify is to end the call and dial a number you looked up yourself from an official source, on a different phone if you have one.
faq.t: "Digital arrest": the scam that keeps you on camera until the money moves

faq.q: Should I keep the caller talking to collect evidence?
faq.a: No. Every extra minute is a minute they get to work on you, and the evidence that matters is already on your device — the number, the timestamps, the documents they sent, and the account details they gave you. End the call, then screenshot everything before you touch anything else.
faq.t: "Digital arrest": the scam that keeps you on camera until the money moves

faq.q: I already transferred money. Is it too late to report?
faq.a: Report anyway, immediately. Call 1930 and file at cybercrime.gov.in, then call your bank's own fraud line. Holds placed in the first minutes have the best chance of catching money still sitting in the chain, but complaints filed days later still matter — they support the investigation, they link your case to others, and they are what makes any later restitution order possible.
faq.t: "Digital arrest": the scam that keeps you on camera until the money moves

faq.q: Will I get my money back?
faq.a: Sometimes partly, often not, and nobody honest can promise otherwise. Only funds still sitting in the chain can be held, a hold is not a refund, and releasing held money usually needs a court order and months of waiting. Anyone who contacts you afterwards promising guaranteed recovery for a fee is running the second scam on the same victim.
faq.t: "Digital arrest": the scam that keeps you on camera until the money moves

faq.q: They have my Aadhaar number and my photograph. How much trouble am I in?
faq.a: An Aadhaar number is an identifier, not a password, and knowing yours proves nothing about a case against you. Nothing said on that call is evidence of anything. Report it, change the passwords on any account whose details you shared, watch your statements, and if you shared banking credentials or installed anything at their request, tell your bank so the account can be secured.
faq.t: "Digital arrest": the scam that keeps you on camera until the money moves

faq.q: Do you charge for the first week, and what do I own at the end of it?
faq.a: Yes, it is paid work, priced as a small fixed piece rather than an hourly open tab. You own the document: the observed process, the counts and their sources, the recommended build and the explicit exclusions. It is written so that it still works if you do the build in-house or give it to somebody else. Free discovery is either not real discovery, or it is priced into a build you have not agreed to yet.
faq.t: What actually happens in the first week of an automation engagement

faq.q: We already know exactly what we want built. Can we skip discovery?
faq.a: Sometimes, and I will say so. One trigger, one system, one person, and a low cost if it breaks — then discovery compresses to a call and one observed run, and I would not charge five days for it. What I will not skip is watching the process once and counting it. Without those two things there is no baseline, so there is no way to tell afterwards whether the build helped.
faq.t: What actually happens in the first week of an automation engagement

faq.q: What access do you actually need, and can we restrict it?
faq.a: Read-only access to the systems named in the discovery conversation, and nothing more in week one. No write scope, no admin. If access cannot be granted at all — regulated data, a vendor contract, a customer’s system — discovery moves to a screen share with your own operator driving, and the document states that the counts came from a sample rather than the full record.
faq.t: What actually happens in the first week of an automation engagement

faq.q: What if the answer at the end of the week is that we should not automate it?
faq.a: Then that is what the document says, with the reasoning and the numbers behind it, and you can act on it without me. It tends to happen when a step is about to change, when the volume is far smaller than remembered, or when the honest fix is to delete the step. I would rather lose a build than ship something that makes a bad process permanent.
faq.t: What actually happens in the first week of an automation engagement

faq.q: Who from our team needs to be involved, and for how long?
faq.a: Three people, usually briefly. The person who does the work, for the conversation and roughly an hour of being watched. Whoever can grant read-only access, for a request that takes minutes once it reaches them. And whoever can make the decision at the end of the week. Start the access request on day one, because it is the step most likely to stall.
faq.t: What actually happens in the first week of an automation engagement

faq.q: How soon after the first week is something actually running?
faq.a: I will not put a number on that before the map exists, which is much of the point of the map. What I can say is what drives it: how many systems the automation has to touch, whether any of them need credentials or approvals you do not already hold, and how much of the work is the exception path rather than the happy path. The exception path is usually the larger half of a build.
faq.t: What actually happens in the first week of an automation engagement

faq.q: Is a SIM swap the same thing as SIM cloning?
faq.a: No, and the difference matters. Cloning means copying the secret key held inside the card onto a second card, so that two SIMs answer to the same identity. Against the SIM generations in use today that is genuinely hard, and it is not what is happening in these cases. A swap copies nothing. It is an ordinary administrative change at the operator — this number now belongs to that SIM profile — performed by staff who are supposed to be able to perform it, because people really do lose phones. Reporting uses the two words interchangeably. Only one of them is common, and it is the one with no cryptography in it.
faq.t: How a SIM swap works, and why an OTP is not the protection you think it is

faq.q: My phone lost signal. Is that a SIM swap?
faq.a: Almost always no. Networks have outages, trays work loose, handsets sulk after an update, and buildings have dead spots. But the cost of checking is about ten minutes and the cost of not checking can be your bank account, so treat it as an incident until it explains itself. Ask whether somebody next to you on the same network still has service, try the card in another handset, and call your own number from a different phone. If nothing resolves it quickly, contact your operator from another line rather than waiting to see whether it comes back on its own.
faq.t: How a SIM swap works, and why an OTP is not the protection you think it is

faq.q: Can I put a port-out lock on my number in India?
faq.a: Not as a self-service switch, the way some carriers elsewhere offer one. What exists here is procedural rather than something you hold: a port needs a unique porting code generated by your current operator, a replacement SIM triggers a re-verification step, and the rules require the SMS facility to be barred for a period after a swap or a port. Those are speed bumps that buy detection time. They are not a lock, the details change without anyone telling you, and none of them is a substitute for moving your accounts off SMS. Ask your operator what is available on your account, take whatever they offer, and treat it as the weaker half of your defence.
faq.t: How a SIM swap works, and why an OTP is not the protection you think it is

faq.q: Does an eSIM make this better or worse?
faq.a: Both, and neither decisively. There is no plastic card to hand across a counter, and the profile is downloaded to a specific device after the operator authorises it, which removes one physical step. But the deciding check is unchanged: somebody at the operator still decides whether the person asking is you, and a profile can be issued to a device on the other side of the country without anyone walking into a shop. Treat the format as close to irrelevant. The control you are relying on is the operator's identity check either way.
faq.t: How a SIM swap works, and why an OTP is not the protection you think it is

faq.q: Can a passkey be defeated by a SIM swap?
faq.a: Not directly. The private key stays inside the device that created it, the browser will only offer it to the site it was registered for, and what crosses the network is a signature that is useless anywhere else. There is no code in existence to intercept, so holding the number gets an attacker nothing. The real risk sits behind the passkey rather than in it: if the account still lets somebody reset their way in with an SMS code, the passkey is a strong lock on a door that has a second door beside it. Adding a passkey and leaving SMS recovery switched on is the most common way people believe they have fixed this and have not.
faq.t: How a SIM swap works, and why an OTP is not the protection you think it is

faq.q: What happens if I lose the phone with my authenticator app on it?
faq.a: This is the honest cost of the advice, and it is why people stay on SMS. If the app is gone and you kept nothing, you are into each service's account-recovery process, which is slow, uneven and occasionally hopeless. So set it up properly on the day you move: save the recovery codes each service offers at enrolment and keep them offline somewhere that survives losing the phone, enrol a second device or a second factor where the service allows it, and prefer an app whose backup you control and have actually tested. Ten minutes of preparation turns a disaster into an inconvenience, and skipping it is why well-meant advice about authenticator apps sometimes ends badly.
faq.t: How a SIM swap works, and why an OTP is not the protection you think it is

faq.q: Will reporting to 1930 get my money back?
faq.a: Sometimes, partly, and it depends almost entirely on speed. What the report can do is put a hold on funds that have not yet moved out of the chain of accounts they were pushed through, which is why minutes matter and days usually do not. It is not a refund mechanism and nobody can promise you an outcome. Report anyway, and through both routes — the helpline and the portal — because the complaint is also what makes a bank dispute, a police investigation and any later restitution possible. Raise the dispute with your bank in writing as well, keep every acknowledgement number, and do not let anyone tell you a rule will rescue you automatically. I am not a lawyer, and none of this is advice on your particular case.
faq.t: How a SIM swap works, and why an OTP is not the protection you think it is

faq.q: Should I tell the consultant my budget?
faq.a: Usually yes. A budget is not a price you will automatically be charged; it is a constraint that lets the consultant propose the largest useful engagement that fits, instead of guessing at a size and being wrong in either direction. If you would rather not name a figure, name a range and ask what they would remove to reach the bottom of it. The answer to that question tells you how they think about priorities.
faq.t: How to brief a security consultant so the quote is accurate

faq.q: Can I ask for a fixed price instead of a day rate?
faq.a: Yes, and it is a reasonable thing to want. Understand where the padding lives, though: a fixed price is only fair to both sides if the scope is genuinely fixed too. If the inventory is vague, the fixed price will contain a margin for the version of your system that turns out to be twice the size you described. Fix the scope first and the fixed price gets cheaper on its own.
faq.t: How to brief a security consultant so the quote is accurate

faq.q: Do I need to tell my hosting or cloud provider before a test?
faq.a: Check the contract and the provider policy rather than assuming. Some providers permit testing of your own resources with no notice, some require notice or approval, and some prohibit particular techniques outright. Either way you cannot authorise testing of infrastructure you do not control, so anything shared or managed on your behalf needs its owner named in the brief.
faq.t: How to brief a security consultant so the quote is accurate

faq.q: Should the tester get an administrator account?
faq.a: It depends on the question. Administrator access finds a different class of problem, mostly around what a compromised or malicious insider could reach and what the audit trail records. It is worth having, but I would not start there. Start with the roles your real users hold, because that is where the authorisation bugs affecting customers live, then add administrator if the budget allows.
faq.t: How to brief a security consultant so the quote is accurate

faq.q: What if the report comes back with almost nothing in it?
faq.a: That is a possible outcome and not automatically a waste, but do not accept it on its own. Ask for the coverage statement: what was reached, what was not, and why. A quiet report from an engagement that spent most of its days waiting for credentials is not evidence of a secure system. A quiet report with a clear account of what was exercised is worth something to you and to your customers.
faq.t: How to brief a security consultant so the quote is accurate

faq.q: How far in advance should the brief go out?
faq.a: Far enough that access has been provisioned and tested before day one, which is the constraint that actually binds. The brief itself can be written in an afternoon. Getting accounts created, allowlists updated, third parties notified and an on-call rota told usually takes longer than people expect, and every one of those is a way to lose the first day.
faq.t: How to brief a security consultant so the quote is accurate

faq.q: Should I apply if I only meet half the requirements?
faq.a: It depends entirely on which half. Sort the list first: the requirements that also appear in the description of the work are the ones being hired for, and the ones that appear nowhere else are usually preferences. If you meet most of the first group, apply. If you meet half the list but none of the load-bearing half, you are a keyword match rather than a candidate, and the application is a slower way of being turned down. The count on its own tells you nothing, which is why the count is the wrong thing to be looking at.
faq.t: How to read a job description

faq.q: Is the statistic about men applying at sixty per cent and women at a hundred real?
faq.a: Not as a study. It comes from an internal Hewlett-Packard report described second-hand in a book, with no published method, sample or measurement behind it, and it has been repeated so often that it now gets cited as research. What is better supported is a survey Tara Mohr ran for the Harvard Business Review in 2014, which asked people who had not applied why not. The most common reason given was not confidence — it was a belief that applying without meeting the stated qualifications would be a waste of effort because they would be screened out. That belief is a model of how hiring works, and models can be corrected.
faq.t: How to read a job description

faq.q: What does it mean when a posting says competitive salary and gives no number?
faq.a: Usually one of three things: the number has not been agreed internally, the range is wide enough that publishing it would invite questions, or the company prefers to anchor on whatever you say first. None of those are scandals. What it does mean, reliably, is that the cost of finding out is being moved onto you, in the form of interview rounds that may end at a number nobody could have worked with. That is the reason to ask early rather than a reason to walk away.
faq.t: How to read a job description

faq.q: Is it rude to ask about salary on the first call?
faq.a: No, and the recruiter is generally relieved, because they are also trying to avoid four wasted rounds. Ask it plainly and late in the call: what is the band for this role, and what separates someone at the bottom of it from someone at the top. The second half is the useful part, because a team with real levels answers it immediately and a team that invented the band answers it vaguely. If asking is treated as distasteful, you have learned something about how the raise conversation will go in eighteen months.
faq.t: How to read a job description

faq.q: How do I explain a gap without making it the whole conversation?
faq.a: Name it first, in one sentence, in your own words, without an apology, and then move to what you are doing now. What it was is usually enough; why it was is only needed when the why is short and unremarkable. Do not stretch dates to hide it, because an inconsistency discovered later converts a non-event into a credibility problem. The question underneath the question is almost always whether the same thing is about to happen again, so answering that directly is what makes the gap stop being interesting.
faq.t: How to read a job description

faq.q: Is it worth applying to a posting that has been open for six months?
faq.a: Sometimes, but read it differently. A long-open posting means one of a few things: the requirements are unrealistic for the budget, the role has been deprioritised and the listing left up, the team is collecting a pipeline rather than hiring, or the description no longer matches what they need. The last one is the interesting case and it is worth one question in the first message or call — has what you need from this role changed since this was written. If the answer is yes, you are now talking about the real job, and most applicants are still answering the old one.
faq.t: How to read a job description

faq.q: Should I tailor my CV for every posting?
faq.a: Tailor it for the ones you would actually take, and let the rest go. Eight tailored applications beat forty untailored ones, and tailoring does not mean rewriting — it means using their words for the concepts you already have evidence for, and reordering so the load-bearing requirements are answered in the first third of the page. What it must never mean is adding a technology you have not used. The interview finds it, and being caught inflating one line makes a reader re-audit every other line on the page.
faq.t: How to read a job description

faq.q: Is a privacy policy actually binding, or is it just marketing?
faq.a: It is generally treated as a representation the organisation can be held to, which is why regulators often pursue the gap between what a policy says and what a company does rather than the processing itself. That is also why the method ends by comparing the document with the page: a policy that overstates its own restraint is a specific, provable failure. I am not a lawyer, and how binding it is varies by jurisdiction and by what else you agreed to.
faq.t: How to read a privacy policy in five minutes

faq.q: Does “we do not sell your data” mean my data stays with them?
faq.a: No. “Sale” is a narrow defined term, generally turning on an exchange for consideration, and the sentence leaves untouched disclosure to processors, sharing for advertising, sharing inside a corporate group, and transfer to whoever buys the company. Read the sharing section and the transfer clause rather than the denial.
faq.t: How to read a privacy policy in five minutes

faq.q: How can I tell a policy was bought from a template rather than written?
faq.a: Search for the company’s own name and see whether a different one appears anywhere in the text. Then check for an effective date, a named contact, and whether the statutes it cites are the ones that govern where the service actually operates. A defined-terms section full of terms the document never uses again is another giveaway.
faq.t: How to read a privacy policy in five minutes

faq.q: What should I do when a policy states no retention period at all?
faq.a: Treat it as indefinite and decide what you hand over on that basis. You can also ask: a short email to the contact address asking how long a specific category is kept costs nothing, and the answer tells you two things. Whether there is a number, and whether anyone replies.
faq.t: How to read a privacy policy in five minutes

faq.q: Does India’s DPDP Act give me a right to have data deleted?
faq.a: The Digital Personal Data Protection Act, 2023 includes rights of access, correction and erasure, a right to withdraw consent, a provision for nominating someone to exercise your rights on your behalf, and a requirement that data fiduciaries publish a grievance officer. The implementation detail has been arriving in stages, and I am not a lawyer, so use this as orientation rather than advice.
faq.t: How to read a privacy policy in five minutes

faq.q: Is five minutes really enough?
faq.a: It is enough for a risk read: who receives this, for how long, and how do I get out. It is not a legal review, it will not catch a clause drafted to be misread, and no amount of reading tells you what runs on somebody else’s servers. If the decision is large — a business contract, health data, a service you cannot leave — five minutes is where you start, not where you stop.
faq.t: How to read a privacy policy in five minutes

faq.q: Which one is cheapest?
faq.a: Nobody can answer that from a price sheet, including me, because the three tools do not meter the same thing. A workflow with few steps and low volume is cheapest on Zapier. A workflow that fans one trigger out into dozens of items is punished hardest on Make and barely noticed by n8n. A workflow running constantly at high volume is cheapest as code on a server you already have. Build the thing, run it for one real week, read the usage counter the tool gives you, multiply by four, then double it for the retries and the growth you have not thought of yet. That number is your comparison. The pricing page is not.
faq.t: n8n, Make, or Zapier: an honest comparison

faq.q: Is n8n open source?
faq.a: Not in the OSI sense, and the distinction matters commercially. n8n is source-available under the Sustainable Use License, which the company describes as fair-code: you can read it, modify it, and self-host it for your own internal business purposes at no licence cost. What you cannot do is host it as a service for other people, or resell it, without a separate commercial arrangement. If you are an agency planning to run one instance and sell workflows on it to clients, read the licence properly before you build the business model on it.
faq.t: n8n, Make, or Zapier: an honest comparison

faq.q: Can I self-host Make or Zapier?
faq.a: No. Both are hosted products only, and that is a deliberate part of what they sell — the uptime, the connector maintenance and the security posture are the product. What they offer instead is a choice of region: Make asks which data zone you want when you create the account, and Zapier has published data-residency options at the enterprise end of its pricing. Neither is a substitute for the data never leaving your own infrastructure, so if a contract requires that, the hosted tools are out before you compare a single feature.
faq.t: n8n, Make, or Zapier: an honest comparison

faq.q: Does self-hosting n8n make me compliant?
faq.a: No. It removes one subprocessor from the path, which can be the specific thing a contract asks for, and it hands you every obligation that vendor was carrying: patching the container, keeping the database backed up and encrypted, protecting the credential encryption key, restricting who can open the editor, and noticing when it stops. I have moved clients off self-hosted instances and onto n8n Cloud precisely because nobody was doing that work. An unpatched server you control is not more compliant than a maintained service you disclosed.
faq.t: n8n, Make, or Zapier: an honest comparison

faq.q: Can I move a workflow from one tool to another?
faq.a: Not automatically. Make exports a scenario blueprint as JSON and n8n exports a workflow as JSON, but they are unrelated formats describing different execution models, and Zapier has no equivalent export at all. Migration means rebuilding by hand, re-authorising every connection, and re-testing every branch. Anything claiming to convert between them is doing a rough translation you will still have to check step by step. Treat the choice as something you live with for a couple of years, not a setting you can change later.
faq.t: n8n, Make, or Zapier: an honest comparison

faq.q: Which one should I use for AI agents?
faq.a: All three can call a model API, so the real question is whether you want the tool to orchestrate the agent or just to make the request. n8n has the deepest native tooling for this — model nodes, tool calling, memory and vector store nodes as ordinary parts of a workflow — which is why I built my open-source AI SDR on it. Zapier and Make both have perfectly good AI steps for the common case of classify this, then draft that. What usually decides it is not the feature list but where the prompt and the customer record are allowed to travel.
faq.t: n8n, Make, or Zapier: an honest comparison

faq.q: How do I stop an automation bill from surprising me?
faq.a: Learn what one run costs in the tool's own unit before you scale it, because each tool counts a different thing: Zapier counts action steps, Make counts module executions including the trigger, and n8n Cloud counts whole executions. Then find the multiplier that is specific to your data rather than to your workflow — usually an array that arrives with a variable number of items — and work out the worst realistic day rather than the average one. Put a usage alert on the account, and write the expected monthly figure into the quote so nobody is surprised in month three.
faq.t: n8n, Make, or Zapier: an honest comparison

faq.q: What about Power Automate, Workato, or the others?
faq.a: The same two questions decide those too. Power Automate is worth a serious look when the organisation already lives in Microsoft 365, for exactly the reason Apps Script is worth a look when it lives in Google — the data does not leave a boundary that has already been accepted. Workato and the enterprise integration platforms sell governance, audit trails and support contracts, which is what a large compliance department is actually buying. I have kept this article to the three I ship production work in, because a comparison written from a marketing page is not worth reading.
faq.t: n8n, Make, or Zapier: an honest comparison

faq.q: The notification says the passwords were encrypted. Do I still need to change mine?
faq.a: Yes. Start with the word itself: passwords are supposed to be hashed, not encrypted, because encryption is reversible with a key and the key often sits in the same system that was breached. So the sentence means either that they did something they should not have, or that whoever wrote the notice did not know the difference — and neither reading tells you your password is safe. Even a correctly hashed password is only as strong as the guessing it survives: bcrypt, scrypt or Argon2 with a real work factor makes each guess expensive, while an unsalted MD5 or SHA-1 hash of a common password falls to a lookup. You cannot check which one they used, so change it at that service and everywhere you reused it, and let the algorithm turn out to be good news you did not need.
faq.t: How to read a data breach notification

faq.q: What does "we have no evidence of misuse" actually mean?
faq.a: It means they looked at what they can see and did not find anything. That is worth having, but notice how narrow the view is. Misuse of your data mostly happens somewhere else — a login attempt at a different company, a phishing message sent from an address they do not control, a loan application at a bank they have no relationship with. None of that is visible from inside the breached company's logs, and none of it would be, however carefully they looked. The useful follow-up question is not whether they found evidence but what evidence would have looked like and whether they were positioned to see it. In most incidents the honest answer is that they were not.
faq.t: How to read a data breach notification

faq.q: Is the free credit monitoring worth taking?
faq.a: Take it, because it is free and it takes ten minutes, but do not treat it as the response. Monitoring is detection after the fact — it tells you a new account or enquiry appeared, which means the fraud already happened. It usually covers one bureau rather than all of them, it expires after a year or two while a leaked identity number is permanent, and it does nothing whatsoever about the risk that actually applies to most breaches, which is somebody replaying your password at other sites. A credit bureau has no view of your email account. In India you are entitled to one free full credit report per calendar year from each credit information company, so a recurring calendar reminder gives you most of the same value permanently and at no cost.
faq.t: How to read a data breach notification

faq.q: My Aadhaar or PAN number was in the breach. What can I actually do?
faq.a: You cannot change the number, so the work is making the number less useful. For Aadhaar, UIDAI lets you lock biometrics and lock the number itself through the mAadhaar app or the portal, generate a Virtual ID to hand over instead of the real number, and review your authentication history to see where it has been used. For PAN, the exposure that matters is credit taken in your name, so pull your credit report from each bureau and read the enquiries section rather than only the score. Beyond that, expect the number to be quoted at you by callers as proof they are genuine — a leaked identity number is worth far more to a social engineer than to a fraudster filling in a form, and treating it as public is the mental adjustment that protects you.
faq.t: How to read a data breach notification

faq.q: How do I tell a real breach notification from a phishing email pretending to be one?
faq.a: Do not try to tell them apart, because both a real notice and a good forgery will look plausible and attackers deliberately send fakes in the days after a real breach becomes news. Instead, never act inside the email. Do not click the link, do not use the phone number in it, and do not type a password into anything it opens. Go to the company the way you normally do — the app on your phone, or an address you type yourself — and look for the notice there. Real notices are published on the company's own site and repeated by the press; a notice that exists only in your inbox and only behind a link is a strong signal on its own.
faq.t: How to read a data breach notification

faq.q: Can I sue the company or get compensation under the DPDP Act?
faq.a: Not under that Act, and this is the part people are most often surprised by. The Digital Personal Data Protection Act, 2023 gives the Data Protection Board power to impose penalties — the Schedule runs up to two hundred and fifty crore rupees for failing to take reasonable security safeguards and up to two hundred crore for failing to give breach intimation — but those penalties are paid to the government, not to you. The Act creates no route to individual compensation. What it does give you is a right to grievance redressal that you must use with the company first, and then a complaint to the Board. If you lost money, the routes that can actually return it are your bank's unauthorised-transaction process, the cybercrime helpline, and a consumer forum claim for deficiency in service.
faq.t: How to read a data breach notification

faq.q: Nothing has happened in six months. Am I in the clear?
faq.a: Silence is weak evidence, because breach data does not expire and it is often used long after it is stolen. A corpus gets traded, merged with other corpora, and worked through by different people at different times; credential lists in particular are replayed for years because a password that was reused in 2024 is frequently still in use. Identity numbers age even more slowly than that. This is not a reason to stay anxious — it is a reason to make the fix structural rather than vigilant. A unique password per site and a phishing-resistant second factor keep working while you forget about the incident entirely, which is the whole point of choosing controls over watchfulness.
faq.t: How to read a data breach notification

faq.q: Is it illegal to use Tor or visit the dark web?
faq.a: In most countries, including India, running Tor and reading a site over it is not itself an offence — the software is public, and news organisations, researchers and privacy-minded people use it openly. What you do with it is judged the same way it would be on any other network: buying prohibited goods or accessing prohibited material is an offence regardless of how the connection was routed. A handful of states restrict or block anonymity tools outright, so this is one of the places to check your own jurisdiction rather than take a general answer from an article. For the Indian statutes that would apply, the IT Act post on this site is the longer read.
faq.t: Surface web, deep web, and dark web: what the three layers actually are

faq.q: Is the deep web dangerous?
faq.a: No, and the question usually comes from the iceberg picture rather than from anything real. The deep web is the part of the ordinary web a crawler cannot reach: your webmail, your bank's logged-in pages, a company intranet, a paywalled journal, results a database generates when you submit a form. You used it this morning. The risk in that layer is the ordinary one — a weak password, a reused password, a phishing page that catches you on the way in.
faq.t: Surface web, deep web, and dark web: what the three layers actually are

faq.q: How big is the dark web really?
faq.a: Small, and nobody can give you an honest number. Published counts of reachable Tor onion services have run in the tens of thousands of addresses, many of which are duplicates, mirrors, or offline within days. The often-quoted claim that the dark web is some large multiple of the visible web is not a measurement of anything — it confuses the dark web with the deep web, which cannot be counted either, because a database that generates a page per query has no fixed number of pages.
faq.t: Surface web, deep web, and dark web: what the three layers actually are

faq.q: Does a VPN make me anonymous the way Tor does?
faq.a: No. A VPN moves your trust rather than removing it: your traffic is hidden from your network and your provider, and handed instead to the VPN company, which can see both who you are and where you are going. Tor's design splits that knowledge across three independently operated relays so no single one holds both halves. A VPN is a reasonable answer to an untrusted café network. It is not an anonymity system, whatever the advertising says.
faq.t: Surface web, deep web, and dark web: what the three layers actually are

faq.q: Can my data be removed from the dark web?
faq.a: No, and any service selling removal is selling something it cannot deliver. Once a breach corpus has been copied, traded and mirrored, there is no registry to delete it from and no party obliged to honour a request. What you can do is make the leaked data useless: change the password everywhere it was reused, turn on multi-factor authentication, and treat the leaked details as permanently public when you choose account-recovery answers.
faq.t: Surface web, deep web, and dark web: what the three layers actually are

faq.q: Why do newspapers run onion sites?
faq.a: For sources. A SecureDrop instance reached over Tor means a whistleblower's connection does not create a record at their internet provider or employer showing they contacted that newsroom. Several major papers run one, and several also publish onion mirrors of the paper itself so readers behind national filtering can reach ordinary news. It is the same technology as the criminal markets, used for the reason it was funded in the first place.
faq.t: Surface web, deep web, and dark web: what the three layers actually are

faq.q: What does a breach-monitoring service actually check?
faq.a: It matches your email address or password against a corpus of already-published breach dumps that somebody collected and indexed. That is genuinely useful — it tells you which of your accounts is exposed — but it is a search of a known dataset, not surveillance of the dark web. No service can see what an unknown criminal holds privately, and none can remove anything. Treat "we scan the dark web for you" as marketing for "we search dumps we already have", and use the breach checker on this site if you want to see the honest version of the mechanism.
faq.t: Surface web, deep web, and dark web: what the three layers actually are

faq.q: Can I rename a HubSpot property without losing its history?
faq.a: Changing the label a property shows in the interface is the safe operation — the internal name it is stored under does not move, so reports, workflows and integrations keep working. The destructive operation is deleting a property, or quietly abandoning one in favour of a new field, because the value history hangs off the property itself. HubSpot changes behaviour and retention windows over time, so check the current documentation for your portal before relying on any specific recovery window, and export before you delete either way.
faq.t: The HubSpot mistakes that cost the most to undo

faq.q: Is a custom object always better than adding more contact properties?
faq.a: No, and treating it as the default is how a small portal gets expensive. Custom objects sit on higher subscription tiers, need their own reporting and permissions, and add a relationship for everyone to reason about. The test is whether the thing has its own lifecycle and a many-to-one relationship to a person or company. A licence that renews, a vehicle that changes owner, an enrolment with its own stages — those want an object. A single flag about a contact does not.
faq.t: The HubSpot mistakes that cost the most to undo

faq.q: How do I tell whether my deal stages are actually measurable?
faq.a: Take ten open deals and ask two people to place each one independently, without discussing it. Where they disagree, the stage is not describing an observable event. It costs an hour and no tooling, and in my experience it finds the unmeasurable stages faster than reading the stage list does, because the disagreement itself is the evidence.
faq.t: The HubSpot mistakes that cost the most to undo

faq.q: Should I clean the data before or after migrating it into HubSpot?
faq.a: Before, wherever the source system still holds the identifier that tells two records apart. Deduplication is a matching problem and matching is easier where the key lives. Once records are in HubSpot without that key you are matching on email and company name, which is exactly the weak matching that created the duplicates. The exception is data that only becomes comparable after normalising, which is worth doing in one deliberate pass rather than inside each import.
faq.t: The HubSpot mistakes that cost the most to undo

faq.q: What should I fix first if most of this list applies to my portal?
faq.a: Order by how many things read it, not by how bad it looks. The property your forecast is derived from, or the stage list your pipeline review runs on, comes before a settings page full of duplicate fields. Sprawl is visible and mostly harmless. A load-bearing value that several workflows write to is invisible, and it is the one producing numbers people act on.
faq.t: The HubSpot mistakes that cost the most to undo

faq.q: Is any of this specific to HubSpot?
faq.a: The mechanics are. Lifecycle stage timestamps, workflow enrolment evaluated against the whole database, and what deleting a property does to its history are HubSpot behaviours, and the equivalents differ in other CRMs. The underlying pattern is not specific to any tool: a choice becomes hard to reverse in proportion to how much has been built on top of it, which is as true of database schemas, file formats and APIs as it is of CRMs.
faq.t: The HubSpot mistakes that cost the most to undo

faq.q: Should the questions be shared in advance?
faq.a: For anything structured, yes, and I do: the format, the rough timings, whether they may look things up, and what the coding round will look like. Nothing on my list gets worse for being known. If somebody prepares for the question about what they would change by genuinely thinking about what they would change, then they have done the work I was trying to measure. The only questions ruined by disclosure are the ones testing whether a candidate has seen a trick before, and that is a reason to drop them rather than a reason to keep them secret. Surprise is not rigour, and it quietly costs you every good engineer who interviews badly under ambush.

faq.q: How long should a technical interview be?
faq.a: Long enough for two substantial questions and their follow-ups, which is about fifty minutes, and no longer than that in one sitting. The value curve is steep at the start and flat quickly: most of what I learn arrives in the follow-ups to the first real question. Past an hour I am mostly measuring stamina and how recently somebody ate. If one round cannot carry the decision, run two short rounds with different people rather than one long round with the same person, because a second interviewer is worth far more than a second half-hour.

faq.q: Is a take-home better than a live coding round?
faq.a: It is better at measuring the code and worse at measuring the person. A take-home shows you what somebody produces with time, their own tools and nobody watching, which is much closer to the actual job. It also charges the candidate several unpaid hours, and charges them unequally — someone with a job and a family pays far more than a student does. If I use one, I cap it at about two hours, say the cap out loud, accept whatever exists when the cap is reached, and then spend the live time talking about their code rather than watching them write more. A small live problem plus a real conversation about something they already built gets most of the same signal for a fraction of the candidate's time.

faq.q: What about a candidate who freezes?
faq.a: Assume it is nerves rather than ability until something proves otherwise, because that is what it usually is. Stop the clock, say plainly that this happens often and is not being scored, and go back to their own project — a question they cannot get wrong. Most people are back within a few minutes. If they are not, the honest move is to say that the format may not be showing me their best work, and to offer another route such as a small piece of asynchronous work. What I try hard not to do is score the freeze itself, because an interview is a performance under artificial conditions and I am not hiring a performer.

faq.q: How many interviewers should be in the room?
faq.a: Two, and mostly for the interviewers rather than for the candidate. One asks and one writes, and then both score independently before either says a word, because the moment one of them speaks first the other's score moves toward it. Three or more turns a conversation into a panel, and a panel makes people perform instead of think. One interviewer is workable if the scoring is written down as it happens, but it leaves the whole anchoring problem resting on the goodwill of a single tired person at four in the afternoon.

faq.q: What if the candidate uses an AI assistant?
faq.a: Let them, and say so at the start, because the alternative is testing people under conditions that no longer exist anywhere. Then interview the interaction rather than the output: what they asked for, what they accepted, what they threw away, and how they checked it. The gap between engineers is no longer who can produce code — it is who can tell when the produced code is wrong. A candidate who pastes in a suggestion and cannot explain why the edge case at the bottom is handled that way has told me something more useful than any closed-book test would have.

faq.q: Does this apply to interviewing interns rather than engineers?
faq.a: The questions survive; the weighting changes. For an intern the project question and the bug question carry almost everything, because they are the only two that still work when the candidate's entire experience is one college project — and they work perfectly well on one college project, honestly described. The two-year question matters more rather than less, because a mismatch of intent costs an intern a much larger fraction of their available time. The coding problem gets smaller and the clarifying-questions part gets larger. What I stop expecting is breadth. What I keep expecting is that they can describe their own part of the work.

faq.q: How long should I stay stuck before I ask?
faq.a: Set the limit before you start, not while you are inside the problem, because the judgement you need is exactly the one the problem has taken away from you. Twenty minutes to an hour is where most things sit. The signal that the window has closed is not the clock alone — it is that you have stopped generating new hypotheses and started re-reading the same page hoping it will say something different. When that happens you are not learning any more, you are only waiting.
faq.t: The mentee mistakes that cost the most time

faq.q: Are tutorials always a waste of time?
faq.a: No, and I would not want that read into this. A tutorial is an efficient way to get the shape of something unfamiliar in an hour. The failure is not the tutorial, it is the loop — finishing one and starting another with nothing in between. The rule worth holding is that the tutorial follows a problem rather than preceding it. You hit something you cannot do, you go and read how it is done, you come back and do it in your own thing. That is a tool. A queue of tutorials with no project attached is a hobby that resembles work.
faq.t: The mentee mistakes that cost the most time

faq.q: What should the first thing I ship actually be?
faq.a: Something you can finish across two weekends, that does one thing, for one person you can name. The best candidates are annoyances that already exist near you: a report someone assembles by hand every Friday, a rename somebody does forty times a week, a reminder that keeps getting missed. Deliberately not a clone of a large product, and deliberately not something that needs accounts, payments and a mobile app before anyone can touch it. Small is not a compromise here — small is what lets it exist at all, and existing is the entire point.
faq.t: The mentee mistakes that cost the most time

faq.q: I do not have any users. Where do the first five come from?
faq.a: From people you already have a reason to talk to. A classmate, a sibling, two people in a group chat about a hobby you share, the person whose spreadsheet you are replacing, a maintainer whose issue tracker you read. They do not have to be strangers and they do not have to be many. What makes a user useful is that they will tell you honestly when it breaks, which is a property of the relationship rather than of the number.
faq.t: The mentee mistakes that cost the most time

faq.q: Should I finish a project I have lost interest in?
faq.a: Usually yes, and I say that knowing how unwelcome it is. The loss of interest very often arrives at exactly the point where the remaining work is unfamiliar rather than boring — deployment, error handling, the parts that only start to matter once someone else touches it. That is the part you have not done before, and therefore the part with the learning in it. There is a real exception: if the premise itself was wrong and nobody wants the thing, stopping is the correct call. The test is whether you can say what changed your mind in one sentence, without using the word boring.
faq.t: The mentee mistakes that cost the most time

faq.q: How do I tell useful feedback from noise?
faq.a: Split every comment into what it observes and what it prescribes. The observation is almost always true and almost always worth having, because it is a report about someone's experience of your work and they are the authority on that. The prescription is one person's suggested fix, and you may take it or not provided you can say why. Noise is the small residue that observes nothing and prescribes nothing — the comment that is only a verdict. Treat that as information about the reviewer's day rather than about your code, and go back to the comments that named something.
faq.t: The mentee mistakes that cost the most time

faq.q: I have been in the tutorial loop for a year. Is it too late?
faq.a: No, and the recovery is faster than people fear, because the knowledge is not absent — it is unpractised. What is missing is retrieval and decision-making, and both come back quickly once something forces them. The way back is unglamorous and takes about two weekends: pick one small problem, build it badly from a blank file, put it in front of one person, and fix the first thing they complain about. The year is not lost. It has simply not been converted into anything yet, and that is the conversion.
faq.t: The mentee mistakes that cost the most time

faq.q: Does NIST still tell organisations to expire passwords every 90 days?
faq.a: No. SP 800-63B tells verifiers not to require periodic changes, and to force a change only when there is evidence the credential has been compromised. Plenty of compliance questionnaires and internal checklists still ask for rotation out of habit, so in practice you may have to argue the case with a form rather than with a standard.
faq.t: The password advice that stopped being true

faq.q: Is a passphrase of three random words really stronger than P@ssw0rd1?
faq.a: Yes, and for a boring reason: guessing effort tracks how many equally likely options the secret was drawn from, not how many character types appear in it. But random is doing the work. Three words you chose because they mean something to you are not three random words, and cracking rule sets already model the @ for a and 0 for o substitutions in P@ssw0rd1.
faq.t: The password advice that stopped being true

faq.q: Should I still change a password after a breach notification?
faq.a: Yes, immediately, for that account and anywhere you reused it. That is the one forced change every current guideline still requires. What got deleted was the arbitrary calendar, not the response to evidence.
faq.t: The password advice that stopped being true

faq.q: Are password managers safe if the vault provider gets breached?
faq.a: A stolen vault is a real risk rather than a hypothetical one. Its contents are encrypted under a key derived from your master password, so the exposure depends on that password and on the provider key derivation settings. It concentrates a risk that was previously spread across every site you reuse a password on. I take that trade because the concentrated risk is the one I can act on, and I would revisit it if stolen vaults started being decrypted at scale rather than merely exfiltrated.
faq.t: The password advice that stopped being true

faq.q: Is SMS two-factor better than nothing?
faq.a: Yes. It is the weakest common second factor, because a phone number is an account at a telecoms company that can be ported or swapped, and because a phishing page can relay the code in real time. It is still a large improvement over a password on its own. Turn it on where nothing better exists, and migrate later.
faq.t: The password advice that stopped being true

faq.q: Do complexity rules ever help at all?
faq.a: Marginally. They push out the very worst passwords, which is not nothing. A blocklist of known-breached and commonly used passwords does that job better, and without teaching everyone to produce the current season and year with an exclamation mark on the end.
faq.t: The password advice that stopped being true

faq.q: What is a loaded hourly rate, and how do I work out mine?
faq.a: Take the annual salary, add everything the business spends to keep that person able to work — statutory contributions, insurance, software licences, the desk and the laptop spread over their life, recruitment and training spread over the expected tenure, and a share of the manager's time — then divide by the hours that person is actually available in a year, which is not 2,080. In the example in this article that is ₹8,10,000 divided by 1,800 hours, or ₹450 an hour, against a salary-only figure of ₹333. If you cannot get the real overhead numbers out of finance, multiply salary by 1.3 and label it an assumption rather than a fact.
faq.t: The real cost of a manual process

faq.q: Our people are salaried, so the time is already paid for. Is it really a cost?
faq.a: It is a real cost and it is not a cash saving, and confusing those two is how automation business cases lose their credibility. The hour is bought whether or not it is spent well, so removing the work does not reduce the payroll — it converts spent hours into available hours. That is worth something only if the available hours get used for something that earns, or for something that was not getting done at all. Say that plainly in the business case. A claim of cash savings that never shows up in the accounts costs you the argument for the next three projects.
faq.t: The real cost of a manual process

faq.q: How do I measure how long the process actually takes?
faq.a: Not by asking. Self-reported durations are wrong in both directions: people quote the good run rather than the median, and they leave out the finding, the chasing and the checking either side of the part they think of as the task. Watch it end to end five or ten times with a timer, on ordinary days rather than a quiet Friday, and record the median and the worst case rather than the average. If you cannot watch it, take the count from whatever system records the work — rows added, emails sent, tickets closed — and divide the observed elapsed time by it.
faq.t: The real cost of a manual process

faq.q: What if the volume is going to grow?
faq.a: Run the arithmetic twice, at today's volume and at the volume you actually believe in twelve months, and present both. Growth shortens the payback, because the manual cost scales with volume and the running cost of an automation mostly does not. The discipline is to use a growth number somebody is willing to be held to rather than the one on the plan, and to check the two thresholds that break a straight line: the point where the manual process needs a second person, and the point where the tool's pricing tier changes. Both are step changes, and both land outside the model.
faq.t: The real cost of a manual process

faq.q: Should I count opportunity cost as well as the salary cost?
faq.a: No — opportunity cost replaces the labour line, it does not stack on top of it. If a salesperson spends an hour on data entry you can count the ₹450 the hour cost you, or the margin that hour would have produced in front of a customer, but counting both charges the same hour twice. Use whichever is larger, state which one you used, and be honest that the opportunity figure only holds if the freed hour genuinely goes to the alternative. Most freed hours do not, at least not in the first month.
faq.t: The real cost of a manual process

faq.q: What payback period is short enough?
faq.a: Under twelve months is usually an easy yes, because neither the volume nor the process is likely to change beyond recognition inside a year. Twelve to twenty-four months is a yes only where the process is genuinely stable and somebody has agreed to maintain the thing. Beyond twenty-four months the answer is no, or the scope is wrong and you should automate the busiest third of the process instead of all of it. Those are rules of thumb rather than finance, and if your business already has a required rate of return, use that instead of mine.
faq.t: The real cost of a manual process

faq.q: What if the honest answer is that we should not automate it?
faq.a: Then you have bought a good outcome for the price of an afternoon, and you should write the decision down with the numbers attached and a date to look again. The write-up is the valuable part: it stops the same conversation being had from scratch every quarter, and it names exactly which number would have to change for the answer to flip, which is usually the volume. I have talked people out of automations more often than into them, and the ones that go ahead afterwards tend to survive, because the reason for them is written down rather than felt.
faq.t: The real cost of a manual process

faq.q: Do I ever need to enter my UPI PIN to receive money?
faq.a: No. Not in any app, not for any amount, not to verify an account, not to claim a refund, not once. The PIN is a signature on a debit and it does nothing else. Receiving needs no approval because there is nothing to approve — the credit simply happens and you are told afterwards. If a screen is asking for your PIN, money is leaving your account, whatever the text above the prompt says.
faq.t: UPI fraud: how the money actually leaves

faq.q: Can somebody empty my account just by knowing my UPI ID or my phone number?
faq.a: No. A UPI ID is an address, like an email address. Somebody who has it can send you money, or raise a collect request asking you for money. A request cannot debit you on its own — it arrives as a prompt on your phone and dies there unless you approve it with your PIN. Almost every account that was supposedly emptied by a stranger who knew the ID was emptied by an approval the owner was talked into giving.
faq.t: UPI fraud: how the money actually leaves

faq.q: Somebody transferred money to me by mistake and wants it back. What should I do?
faq.a: Do not send it back through their link, their QR code or their request. A genuine misdirected transfer is reversed by the sender's own bank, on the sender's written request, with a reference number — so tell them to raise it there. Leave the amount untouched, tell your own bank what happened, and keep the messages. If the money that reached you was itself stolen, handing it onward makes your account a link in the chain, and it is your account that gets frozen.
faq.t: UPI fraud: how the money actually leaves

faq.q: A buyer sent me a screenshot showing the payment. Is that proof?
faq.a: No. A screenshot is an image, and images are edited in seconds. The only thing that settles it is your own side of the transaction: the alert from your bank, or the entry in your own statement or passbook. Wait for that before you hand anything over. The awkwardness of making somebody wait is exactly what the script is built on, which is why the wait is the defence.
faq.t: UPI fraud: how the money actually leaves

faq.q: Can I turn collect requests off completely?
faq.a: Sometimes, and it depends on the app in front of you. Person-to-person collect has been tightened repeatedly — the limits on it are far lower than on an ordinary payment, and some apps have put it behind an extra step or withdrawn it for individuals altogether. Because that keeps changing, look in the app's own payment settings rather than trusting a figure in an article. Where it cannot be switched off, the workable substitute is a habit: an unexpected request is declined first and asked about afterwards.
faq.t: UPI fraud: how the money actually leaves

faq.q: How much of the money usually comes back?
faq.a: Often none of it, and I would rather say that plainly than imply otherwise. A complaint triggers holds down the chain of accounts the money passed through, and only the portion still sitting somewhere in that chain can be held — anything withdrawn in cash, converted or moved abroad is beyond reach. A hold is also not a refund: frozen money is evidence in a live case, and releasing it to you generally needs a court order and months of waiting. Partial recovery is the common good outcome, and nobody can promise more in advance.
faq.t: UPI fraud: how the money actually leaves

faq.q: A parent already installed a screen-sharing app during a call. What now?
faq.a: Treat it as access rather than as an app. End the session, uninstall it, and then revoke the accessibility or screen-recording permission it was granted, because on Android that permission is what outlives the call. Change the UPI PIN and the app passcode from a different device if you can, review and cancel any autopay mandate that appeared, and call the bank to say the screen was shared during a call — that fact changes the conversation, so do not leave it out. Then report it even if nothing moved yet.
faq.t: UPI fraud: how the money actually leaves

faq.q: Is a security review the same as a penetration test?
faq.a: No. A review is a structured read of the system with full access — code, configuration, cloud, and the people who built it — and its output is breadth: the list of ways the system can be made to misbehave, ranked. A penetration test is a bounded attack simulation, usually with much less information, and its output is depth: proof that a specific path is exploitable, with evidence attached. Reviews find more per rupee on a system nobody has looked at before. Penetration tests are what a customer's contract usually means when it asks for one. They answer different questions, and the industry uses both words loosely, so agree the deliverable rather than the noun.
faq.t: What a security review actually finds

faq.q: How long does a review take?
faq.a: For a small SaaS product or an internal tool, usually one to two weeks of calendar time for a few days of actual work, plus a re-test later once the fixes land. The variable is not the size of the codebase — it is how many separate authorisation models are in it. One product with one permission model reads quickly. The same product after three years of bolted-on roles, an admin panel, a partner API and a mobile client is four systems, and each one has to be walked separately.
faq.t: What a security review actually finds

faq.q: Will the review break anything?
faq.a: It should not, because most of the work is reading rather than sending traffic, and what testing there is happens against a non-production environment by default. Where something has to be tried against production — because staging does not reproduce it — that gets agreed in writing first, scheduled, and done with someone from your side on a call. The honest caveat is that rate-limit testing is the one activity that can visibly load a system, so it is always scheduled rather than sprung.
faq.t: What a security review actually finds

faq.q: We already have SOC 2. Do we still need this?
faq.a: They are different instruments. A SOC 2 report attests that you operate the controls you said you operate, over a period, in the judgement of an auditor. It does not involve anyone reading your authorisation logic. I have seen a system with a clean report and an object identifier in a URL that nobody checked. Compliance describes the process around the software; a review looks at the software. Neither substitutes for the other, and a company that has done one is usually well organised enough to get good value from the other.
faq.t: What a security review actually finds

faq.q: What if you find nothing serious?
faq.a: Then you get a short report saying so, the architecture notes, and the same fee, because you paid for the looking rather than for the finding. It is uncommon on a system nobody has reviewed before, and it is not the same as a guarantee — it means the checks I ran on the code I was given, in the time I was given, did not surface a serious issue. If I ever return nothing and cannot tell you specifically what I looked at and what I could not reach, you should not accept the report.
faq.t: What a security review actually finds

faq.q: Can you give us a certificate or a letter for our customer?
faq.a: I can write a factual summary letter stating what was reviewed, when, by whom, and what was fixed on re-test. I cannot certify anything, because a certificate implies a standard and an accreditation body behind it, and a review has neither. If a customer contract specifically requires a third-party penetration test report or an audited attestation, a review will not satisfy it, and you should know that before you buy rather than after.
faq.t: What a security review actually finds

faq.q: How often should we do this?
faq.a: Tie it to change, not to the calendar. The useful triggers are a new authorisation model, a new class of user such as a partner or a reseller, a migration, an acquisition of somebody else's code, and the first enterprise customer whose questionnaire will ask. Once a year is a reasonable default for a product under steady development, and once a year is far less useful than one review timed for the month before you ship a multi-tenant portal.
faq.t: What a security review actually finds

faq.q: Does a VPN make me anonymous?
faq.a: No. It hides your address from the destination and your traffic from the local network. Anything that identifies you at the application layer — logging in, cookies, a browser fingerprint — is completely unaffected.
faq.t: What a VPN does and does not do

faq.q: Is public wifi dangerous without one?
faq.a: Much less than it used to be. Near-universal HTTPS means someone on the same network sees ciphertext rather than your messages. What still leaks is metadata: which sites you visit, through DNS lookups and the server name sent during connection setup.
faq.t: What a VPN does and does not do

faq.q: Does it stop tracking and advertising?
faq.a: Mostly no. Tracking follows identifiers in your browser — cookies, and a fingerprint built from your device's properties. Those are read from the browser, not the network, so a different address does not change them.
faq.t: What a VPN does and does not do

faq.q: Are no-logs claims trustworthy?
faq.a: They are unverifiable from outside by construction. An independent audit is meaningfully better than nothing, but it is a snapshot of one configuration on one day rather than a continuing guarantee.
faq.t: What a VPN does and does not do

faq.q: Should I use a free VPN?
faq.a: Servers and bandwidth cost money, so if you are not paying, the arrangement is funded another way. That question has only a few possible answers and most of them involve the traffic you were trying to protect.
faq.t: What a VPN does and does not do

faq.q: When should I use Tor instead?
faq.a: When identification would genuinely harm you. A VPN concentrates trust in one provider; Tor is designed so no single party sees both ends of the connection. It is slower and less convenient, and that is the trade being made.
faq.t: What a VPN does and does not do

faq.q: Is a workflow with a single model call an agent?
faq.a: By the loose usage, people will call it one. By any definition that helps you plan, no — there is no loop, so there is no runtime decision about what to do next, and the things that make agents hard to maintain all follow from that decision. The label matters because it sets expectations about cost, testing and blast radius. A single call has a cost you can bound in advance, an ordinary trace, and one place to look when it misbehaves.
faq.t: What “AI agent” means once you have to maintain one

faq.q: How large should an evaluation set be?
faq.a: I do not have a defensible number, and I would distrust anyone who offers one without knowing your task. The principles I use: one case for every distinct behaviour you actually care about, one new case every time something fails in production, and enough repeat runs per case that the run-to-run noise is smaller than the difference you are trying to detect. A small set that grew out of real failures is worth more than a large one invented in an afternoon.
faq.t: What “AI agent” means once you have to maintain one

faq.q: Can prompt injection be fixed with a stronger system prompt?
faq.a: Not reliably. Instructions and retrieved content arrive on the same channel, and a system prompt is one more piece of text competing with everything else in the context window. Careful wording helps at the margin and is worth doing, but it is not a control you can point at in a security review. The controls that hold are structural: restrict what the tools can do, scope credentials separately, and require human confirmation for any side-effectful action taken during a run that touched content someone outside your organisation can write.
faq.t: What “AI agent” means once you have to maintain one

faq.q: What should I log for every agent run?
faq.a: The rendered prompt rather than the template, every tool call with its exact arguments and the raw result, the model identifier and sampling settings, per-step token counts and timings, and the stop reason. The stop reason is the field most often left out and the one you will want most, because a run that finished and a run that hit its step cap are indistinguishable from the output alone. Decide the retention period and the redaction rules at the same time, since traces routinely contain personal data.
faq.t: What “AI agent” means once you have to maintain one

faq.q: How do I stop an agent costing an unbounded amount?
faq.a: Cap steps per run, tokens per run, wall-clock time per run and spend per day, and enforce every one of them in the code that drives the loop rather than in the prompt. Each bounds a different runaway: steps catch a loop that will not terminate, tokens catch one oversized document, wall clock catches a hung tool, and the daily cap catches a trigger firing far more often than you assumed. Alert whenever a cap is hit, because a cap that fires silently just looks like a bad answer.
faq.t: What “AI agent” means once you have to maintain one

faq.q: When is a multi-agent system worth the trouble?
faq.a: Less often than it gets built, in my view. It multiplies every maintenance cost in this article by the number of loops and adds a failure mode of its own, where two agents pass a confident mistake back and forth and neither has any way to notice. What would persuade me is genuinely disjoint sub-tasks with different tool sets that can run in parallel and hand back structured results — not prose — to a coordinator that validates them. If your sub-agents are exchanging free text, you have added coordination cost and kept every original problem.
faq.t: What “AI agent” means once you have to maintain one

faq.q: Does ISO/IEC 27001 require annual security awareness training?
faq.a: No. Neither Annex A 6.3 nor clause 7.3 names a frequency. The control asks for appropriate awareness, education and training together with regular updates of your policies, as relevant to a person's job function. Annual is a widespread convention, not a requirement. What actually binds you is your own policy: if it commits you to quarterly refreshers and your records show one session a year, the auditor raises a nonconformity against your document rather than against the standard.
faq.t: What an auditor actually wants from security training

faq.q: Will a training certificate make us ISO 27001 certified or SOC 2 compliant?
faq.a: No. ISO/IEC 27001 certification is issued by an accredited certification body after auditing your management system, and a SOC 2 report is an opinion signed by a licensed CPA firm after testing your controls. A training record is evidence for one control inside those audits, and a useful piece of evidence, but it is not a shortcut to either outcome. Any vendor implying otherwise is describing something that does not exist.
faq.t: What an auditor actually wants from security training

faq.q: Does training have to be in-house, or can an external trainer count?
faq.a: Either counts. Nothing in the standard names who delivers it. What gets tested is whether the right people received training appropriate to their job function, whether the content lined up with your policies, and whether you retained the record. An external session with a clean register is stronger evidence than an internal one nobody wrote down.
faq.t: What an auditor actually wants from security training

faq.q: What will the auditor actually sample?
faq.a: People. Expect them to take your personnel list, pick a handful of names across different roles and joining dates, and ask you to produce the evidence for each of them. New joiners are the usual weak point, because the original session is documented well and the person who started three months later is not.
faq.t: What an auditor actually wants from security training

faq.q: Is a click-through video enough?
faq.a: It depends entirely on what the platform records. A module that logs per-user completion with a timestamp is decent evidence. A video that logs only that a link was opened proves distribution rather than participation, and an assessor can tell the difference with one question about what the system stores.
faq.t: What an auditor actually wants from security training

faq.q: Does India's DPDP Act 2023 require security training?
faq.a: Not by name. Section 8(5) requires a Data Fiduciary to protect personal data by taking reasonable security safeguards to prevent a personal data breach, and leaves what counts as reasonable to be argued on the facts. Training is one of the things you point to in that argument, which is a different job from ticking a box. This is orientation rather than legal advice, and the penalty for getting safeguards wrong is the largest in the Act.
faq.t: What an auditor actually wants from security training

faq.q: Are you an accredited training partner of a certification body?
faq.a: No, and I would rather say it here than let you find out after the invoice. I hold no instructor certification either, and none of the certificates I list is a teaching credential. If your requirement is a scheme-recognised qualification printed on the certificate, book an accredited provider. What I offer instead is material built for your team after an intro call, delivered by the person you booked, with the attendance record, the material as delivered, and per-attendee certificates carrying an ID your auditor can check on the verification page without going through me.
faq.t: What an auditor actually wants from security training

faq.q: Are these gates a replacement for tests?
faq.a: No, they cover different things. Tests exercise code that runs. These gates check artefacts that nothing runs — structured data, sitemaps, precache lists, share images — where a defect is invisible in review and silent in production. A project wants both.
faq.t: What build-gate failures taught me about CI

faq.q: Why fail the deploy instead of logging a warning?
faq.a: Because a warning in a build log is read once, by the person who added it. Stopping the deploy is the only setting at which the check reliably changes what happens next. If a problem is not worth stopping for, it is probably not worth a gate.
faq.t: What build-gate failures taught me about CI

faq.q: How do you know a gate actually works?
faq.a: By making it fail on purpose. The gates in this build are exported from the script so they can be pointed at a deliberately broken copy of the site and proven to throw. A gate nobody has ever seen fail is a gate nobody knows works.
faq.t: What build-gate failures taught me about CI

faq.q: Does this approach scale to a large codebase?
faq.a: The principle does; the economics may not. These checks are cheap because the artefacts are files and the site is small, so the whole pass runs on every deploy. On a large codebase equivalent checks are slower, and a slow check tends to get moved to a nightly job, at which point it is a warning again.
faq.t: What build-gate failures taught me about CI

faq.q: What is the single most useful gate to add first?
faq.a: Whichever one covers a fact that currently lives in two places. That is where drift is guaranteed rather than possible, and it is usually the cheapest gate to write, because you are comparing two lists you already have.
faq.t: What build-gate failures taught me about CI

faq.q: Do we still need consent from a customer who is already paying us?
faq.a: For most of what you want to do with their data, yes. This is the difference from Europe that catches people: DPDP has no lawful basis of processing necessary for the performance of a contract, and no legitimate-interests ground either. The nearest thing is the legitimate use for data the individual voluntarily provided for a specified purpose and has not indicated she does not consent to — which fairly covers using the address she typed into the delivery field in order to deliver the thing. It does not stretch to marketing her later, profiling her, or handing her number to a partner. Paying you is not consent to anything beyond the purpose the payment was for.
faq.t: What consent actually means under the DPDP Act

faq.q: Does DPDP apply to a company as small as ours?
faq.a: Yes. There is no revenue threshold, no headcount threshold and no small-business carve-out in the Act. If you process digital personal data in India, or you process it anywhere in connection with offering goods or services to people in India, you are in scope. The Act does let the Central Government exempt notified classes of startups from a few specific provisions by notification, which is narrower than it sounds and is not something to plan around. What genuinely reduces a small company's obligations is not size — it is holding less data for fewer purposes.
faq.t: What consent actually means under the DPDP Act

faq.q: Does it cover our employees, or only our customers?
faq.a: Both. Your employees are Data Principals and you are their Data Fiduciary, which surprises teams that thought of the Act as a customer-facing thing. The relief is that employment is one of the enumerated legitimate uses, so payroll, benefits, and measures to safeguard the employer from loss or liability — protecting trade secrets and confidential information, for instance — do not need consent. That ground is narrower than the whole HR relationship, though. It is a poor fit for open-ended employee monitoring, and it says nothing about how long you keep the file of someone who left four years ago.
faq.t: What consent actually means under the DPDP Act

faq.q: We already comply with GDPR. Are we finished?
