faq.a: You are much closer than a company starting cold, and you can reuse the data map, the retention schedule, the breach runbook and most of the vendor paperwork. Four differences will still cost you work. Your lawful bases collapse from six to two, so anything you run on legitimate interests or contract necessity has to be re-based on consent. A child is anyone under 18 rather than under 16 or 13. Your notice has to be available in English or any of the 22 Eighth Schedule languages. And there is no sensitive-data tier, so the extra protection you built for health or financial data is good practice rather than a separate legal regime. Treat GDPR work as a head start, not as an equivalence.
faq.t: What consent actually means under the DPDP Act

faq.q: Do we have to keep Indian personal data inside India?
faq.a: Not as a general rule under DPDP itself. The Act takes the opposite approach to Europe: rather than permitting transfers only to approved countries, it lets the Central Government restrict transfers to countries it names. So the default is that transfer is allowed until a restriction exists. Two caveats matter more than that default. Sectoral rules already localise plenty of data — the Reserve Bank's payment-data directive is the one most fintechs meet — and DPDP expressly does not lower any stricter requirement in another law. And a fiduciary notified as significant can be restricted from moving specified categories of personal data out of the country at all.
faq.t: What consent actually means under the DPDP Act

faq.q: If we get consent wrong, is a crore-scale penalty the first thing that happens?
faq.a: No. The figures in the Schedule are ceilings, and the Act tells the Data Protection Board what to weigh before it lands on a number: the nature, gravity and duration of the breach, the type of personal data affected, whether the conduct was repetitive, any gain made or loss avoided, and whether mitigating action was taken and how promptly and effectively. Fast, honest, well-evidenced mitigation is written into the statute as a reason to reduce the penalty. It is also worth knowing that DPDP carries no imprisonment and gives an individual no statutory right to claim compensation from you, which is a real change from Section 43A of the IT Act that it repeals.
faq.t: What consent actually means under the DPDP Act

faq.q: When do we actually have to be ready?
faq.a: Later than the headlines suggest and sooner than is comfortable. The Act passed in 2023 but sat largely un-operational until the Rules were notified in November 2025, and those Rules commence in phases: the Board first, Consent Manager registration around a year on, and the substantive obligations — notice, consent, rights, breach notification, Significant Data Fiduciary duties — roughly eighteen months on, which is when the old Section 43A and the SPDI Rules also stand repealed. Dates in a phased rollout move, so check the current position rather than trusting this paragraph. What should not wait is knowing what personal data you hold, where it lives and who you share it with, because that work takes months, is the input to everything else, and is worth doing under any regime.
faq.t: What consent actually means under the DPDP Act

faq.q: Can you just tell me whether this video is real?
faq.a: Usually not from the file alone, and anyone who answers that question quickly is guessing. What I can tell you is what the file supports: whether it carries a signed provenance record, what its encoding history looks like, whether its geometry and lighting hold together, and where the earliest copy I can find came from. Often the decisive fact sits outside the file entirely — the account that posted it, the date it first appeared, or a second recording of the same moment. I would rather hand you that than a percentage.
faq.t: What deepfake detection can and cannot do

faq.q: Are AI detectors useless, then?
faq.a: Not useless, but badly mismatched to the way people use them. A detector is a classifier trained on the output of the generators whoever built it had access to, so it is strongest on those and weakest on the model released after the training set was frozen — which is the one you are actually being attacked with. Used as one input among several, by someone who knows what it was trained on, it has a place. Used as a verdict on a single file, it produces a confident answer with nothing under it, and a confident wrong answer is worse than no answer.
faq.t: What deepfake detection can and cannot do

faq.q: The photo has no metadata at all. Does that mean it was faked?
faq.a: No. Missing metadata is the normal state of almost every image you will ever be sent. Large platforms strip it on upload, chat apps re-encode and strip it, and a screenshot never had any to begin with. Absence proves nothing whatsoever. The reverse holds too: metadata that is present is trivially editable, so unless it sits inside a signed provenance manifest it is a claim about the file rather than evidence about it.
faq.t: What deepfake detection can and cannot do

faq.q: What does a Content Credentials badge actually prove?
faq.a: That a particular device or piece of software signed this asset with this stated history, and that the bytes have not changed since. That is genuinely valuable, and it is the strongest thing in the field. It does not prove the scene in front of the lens was real, because a signing camera pointed at a screen produces a validly signed photograph of a fake. It does not prove the signer is honest, only that the certificate chains to something you decided to trust. And an asset with no credential is not thereby fake — it is an asset with no credential, which describes most of the internet.
faq.t: What deepfake detection can and cannot do

faq.q: Is error level analysis proof that an image was edited?
faq.a: No, and this is the most misread tool in the field. ELA maps where compression history differs across an image. Sharp edges, saturated colour and fine texture are bright in the ELA of every untouched photograph ever taken, and one extra re-save flattens the whole map into uniform noise. Bright does not mean pasted. It is also worth asking what amplification factor produced the picture you are being shown, because turning the gain up until something looks suspicious is how ELA is usually used to mislead.
faq.t: What deepfake detection can and cannot do

faq.q: How do I stop a cloned voice from getting a payment out of my company?
faq.a: Not by detecting it. Make the payment process indifferent to how convincing the voice was. No payment and no change of bank details is ever approved on the channel the request arrived on. Verification is a callback to a number from your own records, never a number offered during the call. A second approver is reached separately. Urgency and seniority become stop conditions rather than reasons to skip a step, and stopping a payment has to be safe for the most junior person in the chain. None of that requires anyone to judge whether a voice was synthetic.
faq.t: What deepfake detection can and cannot do

faq.q: Someone has made a fake video of me. What should I do first?
faq.a: Preserve before you react. Save the original file rather than a screenshot of it, record the exact address, the account and the time you saw it, and take a hash of the file so you can later show that the copy you handed over is the copy you found. Then report it: in India that means the national cybercrime portal or the 1930 helpline, and the platform's own reporting route in parallel. Do not pay anyone offering removal, and do not argue with the poster. What you preserve in the first hour is usually worth more than any analysis done a week later.
faq.t: What deepfake detection can and cannot do

faq.q: Can my family just show a death certificate and get into my account?
faq.a: Generally not into the account. Providers draw a firm line between releasing a copy of data to a relative and handing over a working login, and their next-of-kin processes almost always produce the former. Even where a court gets involved, the usual outcome is disclosure of content rather than credentials. Plan on your family receiving an export, not a password.
faq.t: What happens to your accounts when you die

faq.q: Is it safe to keep my authenticator seeds in the same vault as my passwords?
faq.a: It weakens the separation between your two factors, which is a real cost, and the purist answer is no. The practical answer for most people is that it is worth it: seeds in a vault survive a lost or locked phone, they can be inherited through emergency access, and the more common failure by far is losing access yourself rather than an attacker defeating a well-protected vault. Decide it deliberately rather than by accident.
faq.t: What happens to your accounts when you die

faq.q: What happens to subscriptions and purchased digital media?
faq.a: Subscriptions usually keep billing until the card is cancelled or somebody cancels them, which is why the account list matters as much as the passwords. Purchased media is generally licensed to a person rather than owned, and those licences are typically not transferable, so a large digital library often does not pass to an estate at all. Terms differ by provider and change, so check the ones that matter to you.
faq.t: What happens to your accounts when you die

faq.q: Should digital accounts be mentioned in a will at all?
faq.a: Yes, but as people and permissions rather than as secrets. Name who should deal with your accounts and what you want done with them, and give your executor explicit authority to act. Never put a password, a recovery phrase or a PIN in the document, because in many jurisdictions a will becomes a public record once it is admitted to probate.
faq.t: What happens to your accounts when you die

faq.q: Does a nominee on my bank account override my will?
faq.a: Broadly, and with exceptions that matter, a nominee in India is the person the institution is permitted to pay rather than the person entitled to keep the money. Succession is decided by the will where there is one and by personal law where there is not, and personal law differs by religion. I am not a lawyer and this is not legal advice; if there is anything substantial involved, this is the question to take to one.
faq.t: What happens to your accounts when you die

faq.q: Someone has died and none of this was set up. What can I actually do?
faq.a: Do not cancel the mobile line yet, because it may still be the only route to several accounts. Identify the primary email address, since most other recoveries run through it. Get several certified copies of the death certificate, start each provider’s own next-of-kin or memorialisation process, and approach banks and insurers with the nomination details. Expect data and closures rather than working access, and expect it to take a while.
faq.t: What happens to your accounts when you die

faq.q: Can just opening a phishing link hack my phone?
faq.a: Almost never, on a phone that is still getting updates. Loading a page runs the page's code inside the browser's sandbox, where it cannot read your other tabs, your saved passwords, your files or your messages. Compromise through rendering alone needs a working exploit chain against your exact browser and operating system version, and those are expensive enough to be aimed at named individuals rather than sprayed at a mailing list. The realistic risk on a phone is the ordinary one: the page asks you to sign in, or to install a profile or an app from outside the store, and you do it.
faq.t: What happens when you click a phishing link

faq.q: I clicked the link but did not type anything. Do I need to change my password?
faq.a: No. If nothing was entered and nothing was downloaded, no credential left your device, and there is nothing for a password change to undo. What the click did disclose is that your address is live and that a person reads it, which is worth money to whoever sold the list, so expect the volume of similar mail to rise. Report the message, keep it rather than deleting it, and carry on.
faq.t: What happens when you click a phishing link

faq.q: Does changing my password fix it?
faq.a: Only half of it, and it is the half people stop at. A modern credential-harvesting page steals the session cookie the real service issued, and a session cookie is not a password — it is a token saying this browser has already signed in. Until that session is ended, the new password changes nothing for the attacker. Change the password, then use the sign-out-everywhere or revoke-sessions control, in that order, and then look for what outlives both: mail rules, forwarding addresses, connected apps and recovery details.
faq.t: What happens when you click a phishing link

faq.q: I have two-factor authentication. Does that not stop this?
faq.a: It stops the reused-password attack, which is worth having. It does not stop a page that relays your login to the real site in real time. A code from an app or an SMS is valid for a short window and the attacker needs about a second of it; a push approval is easier still, because the prompt you approve is the attacker's genuine login attempt. The factors that survive are the ones bound to the address you are actually on — a passkey or a hardware security key — because the signature they produce verifies nowhere except the real site. That only holds if the weaker methods are removed from the account, because an attacker will simply choose the fallback.
faq.t: What happens when you click a phishing link

faq.q: Should I delete the email?
faq.a: Not yet. The headers are the only reliable record of where the message came from and how it authenticated, and deleting it removes that record from the place anyone investigating would look. Report it with whatever button your mail client provides, tell whoever handles security where you work, and leave the message alone until they say otherwise. If there is nobody to report it to, move it to a folder rather than deleting it.
faq.t: What happens when you click a phishing link

faq.q: I downloaded the attachment but did not open it. Is that bad?
faq.a: No. A file sitting on disk has not run, and a file that has not run has not done anything. Delete it, empty the bin, and you are back where you started. The line that matters is execution, not download, which is exactly why the answer to what you actually did has to separate the two: the response on either side of that line is completely different.
faq.t: What happens when you click a phishing link

faq.q: Is an antivirus scan enough after I ran something?
faq.a: No, and this is where people most often stop too early. A clean scan means the scanner recognised nothing, not that nothing is there, and the tooling used for initial access is rebuilt specifically to be unrecognised for its first days in the wild. If something ran, treat every credential typed on that machine as exposed, change them from a different device, and have the machine rebuilt rather than cleaned. Rebuilding is inconvenient and reliable. Cleaning is convenient and a guess.
faq.t: What happens when you click a phishing link

faq.q: How would I know if someone is already reading my mailbox?
faq.a: Look for the housekeeping rather than for drama. Check the mailbox rules and any forwarding address, because a rule that files security alerts and banking mail somewhere you never look is the standard first move and it survives a password change. Check the sent and deleted folders for messages you did not write. Check the list of connected or authorised applications, because an app you once approved holds its own token. Then read the recent sign-in activity your provider records, which shows locations and devices even when nothing else looks unusual.
faq.t: What happens when you click a phishing link

faq.q: Does a VPN hide my browser fingerprint?
faq.a: No. A VPN changes the address a server sees and nothing else. Your screen, time zone, core count, GPU string and canvas hash are read inside the browser and are identical with the VPN on or off. Worse, if WebRTC escapes the tunnel then even the address leaks, which is what the leak page lets you check: compare the public address it finds against the one your provider says it is giving you.
faq.t: What your browser tells every site you visit

faq.q: Does private browsing or incognito change my fingerprint?
faq.a: Mostly no. Private browsing starts with empty storage, so it defeats cookies and anything else a site saved. It does not change your hardware, your fonts, your screen or your time zone, so the values that make up a fingerprint come out the same. Firefox and Tor Browser go further than ordinary private windows do, but an ordinary private window is a storage feature rather than a fingerprinting defence.
faq.t: What your browser tells every site you visit

faq.q: Can a website really see which fonts I have installed?
faq.a: It can probe for them. The usual method renders the same string in each candidate font and measures how wide the result comes out; a font that is missing falls back to a default and measures differently. Safari and Firefox have restricted this to system fonts, which limits how much a page can learn. The leak page on this site does not run a font probe, so you will not find a font row in its table.
faq.t: What your browser tells every site you visit

faq.q: Will turning JavaScript off stop this?
faq.a: It stops the second half. Without scripts a page cannot read your screen, your core count, your GPU or a canvas hash. It still receives your IP address, User-Agent, Accept-Language and Referer, because those arrive with the request before any code runs. Browsing with JavaScript disabled is also rare enough to become a distinguishing feature in itself, and a large part of the web stops working.
faq.t: What your browser tells every site you visit

faq.q: Is fingerprinting legal?
faq.a: It depends on the jurisdiction and the purpose, and I am not a lawyer. Under consent-based regimes such as India's DPDP Act or the GDPR, reading device characteristics in order to identify a person is generally the kind of processing that needs a lawful basis, and consent is the usual one. The practical problem is that enforcement happens after the fact. Nothing in the browser stops the read while it is occurring.
faq.t: What your browser tells every site you visit

faq.q: Is my phone safer than my laptop for this?
faq.a: Different rather than safer. Phones are more uniform, because a given model has one screen, one GPU and one core count, so you blend in with everyone carrying the same handset. Against that, the model itself is readable, and a phone carries an app layer with permissions that a browser tab does not have. Which of the two is easier to fingerprint in practice, I have not measured.
faq.t: What your browser tells every site you visit

faq.q: Does static mean the site cannot be interactive?
faq.a: No. Interactivity is a client-side property and has nothing to do with how the page is served. This site runs language compilers, an operating system emulator and a forensics suite in the browser, all from static files.
faq.t: When a static site outgrows being static

faq.q: What is the single clearest sign you need a server?
faq.a: A feature that requires a secret. A key shipped in client-side code is public, whatever it is named. Everything else on the list has workarounds of varying quality; that one does not.
faq.t: When a static site outgrows being static

faq.q: Is a shipped search index a real limit?
faq.a: Eventually. This site's index is around 957 KB for 272 pages and is fetched once, on first use rather than on page load. It grows roughly linearly with the site, so at some size asking a visitor to download it becomes a worse deal than a query against a service.
faq.t: When a static site outgrows being static

faq.q: Should I move the whole site when one feature needs a backend?
faq.a: Usually not. Give that feature an edge function or a hosted service and leave the rest static. Architecture changes tend to be justified by one requirement and then paid for by every page.
faq.t: When a static site outgrows being static

faq.q: What do you lose by going dynamic?
faq.a: An attack surface you did not have, an availability dependency, a bill that scales with traffic, and the ability to make simple verifiable promises about data never leaving the visitor's machine — which for a site full of security tools is the product itself.
faq.t: When a static site outgrows being static

faq.q: Is this not over-engineering for a personal site?
faq.a: The mechanism is a few dozen lines: find elements carrying a key, count the thing, rewrite the text. It was written after one fact was found typed into six separate files with no way for any copy to notice it had gone wrong.
faq.t: Why every number on this site is counted rather than typed

faq.q: What happens to the committed value in the repository?
faq.a: It stays as the last deploy's number, so the repository copy is always a real figure rather than a placeholder. The next deploy corrects it. That also means a page opened straight from the repository reads correctly.
faq.t: Why every number on this site is counted rather than typed

faq.q: Why not just count at page load in JavaScript?
faq.a: Because the number would then be absent for anyone without JavaScript, and for crawlers reading the raw HTML. Counting at build time puts a real figure in the delivered markup, which is where it needs to be.
faq.t: Why every number on this site is counted rather than typed

faq.q: Which numbers does this not cover?
faq.a: Anything about the world outside the repository — clients, people mentored, years of experience. Those are still typed and still go stale at the same rate. The technique does not touch the numbers most likely to be wrong on a professional site.
faq.t: Why every number on this site is counted rather than typed

faq.q: Should every number be automated then?
faq.a: No. Some figures are accurate at every deploy and still misleading, because a total reads as a finished total. Where a section is still growing, dropping the number is more honest than automating it.
faq.t: Why every number on this site is counted rather than typed

faq.q: What do you do about a number recorded in a video?
faq.a: Nothing a build can do. A figure spoken in a walkthrough, or captured in a recording of an interface that displayed it, is part of the picture. Either re-record it, or say plainly beside the video that the figure has moved on.
faq.t: Why every number on this site is counted rather than typed

faq.q: Will you quote fixed price without a written scope?
faq.a: No. The number is meaningless on its own — it is a price for a specific document, and without the document there is nothing for it to be a price of. The scope does not have to be long. One page covering what is included, what is not, what I need from you and what done looks like is usually enough for a small engagement.
faq.t: Why I quote fixed price, what it costs me, and when I refuse

faq.q: What happens if the work finishes faster than you expected?
faq.a: The price does not change. That is the same deal running in the other direction: you bought a number rather than a quantity of my hours, so a good week belongs to me in the same way a bad one does. If that feels wrong to you, capped time and materials is probably the structure you want instead, and I am happy to work that way.
faq.t: Why I quote fixed price, what it costs me, and when I refuse

faq.q: Can a fixed price be paid in stages?
faq.a: Yes, and I prefer it. Payments tied to observable milestones let you stop after any stage rather than being committed to the whole engagement from the first invoice. Where a scope has not agreed something more specific, my refund policy treats advances for work not yet started as refundable in full and accepted milestones as not.
faq.t: Why I quote fixed price, what it costs me, and when I refuse

faq.q: How long is a fixed quote valid for?
faq.a: I put a validity window on it, but the window is not really the point. In my experience quotes go stale because their assumptions go stale, not because prices move. So the quote lists the assumptions it depends on, and if one of them turns out to be false the quote reopens whether or not the window has closed.
faq.t: Why I quote fixed price, what it costs me, and when I refuse

faq.q: What if I want to change something halfway through?
faq.a: It gets priced as an addendum: a small separate agreement for the change, with its own effect on the timeline. It is not a renegotiation of the original quote, and you can decline it and keep the original deliverable. The important part is that this happens the week the change is raised, not at the end when both of us are arguing from memory.
faq.t: Why I quote fixed price, what it costs me, and when I refuse

faq.q: Is a paid discovery refundable if the conclusion is not to build?
faq.a: No, and that is deliberate. You paid for an answer, and “do not build this” is often the answer with the highest return in the whole engagement. If a discovery were refundable on that outcome, everyone involved would face a quiet incentive to recommend a build. You keep the written recommendation either way, including if you take it elsewhere.
faq.t: Why I quote fixed price, what it costs me, and when I refuse

faq.q: Is a password manager’s vault the same problem?
faq.a: It is the same mathematics with a much better shape. A well-built manager encrypts the vault on your device with a key derived from your master password, so the provider stores a blob it genuinely cannot read — that claim is closer to true than the one on most login pages. The caveat is identical, though: a stolen vault is an offline guessing attack on your master password, and the only thing standing between an attacker and the contents is how long and how unusual that one password is, plus the key-derivation cost the vendor chose.
faq.t: Why “we don’t store your password” is usually false

faq.q: Is SHA-256 a bad hash function?
faq.a: No. SHA-256 is an excellent hash function for the job it was designed for, which is integrity: checking that a file or a message has not changed. It is a bad password hash for exactly the reason it is a good integrity hash — it is fast, and speed is the attacker’s ally when the work is guessing. Password hashing wants a function that is deliberately slow and memory-hungry, which is what bcrypt, scrypt and Argon2 are for.
faq.t: Why “we don’t store your password” is usually false

faq.q: Does the salt need to be kept secret?
faq.a: No, and expecting it to be is a common misunderstanding. A salt lives in the database next to the digest it belongs to and is assumed to leak with it. Its job is to make each stored value unique so that precomputed tables and shared-password patterns stop working, not to be a secret. The secret value is the pepper, and the whole point of a pepper is that it is stored somewhere the database is not.
faq.t: Why “we don’t store your password” is usually false

faq.q: If a site emails me a reset link, does that mean it stores my password?
faq.a: No — that is the correct behaviour. A reset link proves control of the mailbox and then lets you set a new password, which requires knowing nothing about the old one. The red flag is recovery: an email that contains your existing password, or a flow that reads it back to you. Reset is fine. Recovery is proof that the plaintext was reachable.
faq.t: Why “we don’t store your password” is usually false

faq.q: Can I find out which algorithm a service uses without asking?
faq.a: Usually not. Nothing in the login flow exposes it, and I would be suspicious of any tool claiming to detect it from outside. Your options are the ones that involve people: the service’s own engineering documentation, its source if it is open, an audit or certification report, or simply asking support and seeing whether anyone can answer. A vague answer is itself information.
faq.t: Why “we don’t store your password” is usually false

faq.q: If I use a strong unique password everywhere, does any of this matter to me?
faq.a: Much less, and I would rather say so than overstate the case. A long random password that appears in no wordlist is out of reach whether it was stored under MD5 or Argon2, because the search space rather than the per-guess cost is what defeats the attack. What still matters to you is rung two: reversible storage means an attacker who reaches the application reads your password directly, and no amount of length helps with that.
faq.t: Why “we don’t store your password” is usually false

faq.q: My automation stopped and the logs are completely empty. Where do I start?
faq.a: An empty log is itself the finding: it means nothing executed, so the fault is at the edge rather than in the middle. Check three things in this order. First the credential — open the connection in the platform and look for a reauthentication prompt, or call a cheap authenticated endpoint by hand and see whether you get a 401. Second the trigger — confirm the workflow is still active, that a schedule survived any recent platform migration, and that a webhook endpoint registered with the vendor still points at a URL that exists. Third the vendor's status page and changelog for the window in which the last successful run sits. Between them those three cover the large majority of empty-log cases, and all three are faster to check than reading the workflow.
faq.t: Why your automation broke, and how to build one that fails loudly

faq.q: How often does this actually happen?
faq.a: Often enough that I plan for it rather than react to it, and I would rather give you a rule than a statistic I cannot back with published data. The rule is that the expected lifetime of an integration without maintenance is roughly the interval at which its slowest-moving vendor ships a breaking change, and for mainstream business software that is a matter of months rather than years. If a workflow matters, budget for it to need attention two or three times a year, and treat a year of complete silence as a sign that nobody is checking rather than evidence that nothing has moved.
faq.t: Why your automation broke, and how to build one that fails loudly

faq.q: Is self-hosting more or less reliable than a hosted platform?
faq.a: Neither, and the question is really about which failures you would rather own. A hosted platform absorbs patching, uptime and connector maintenance, and in exchange you get their outages, their retry policy and their deprecations on their timetable. Self-hosting gives you control over every one of those and hands you the pager. What actually changes reliability is not the hosting model — it is whether anybody is alerted when the thing stops. I have seen self-hosted workflows with better monitoring than enterprise deployments, and the reverse, and in both cases the monitoring was the variable.
faq.t: Why your automation broke, and how to build one that fails loudly

faq.q: Do I really need a dead-letter queue for a five-step workflow?
faq.a: Probably not, and I would not build one first. For a small workflow the useful order is: alert on absence, then handle retries safely with an idempotency key, then add a dead-letter queue when you find yourself losing items you cannot reconstruct. The signal that you need one is specific — a failure where you cannot answer the question "which records did not get processed, and can I run them again". Until you have hit that question, the queue is scaffolding for a problem you do not have, and the monitoring is not.
faq.t: Why your automation broke, and how to build one that fails loudly

faq.q: How do I test a change without touching the vendor's live data?
faq.a: Use a sandbox where the vendor offers one, and check whether its schema matches production before you trust a green result. Where there is no sandbox, the workable pattern is a disposable record you create and delete in the same run, tagged clearly enough that a human finding it in the CRM knows what it is. Keep a separate set of credentials for testing so a mistake is contained, run tests against a copy of the workflow rather than the live one, and get written agreement from whoever owns the account before anything scheduled starts writing into their production system.
faq.t: Why your automation broke, and how to build one that fails loudly

faq.q: The vendor emailed about a deprecation months ago. Why did it still surprise us?
faq.a: Because the notice went to an inbox rather than to a system. Vendor announcements arrive as email to whoever created the account, at a moment when the change is not yet actionable, and they are read by a person who is not the person who will have to do the work. The fix is mechanical rather than cultural: route changelog and status feeds to a shared address that a team reads, record every pinned version and its announced end date in the same place you track other dated obligations, and let a contract test be the backstop for the notices that get missed anyway. Assume some will always get missed.
faq.t: Why your automation broke, and how to build one that fails loudly

faq.q: Should I just rebuild it in code instead?
faq.a: Only if the reason is one of a short list: volume that makes per-operation pricing absurd, logic that has outgrown what a visual canvas can express readably, or a requirement for tests and review that the platform cannot give you. Rebuilding in code does not remove a single cause from the first half of this article — the vendor still deprecates, the token still expires, the page size still changes. What it changes is that the guards become ordinary code you can test, and the workflow becomes a diff. That is a real gain, and it arrives with a maintenance burden that a no-code platform was carrying for you.
faq.t: Why your automation broke, and how to build one that fails loudly

faq.q: Can someone hack my phone just from my number?
faq.a: Not in the way the phrase suggests. A number lets somebody send you things — a message with a link, a call, an invitation to install something — and every one of those still needs you to act before it works. What a number does enable without your involvement is an attack on the number itself: persuading your operator to move it to a new SIM, after which every code sent by text arrives on somebody else's phone. That is why moving your important second factors off SMS buys more safety than any app you could install.
faq.t: Why your phone feels hacked, and probably is not

faq.q: My battery drains fast and the phone gets hot. Does that mean spyware?
faq.a: Almost never on its own. Battery capacity falls with age and with heat, so a two-year-old phone genuinely lasts less than it did when you bought it. A major operating system update makes the phone re-index photos and search for several days. And one app that changed in the last week is the single most common cause of a sudden overnight difference. Check the battery screen for one app you cannot explain, check that storage is not nearly full, and give the phone a week after an update. If the drain survives all three, it is worth looking further.
faq.t: Why your phone feels hacked, and probably is not

faq.q: Is my phone listening to my conversations to choose adverts?
faq.a: The evidence says no, and the real explanation is more interesting than the myth. Both platforms now show an indicator whenever the microphone is live and keep a log you can read, so a permanently listening app would be visible; continuous audio would also cost battery and data that somebody would have measured by now. What actually happens is that ad networks already link your devices to the people around you through a shared home connection, shared logins, uploaded contact lists and overlapping locations, so a search somebody else made can select the advert you see. Then memory does the rest: you scroll past thousands of adverts a week and remember only the handful that echo something recent.
faq.t: Why your phone feels hacked, and probably is not

faq.q: I received a one-time code I did not ask for. What should I do?
faq.a: Treat it as somebody standing at your door holding your key. Do not read the code out to anyone, whatever they claim to be, and do not approve a sign-in prompt you did not start. Change that account's password from a different device you trust, sign out every other session, and then check the account for a forwarding rule or a recovery address you did not create. One stray code can be a wrong number. A second one is not.
faq.t: Why your phone feels hacked, and probably is not

faq.q: Will an antivirus app tell me if my phone is compromised?
faq.a: Much less than the advertising implies. On iOS an app cannot inspect other apps at all, so anything sold as an iPhone virus scanner is checking almost nothing. On Android, Play Protect and the reputable scanners do catch commodity stalkerware and known malicious apps, which is worth having and is already built into the phone. Neither will find a targeted implant, and neither is a substitute for the account checks, because the account is where the real finding usually is.
faq.t: Why your phone feels hacked, and probably is not

faq.q: Does a factory reset fix a hacked phone?
faq.a: It fixes the device and nothing else. A reset removes apps, permissions, device administrators and configuration profiles, so if the problem lived on the phone it is genuinely gone. It does not sign out a session on your account, delete a mail-forwarding rule, revoke a third-party app's access, or move your number back after a SIM swap. And restoring from a backup taken while the problem existed puts the problem straight back, which is why people conclude the reset did not work. Fix the accounts first, then reset, then set the phone up as new.
faq.t: Why your phone feels hacked, and probably is not

faq.q: Somebody I live with may have put something on my phone. What is the safe first step?
faq.a: Not a technical one. Monitoring tools report, so removing one tells the person watching that you found it, and the period after surveillance stops is a known point of escalation. Use a device that person cannot reach, and speak to a support organisation before you change anything on the phone, so that there is a plan covering your safety rather than only the software. In India that means 181 for the women's helpline, 112 in an emergency, and cybercrime.gov.in or 1930 to report. If evidence might matter later, photograph what you found rather than deleting it.
faq.t: Why your phone feels hacked, and probably is not

faq.q: Is this not just an argument for self-documenting code?
faq.a: It sits alongside it. The first move should always be to make the code express the mechanism. But a measured contrast ratio, a bug that was actually hit, or an alternative that was rejected cannot be expressed in a better variable name — those are facts about history and constraints, not about behaviour.

faq.q: Won't a comment recording a bug become misleading once the bug is fixed?
faq.a: It records why a guard exists, which stays true for as long as the guard does. The failure case is when the guard is removed and the comment is left, and that reads as obviously strange — which is better than a restated mechanism going quietly wrong.

faq.q: Isn't this level of commenting expensive?
faq.a: Yes, and it suits a codebase with one maintainer and no review conversation carrying the context. On a team some of this belongs in a pull request instead. The kinds worth keeping everywhere are the measurement, the load-bearing constraint and the stated limit.

faq.q: Does all this text slow the site down?
faq.a: Not for visitors. The deploy strips comments out of the delivered CSS and the two scripts that load on every page, so the source keeps them and the browser does not. That only works because the published file is generated rather than served straight from the repository.

faq.q: Where should a comment go?
faq.a: Where the mistake would be made. A wiki page is not read by the person about to reorder two lines, and a commit message is only found by someone who already suspects there is something to find. The comment has to be adjacent to the edit it is trying to prevent.

faq.q: Is my board saved?
faq.a: Yes, after every move, in your own browser storage. Close the tab and come back and the board, the score and the move count are where you left them.

faq.q: How much can I undo?
faq.a: One move. Enough to take back a misfire, not enough to play the board backwards.

faq.q: Can I keep going after reaching 2048?
faq.a: Yes. Reaching 2048 is announced but the run carries on, so 4096 and 8192 are both on the table if the board holds together.

faq.q: Does it work on a phone?
faq.a: Yes — swipe in any direction on the board, or use the pad.

faq.q: Is this the real aafire?
faq.a: No. It is the same effect written from scratch for a browser. The original is a C program driving aalib, but the arithmetic is the same idea and the character ramp is chosen the same way.

faq.q: Why does the flame stop short of the top?
faq.a: The decay. Each row up costs a fixed slice of heat, so the fire runs out at a predictable height. Inferno lowers the decay far enough that it reaches the ceiling.

faq.q: Is there anything to do?
faq.a: Change the wind and watch it lean. That is it, which is why this is filed under toys rather than games.

faq.q: Is this Colossal Cave?
faq.a: No. It is the same kind of game — rooms, a lamp, a locked way, treasure to carry home — but the map, the puzzles and the prose are written for this page. Eighteen rooms against the original's hundreds.

faq.q: I am stuck at the gas. What now?
faq.a: Read the board nailed to the timbering in the pump chamber, then look at what is lying on the floor of that same room. The mine tells you the answer before it kills you for not having it.

faq.q: Do I need to draw a map?
faq.a: Not really. Once you have been somewhere, the exit that leads back to it is labelled with its name, so the list does most of the mapping for you. A pen still helps below the ladderway.

faq.q: What happens when I die?
faq.a: The run ends and scores nothing, and you start again at the stile. There is exactly one way to die in this mine and it is signposted twice, so it is a decision rather than an accident.

faq.q: Can I put things down?
faq.a: No, and nothing needs it. There is no carrying limit and no puzzle that turns on leaving something behind, so a drop command would only be one more line in the list to scroll past.

faq.q: What is a good average?
faq.a: Around 600 ms per target on medium is respectable, and under 450 is quick. Small targets add roughly 150 ms for most people — that gap is Fitts's law, and it is remarkably consistent.

faq.q: Does the mouse matter?
faq.a: Some. Polling rate and sensitivity change the number more than most people expect, so compare yourself against yourself rather than against anyone else.

faq.q: Why does the raw time differ from my score?
faq.a: The result shows both: raw speed, and the adjusted figure after the misses are charged. The gap between them is what accuracy is costing you.

faq.q: Can I cross the halfway line?
faq.a: No. Your mallet is confined to your own half, which is the one rule air hockey really has.

faq.q: Why did my puck barely move?
faq.a: You blocked it rather than hitting it. Standing still returns the puck at the speed it arrived; moving into it adds yours on top.

faq.q: Does the computer cheat?
faq.a: No. It moves at a fixed speed toward an aim point and cannot exceed it, so on Brutal it is fast but it is not teleporting.

faq.q: Why are there no songs?
faq.a: Film lyrics are copyrighted, and a database of them is not something this site will publish. Every sound in this section is also synthesised rather than stored, so there is no audio here at all. Keeping the rule and swapping the content was the honest way to build it.

faq.q: My word is real but it was refused. Why?
faq.a: The word list is closed and hand-written, so it does not know every real word. That is a genuine limitation. It is also what lets the game count the remaining words on a letter, which is the part worth having.

faq.q: What is the difference between the two word lists?
faq.a: One is ordinary English nouns. The other is well-known Indian words in Latin script — places, foods and everyday objects. Neither contains anything taken from a film or any other copyrighted work.

faq.q: How is the score worked out?
faq.a: It is the length of the chain you kept going. Higher is better, and your best is kept in this browser on this device, under a key you can clear with your site data.

faq.q: Can two people play on one phone?
faq.a: Yes. Choose pass and play, and the game names each side in turn. Nothing is sent anywhere and there is no online mode, here or in any game on this site.

faq.q: Can I stop it going dark?
faq.a: Yes. The lighting dropdown offers Daylight and Night as fixed settings as well as the automatic cycle, and it eases between them rather than switching, so choosing one halfway through a dusk is not a light switch being thrown.

faq.q: Why do two of the fish ignore the shoal?
faq.a: Because two of them are meant to. The angelfish and the wrasse have their schooling weight set to zero, so they take no heading and no company from anything in the tank and simply wander it. A tank where every fish shoals reads as a screensaver; the loners are what make it read as a tank somebody keeps.

faq.q: What does the food do?
faq.a: Fish within about a hundred units of a flake break off whatever they were doing and go for it, and the flake is gone the moment one reaches it. Anything nobody finds settles on the sand and dissolves after a few seconds. They are a good deal less interested at night.

faq.q: Can I fail it?
faq.a: No. Every screen accepts every answer, including no answer at all. That is the point being made rather than a shortcut — a fail state would teach the opposite of what the last screen says.

faq.q: Does it record anything about me?
faq.a: It counts your pointer moves, your clicks and the seconds you spent, in variables in your own tab, so the last screen can show you the one signal a real check would care about. The numbers are shown once and are gone when you reload. Nothing is stored and nothing is sent.

faq.q: Are the pictures real photographs?
faq.a: No, they are labelled boxes. Nothing loads over the network on this page. It also means a screen reader can read the challenge out, which real image grids manage badly if at all.

faq.q: Could this be used as a real CAPTCHA?
faq.a: No, and it would stop nothing. A script would clear all eight screens in milliseconds, which is roughly the situation genuine puzzle-based checks are in as well.

faq.q: Why do real ones keep getting harder?
faq.a: Because it is an arms race with a scoreboard only one side reads. Each time recognition software catches up, the puzzle gets more awkward, and the awkwardness is felt by people rather than by the software. That is why the newest systems gave up on puzzles and went to scoring behaviour instead.

faq.q: Can I turn off division?
faq.a: Yes. The dropdown picks addition only, addition and subtraction, those plus multiplication, or all four. It takes effect on the next question rather than the next run.

faq.q: Are the answers ever negative?
faq.a: No. Subtraction swaps the operands if it needs to, so the answer is always zero or more and you only ever type digits.

faq.q: What is the score made of?
faq.a: Each sum is worth its level plus a weight for the operation — one for addition, four for division. So a hard division late in a good run is worth about ten times an easy addition at the start.

faq.q: Does it work on a phone?
faq.a: Yes. Tapping the panel opens a numeric keypad rather than a full keyboard, which is the only thing this game needs.

faq.q: Is this the real asciijump?
faq.a: It is a rebuild, not the original binary. Same three phases, same screenful of characters, written in JavaScript so it runs in a browser tab instead of needing a terminal and a package manager.

faq.q: When exactly should I let go?
faq.a: At the red lip post, and about a twentieth of a second either side of it still counts as perfect. The results panel tells you which way you missed, which is faster to learn from than any advice here.

faq.q: What are the arrow keys for?
faq.a: The air is unstable. Your lean drifts, and drifting further makes it drift faster, so left and right are a constant small correction rather than a steering wheel. The bar along the bottom shows where you are against where the judges want you.

faq.q: Does the wind matter?
faq.a: A headwind is airspeed and airspeed is lift, so it is worth a few metres either way. It is deliberately small: something you notice, not something that decides a jump your takeoff already decided.

faq.q: Does it work on a phone?
faq.a: Yes, in landscape. Hold the Action button down the in-run and lift your thumb at the lip; left and right hold the lean once you are in the air.

faq.q: How is this different from the assembly puzzles game?
faq.a: Different machine and a different rule. That one hands you an input tape, asks for an output tape, and scores instructions plus cycles added together, so a working program is most of the win. Here the arguments arrive in registers and memory, there is a stack with CALL and RET, and the score is the length of your program on its own.

faq.q: Why does it say my program did not terminate?
faq.a: It ran past forty thousand cycles and was stopped. That usually means a loop whose exit test can never be true — a counter tested before it is changed, a DJNZ that started at zero, or a jump that lands above the instruction doing the work. The cap is a cap, not a diagnosis: no checker can decide in general whether a program will stop.

faq.q: Is par really the shortest possible?
faq.a: No, and nothing here claims it is. Par is the shortest program I found for that level, measured by running it rather than by writing a number down. If you beat it, the page says so, and you are right and it is wrong.

faq.q: Why is my shorter program slower than par?
faq.a: Because those are two different competitions and this game only scores one of them. Level seven is the clearest case: the ten instruction answer does far more work than the twelve instruction one. Both figures are shown so you can see what the length cost you.

faq.q: Can I see the test cases?
faq.a: Two of them, from the start. The rest stay hidden until one of them fails your program, at which point that case is shown with the value it wanted and the value it got, and loaded into the machine panel so you can step through it.

faq.q: Are my programs saved anywhere?
faq.a: They are kept in this browser, per level, and nothing is sent anywhere — there is no network call in the game at all. Restart clears your scores but leaves the code; clearing your site data removes both, along with your best.

faq.q: Is this x86, ARM or MIPS?
faq.a: None of them. It is invented, and deliberately small, so the whole instruction set fits on one screen. The register-and-flag model is closest to x86 in spirit.

faq.q: Why does it say "still running after 20000 instructions"?
faq.a: A loop with no way out. Usually the counter is being tested before it is decremented, or the jump goes back above the instruction that changes it.

faq.q: Can I have more than four registers?
faq.a: No, and that is most of the difficulty from level seven onwards. Memory is the answer: 32 cells, addressed as [6] or as [R1] when the address is in a register.

faq.q: Are my programs saved?
faq.a: They are kept in this browser only, per level, and nothing is sent anywhere. Restart clears your progress but leaves the code; clearing site data removes both.

faq.q: Is a lower score better?
faq.a: Yes. Cost is the one number where less is better, so your best is the lowest total you have posted on this device.

faq.q: Why does the ship keep moving after I stop thrusting?
faq.a: Because that is the game. There are no brakes. The only way to slow down is to turn around and thrust the other way, and the drag is deliberately light so that most of the speed you build is still yours to deal with a few seconds later.

faq.q: How many times does a rock split?
faq.a: Twice. A large one becomes two mediums, each medium becomes two smalls, and a small is destroyed outright. One large rock is therefore seven rocks in total, worth 20, 50 and 100 points as they get smaller.

faq.q: What is the saucer worth?
faq.a: The large one is 200 points and fires in random directions. The small one is 1000 and aims at you, with an error that narrows as your score climbs. It turns up more often the better you are doing. Either can be destroyed by a rock, and its shots break rocks too, though you are not paid for those.

faq.q: What does hyperspace do?
faq.a: Down drops you at a random point on the board with your speed reset to zero. It does not check what is already there, so it can put you inside a rock. It is an escape from a situation you cannot fly out of, not a safe one.

faq.q: Do I get extra lives?
faq.a: One every 10,000 points, on top of the three you start with. Your best score is kept in this browser only; there is no server and no leaderboard.

faq.q: How do I get an aircraft off the radar?
faq.a: Point it at its own numbered exit and climb it to altitude nine. It leaves the moment it reaches that exit at that altitude. At any other altitude it flies straight over the exit and off the edge, and that loses the shift.

faq.q: How do I land one?
faq.a: Match the runway heading printed beside the airport, then time the descent so the aircraft reaches altitude zero on the airport square itself. One level a sweep, so from altitude three you commit three squares out.

faq.q: What exactly counts as a collision?
faq.a: Two aircraft in touching squares at the same altitude. One level of separation is enough, which is why altitude rather than heading is the tool that gets you out of trouble.

faq.q: Why is an aircraft sitting on a runway doing nothing?
faq.a: It is a departure waiting for clearance. It will not move until you give it an altitude, and it costs you nothing while it waits — which makes it the one thing on the screen you are allowed to ignore.

faq.q: Does it work on a phone?
faq.a: Yes. Tap an aircraft to pick it, then use the pad. It is a sixty-six column screen, so turn the phone sideways.

faq.q: Is it actually impossible?
faq.a: No. It is very hard. The solver models a decent player rather than a perfect one, and a shape with nowhere at all to go is skipped rather than served — an instant unavoidable loss reads as a broken game, not a cruel one.

faq.q: How is this different from just bad luck?
faq.a: Bad luck is a distribution. This is a search: it evaluates your actual board before choosing. Twenty S-pieces in a row from a random generator is a story; here it is a plan.

faq.q: What is a good score?
faq.a: Far lower than your Tetris score, and that is the point. Clearing thirty lines against this is a genuinely good run.

faq.q: Why is it called that?
faq.a: Short for "bastard Tetris", which is what its author called it, and which is fair.

faq.q: Is the number chosen before I start guessing?
faq.a: Yes. In the rounds where you search, the number is drawn when the round begins and does not move afterwards. Nothing here adapts to your guesses to keep the game going longer — which is exactly the trick the second half invites you to try on me, and the reason the second half has a checker in it.

faq.q: Can I beat par?
faq.a: Yes, by luck. Par is the worst case: it is the number of guesses that is always enough and sometimes necessary. Guess 50 in a range of 1 to 100 and hit it, and you have used one guess for a job that needs seven. The page says so rather than congratulating you, and the score treats any round at or under par as clean, so luck cannot improve your record either.

faq.q: What counts as cheating in the half where I answer?
faq.a: Only an answer that contradicts one you have already given — and it is detected rather than suspected, because the interval your answers imply becomes empty, and an empty interval means no number of any kind would have produced that sequence. Answering to keep the search working as long as possible is not cheating and is not penalised: it is the adversary argument, and the game names it and then finishes in exactly par.

faq.q: How is the score worked out, and why is lower better?
faq.a: It is the guesses you spent over par in the two rounds where you searched, plus two for each contradiction caught in the rounds where you answered. A flawless duel is worth nothing over par, so it shows as "par". The number written to your browser is actually one higher, because the shell reads a zero as "no run happened"; that offset never reaches the page, and it only matters if you go looking in local storage.

faq.q: Does the overflow really happen in JavaScript?
faq.a: No, and the page says so where it shows it. JavaScript numbers are doubles, so lo + hi stays exact well past two billion. To reproduce what a Java or C int does, the sum is pushed through a bitwise OR with zero, which truncates it to 32 signed bits. The wraparound is simulated; the arithmetic and the negative index that comes out of it are real, and are the bug Joshua Bloch wrote up in 2006.

faq.q: Is anything uploaded, or kept?
faq.a: Nothing is uploaded. Your best score, your chosen range and whether you want the midpoint shown are kept in this browser on this device, and the reset strip under the game clears exactly those and nothing else.

faq.q: Is the day of the week right for old dates?
faq.a: Back to 1583 it is, on the Gregorian calendar. Earlier than that the form refuses, because the Gregorian calendar arrived in 1582 in some countries, 1752 in Britain and its colonies and 1918 in Russia — so the weekday for a date in 1650 depends on where you are asking about, and one answer would be a guess dressed as a fact.

faq.q: What if I was born on 29 February?
faq.a: Your age and day counts are exact either way, since they never need an anniversary. For the next birthday in an ordinary year this page uses 1 March; some places use 28 February instead. The result says which it used.

faq.q: Another calculator gives a different age. Which is right?
faq.a: Both, probably. The disagreement will be in the months-and-days part, near the end of a short month, and it comes from how each one adds a month to the 29th, 30th or 31st. Total days alive is not a matter of opinion and should match exactly.

faq.q: Is my date of birth sent anywhere?
faq.a: No. It is typed into a field, used for arithmetic in the same tab, and never leaves it. It is not stored either — no localStorage, no cookie. Reload the page and the field is empty.

faq.q: How accurate is the heartbeat number?
faq.a: It is arithmetic, not measurement: days alive times 1,440 minutes times 70 beats. Treat it as the right size rather than the right number.

faq.q: Why is Pluto not in the table?
faq.a: It has not been a planet since 2006. If you want the figure anyway, its orbit is about 90,560 Earth days, so divide your days alive by that.

faq.q: What happens if I turn separation off?
faq.a: They collapse into a single point and stay there. Separation is the only rule pushing outward, so without it cohesion wins completely.

faq.q: And alignment?
faq.a: You get a milling swarm rather than a flock — they stay together but never agree on a direction. It looks like insects instead of birds.

faq.q: Is this how real flocks work?
faq.a: Broadly, yes. Reynolds proposed it in 1986 as a model rather than a measurement, and later studies of actual starlings found birds do track a small fixed number of neighbours rather than everything they can see.

faq.q: How do I control the bat?
faq.a: Any of three ways: the arrow keys, moving your mouse across the playfield, or the on-screen pad on a touchscreen. The mouse is the most precise.

faq.q: Do the bricks all take one hit?
faq.a: Not after the first level. The darker bricks take two hits, and from level four there are bricks that take three. Their colour tells you how much is left in them.

faq.q: Does the ball speed up?
faq.a: Yes, slightly, each time you clear a row and again on each new level. It is capped, so it never reaches a speed you cannot react to.

faq.q: What happens when I clear a level?
faq.a: The next layout loads and you keep your score and remaining lives. There are six layouts; clearing the sixth wins the run.

faq.q: Is this a real cache from a real processor?
faq.a: No. The parameters are invented and deliberately tiny — sixty-four to five hundred and twelve bytes, sixteen-bit addresses — so that the whole cache fits on screen and the binary split of an address is short enough to read. The arithmetic is the real thing: an L1 data cache on a current desktop is typically 32 or 48 KB, 64-byte lines and eight to twelve ways, and it computes its index and tag exactly the way this does. Nothing is measured from your machine here; the processor explorer is the page that does that.

faq.q: How am I allowed to beat LRU? Is Belady cheating?
faq.a: You are shown the whole access stream, including the part that has not happened yet, and you are allowed to read it. That is the only advantage you have, and it is the same advantage Belady has. A cache has neither. So beating LRU here proves nothing about LRU and everything about how much information a replacement policy is missing — which is the point of putting the two numbers side by side.

faq.q: What is the difference between a capacity miss and a conflict miss?
faq.a: A capacity miss would have happened even in a perfect cache of that size: the working set is simply bigger than the cache. A conflict miss would not have: the block was thrown out only because the index bits sent it to a set that was already busy, while lines elsewhere sat idle. The game separates them by running a fully associative LRU cache of the same capacity alongside yours and asking whether it would have hit. That reference model is the conventional one, and it is a choice — use a different policy for the shadow and a few misses change category.

faq.q: Does write-back change the hit rate?
faq.a: No, and that is why the counter for it is separate. Write-back and write-through place identical demands on the cache and produce identical hits and misses; what changes is memory traffic. Write-back marks the line dirty and defers the write until eviction, so repeated stores to one line cost one write instead of many, at the price of one dirty bit per line and a slower eviction. Level three is the one with stores in its stream, and level four turns its second pass into a read-modify-write.

faq.q: What happens if I change the policy or the level halfway through?
faq.a: Changing the replacement policy or the write mode restarts the current level, because your misses are scored against a reference run of the same stream and the two have to have been made under the same rules. Points already banked from earlier levels are kept. Changing the level restarts the whole run at that level, which is there for practice: starting at level seven can earn a hundred points and starting at level one can earn seven hundred, so there is nothing to gain by skipping.

faq.q: Is anything stored or sent anywhere?
faq.a: Nothing is sent. There is no network call in the game at all. The only things kept are your best total, your chosen level and the three toolbar settings, all in this browser under keys the reset button below the board will clear for you.

faq.q: Will this tell me which job to apply for?
faq.a: No. It can say which kind of work you find appealing to think about, which is not the same as what you are good at, what is hiring near you, or what you will still want in ten years. The result says so under the bars rather than in small print.

faq.q: Why only six tracks?
faq.a: Because six is what could be balanced properly across eighteen questions. There is no option here for QA, technical writing, support engineering, research, or the other jobs that keep software running, and their absence is not a judgement on them.

faq.q: What if all six come out about level?
faq.a: Then the result says that outright instead of picking a winner from noise. A flat spread is common and is usually a sign you have not done enough of any of it yet to have preferences — which is a fine place to be.

faq.q: Is anything sent anywhere?
faq.a: No. The scoring runs in the page, nothing is uploaded, and nothing is stored, not even locally. Reloading loses your answers.

faq.q: How do I aim?
faq.a: Tap along your baseline to slide the striker sideways, then put your finger down anywhere clear of the baseline and pull back behind the striker — the catapult is anchored at the striker, not at your finger. The dashed line shows where the shot is actually going.

faq.q: What is the queen worth?
faq.a: Three points, against one for an ordinary coin. The computer will go for it when the line is there.

faq.q: What happens if I pocket the striker?
faq.a: A foul: everything you sank on that stroke comes back to the centre — the queen included — plus one of your own pocketed coins. If you have none pocketed yet, you owe one, and it is paid out of the first coin you do sink.

faq.q: Do I keep the board if I score?
faq.a: Yes. Sink a coin cleanly and you shoot again. Miss, or foul, and it passes over.

faq.q: Can I grow the same tree twice?
faq.a: Yes — that is what the seed under the pot is for. The same seed always produces the same tree.

faq.q: Why does it grow slowly?
faq.a: Because watching it is the point. The button next to Grow another switches to instant if you would rather.

faq.q: Can two people play?
faq.a: Yes — switch to Pass & play and the engine steps out entirely. Both sides are yours to move, which is what a chessboard on a table already is. Take back then undoes one move rather than a pair.

faq.q: How strong is it?
faq.a: Club level at the default setting — it searches three ply plus captures, so it will punish a hanging piece and a one-move tactic every time, and it will not see a deep combination coming. Strong searches four and takes a second or two to reply.

faq.q: Can I take a move back?
faq.a: Yes, and it takes back the pair, so it is your turn again. Useful for exploring rather than for cheating, though nothing stops you.

faq.q: Does it do under-promotion?
faq.a: No — a promoted pawn always becomes a queen. Under-promotion matters in perhaps one game in a thousand and the dialogue it needs is miserable on a phone.

faq.q: Is there an opening book?
faq.a: No. It works everything out from the position, which is why its first few moves are sensible but not fashionable.

faq.q: Is anything sent anywhere?
faq.a: No. The engine runs in your tab. There is no server, no analysis upload, and no account.

faq.q: Is any of this a recording?
faq.a: No. There is no audio file anywhere in this section of the site. Every partial of every strike, and the wind behind them, is generated in your browser as you listen.

faq.q: Why does the size slider change the pitch so violently?
faq.a: Because pitch goes as one over length squared, not one over length. Halving a tube raises it by two octaves. That is the single most surprising thing about tuned tubes and the slider exists to make it audible.

faq.q: Are these real chime tunings?
faq.a: The scales are real and the relationship between length and pitch is real. The absolute frequencies are the ideal thin-tube formula rather than a measured instrument, so treat it as the right shape rather than a tuning reference.

faq.q: Is there a score?
faq.a: No. Nothing here can be won or lost, so no best score is kept and none is stored. It is a toy, and the page says so rather than inventing a number to chase.

faq.q: Why is the sound off when I arrive?
faq.a: Every game and toy here starts muted, because a page that makes noise unasked is a page people close. This is the one in the section most worth turning on.

faq.q: Do I need to know any cryptography to start?
faq.a: No. Room one is a slider you drag until the text turns into English, and each room explains the measurement it wants before it asks for it. The two rooms that are genuinely work — the Vigenere and the substitution — both have tools that do the arithmetic and leave you the judgement, which is the part worth having.

faq.q: Are the answers hidden from me?
faq.a: Not really. The ciphertexts and the right settings are in the page's JavaScript, and anyone determined can open the file and read them. This is a teaching chain rather than a competition, so there is nothing to protect. The plaintexts themselves are not stored anywhere — each one is produced by running that room's own decoder over its own ciphertext with the right key, which is the same code path your slider is using.

faq.q: Is the Kasiski analysis real, or a picture of one?
faq.a: Real, and computed from the ciphertext every time the panel opens. The repeated trigrams, their spacings, the factor tallies, the per-column index of coincidence and the chi-squared scores are all measured on the message in front of you rather than looked up. Paste any of these ciphertexts into the cipher playground in Labs and you will get the same numbers.

faq.q: What if I get stuck in one room?
faq.a: Every room has up to two hints, each costing a quarter of that room, and the cost is only taken off if you then solve it — reading a hint and still failing can never leave you worse off than not reading it. Beyond that there is "Open this room for me", which sets the room to its answer so the note behind the door is readable and the chain carries on. That room scores nothing and the rest of the run is unaffected.

faq.q: How is the score worked out?
faq.a: A thousand points across the five rooms: 150, 250, 150, 250 and 200, in that order. Each hint takes a quarter of the room it was taken in, and a room opened for you scores zero. There is no clock and no penalty for a wrong setting, because trying settings and looking at what comes out is the entire method.

faq.q: What are the characters?
faq.a: Half-width katakana plus digits and punctuation, which is what the original used — chosen because they are visually dense and unfamiliar enough not to read as words.

faq.q: Is there anything to do?
faq.a: No. It is a screensaver. That is why it is filed under toys.

faq.q: Is Connect Four solved?
faq.a: Yes — with perfect play the first player wins, and it has been proven since 1988. This opponent is not perfect at six ply, so you can beat it; it is perfect at spotting immediate wins and blocks.

faq.q: Why does it always go in the middle first?
faq.a: Because the centre column is genuinely the strongest opening square, for the reason above. It is not being predictable, it is being right.

faq.q: Can two of us play?
faq.a: Yes — pass and play on one device.

faq.q: What format should the answer be in?
faq.a: The whole flag, from CTF{ to the closing brace. Spaces around it and the wrong case are both forgiven; leaving the braces off is not, because the wrapper is part of the flag in every competition you will enter.

faq.q: Do I need any tools to solve these?
faq.a: No. Every challenge can be done by hand, and each explanation links to the lab that does the same job if you would rather not. Nothing is timed, so take as long as you like over one.

faq.q: Are the answers hidden from me?
faq.a: Not really — the flags are in the page's JavaScript, and anyone determined can open the file and read them. This is a practice ladder rather than a competition, so there is nothing to protect and no reason to pretend otherwise.

faq.q: Is this a real capture the flag?
faq.a: It is one slice of one. Real events add exploitation, reversing and forensics, which need a target you have permission to attack — and there is one on this site: HackLab holds forty-two of those, from SQL injection on a live engine through JWT forgery, SSRF and path traversal, each with hints, the full solution and the real-world fix. This ladder covers recognising and undoing encodings, which is where almost every challenge begins.

faq.q: Does anything I type leave the browser?
faq.a: No. There are no network calls in the game at all, and the only thing stored is your best score, in this browser on this device.

faq.q: Is this an audit?
faq.a: No. It asks what you do, not what your systems are. A real assessment looks at your actual accounts and devices; this is a two-minute prompt to notice the obvious gaps.

faq.q: Why is a VPN barely worth anything here?
faq.a: Because HTTPS already encrypts what a VPN was sold to protect. A VPN moves who can see your traffic; it does nothing about reused passwords, which is what actually gets people.

faq.q: Do you store my answers?
faq.a: No. Nothing is sent and nothing is saved — reloading the page loses the lot.

faq.q: Is this based on anything?
faq.a: No. The six archetypes are made up — they are patterns you can recognise in a team, not categories anybody has measured. The Big Five test elsewhere on this site is the one with actual research behind it.
faq.t: What kind of developer are you

faq.q: I got a different result the second time. Which is right?
faq.a: Neither, particularly. Most people are three of these depending on the week and the codebase, which is why the result also shows your second reading and says when the top two are too close to separate.
faq.t: What kind of developer are you

faq.q: Can I use this to hire people?
faq.a: Please do not. It asks how somebody would like to describe their habits, which is a long way from how they work under a deadline with a codebase they did not choose.
faq.t: What kind of developer are you

faq.q: Are my answers stored?
faq.a: No. Everything is computed in the page, nothing is sent anywhere, and reloading loses it.
faq.t: What kind of developer are you

faq.q: Is there a seizure risk?
faq.a: The strobe is the only part that flashes, it is off until you turn it on, it warns you first, and it is rate-capped. If your system asks for reduced motion the strobe is disabled outright. If you are photosensitive, leave it off — the rest of the rig does not flash.

faq.q: Where does the music come from?
faq.a: It is generated in the tab with the Web Audio API — a kick, hats, a bass line and a pad, sequenced live. Nothing is streamed, nothing is downloaded, and there is no copyright on it.

faq.q: Why does the haze slider change the frame rate?
faq.a: Haze is drawn as stacked translucent wedges, so it is the most expensive thing on the canvas. Turn it down on a weak machine and everything else keeps its timing.

faq.q: Can I put the fire out?
faq.a: Yes. Draw water on it, or over the wood in front of it. Fire that runs out of fuel burns down on its own and leaves smoke.

faq.q: Does it save what I draw?
faq.a: No. It is a toy, and reloading gives you a fresh scene.

faq.q: Why is stone different from wood?
faq.a: Stone does nothing at all — it just blocks. Wood also blocks, but it burns, so it is what you build things out of when you want to set fire to them later.

faq.q: Why am I losing points for blocking traffic?
faq.a: Because most of what walks down that wire is your own business. Blocking a customer costs twelve points and blocking an attack earns ten, so a firewall that refuses everything is scored as the outage it is. This is the one thing the game exists to say: a rule set is judged by what it lets through as much as by what it stops, and the second number is the one nobody puts on a dashboard.

faq.q: What is the difference between DROP and REJECT?
faq.a: Both stop the packet and both score the same here. DROP says nothing at all, so the sender waits for a timeout and learns nothing. REJECT returns an error immediately, which is kinder to a legitimate client that would otherwise hang, and which also confirms to whoever is scanning you that something is there. On screen a rejected packet turns round and goes back the way it came.

faq.q: What does the SHADOWED label mean?
faq.a: That every packet the rule could match is already matched by a rule above it, so it can never fire. It is the commonest way a rule set rots: somebody adds a broad accept near the top, and three carefully written rules underneath quietly stop existing. Nothing warns you in production, which is why it is drawn here.

faq.q: Are these real IP addresses?
faq.a: No, and none of them can ever belong to anybody. The public ranges are 192.0.2.0/24, 198.51.100.0/24 and 203.0.113.0/24, which RFC 5737 reserves for documentation, plus the benchmarking range 198.18.0.0/15 for the distributed flood. The office is RFC 1918 private space. No real company, network or campaign is being reproduced.

faq.q: Can it actually be won?
faq.a: Yes. Six hundred is the maximum — sixty attacks blocked, nothing legitimate dropped — and it fits inside the seven slots with a rule to spare. Your best is kept in this browser on this device and nowhere else, because there is no server behind any of this and so no leaderboard to put it on.

faq.q: Why does a shell take so long to go up?
faq.a: Because it does. A six-inch shell leaves the tube at about 72 m/s and needs five and a quarter seconds to reach 170 m. An earlier version used a brisker gravity to make the rise snappier and it had to come out: with time compressed and distance not, the report arrived a quarter of the way through the burst, and the one detail this toy exists for looked like audio latency.

faq.q: Why does a high burst sound duller than a low one?
faq.a: Air absorbs high frequencies far faster than low ones — roughly 0.005 dB per metre at 1 kHz against about 0.09 at 8 kHz. Over 200 m that is a decibel lost down low and eighteen up top, so the sharp crack of a close break has gone by the time a high one reaches you and only the roar is left. The report rolls its own top end off with distance for exactly that reason.

faq.q: Is the sound recorded?
faq.a: No. Every thump, report and crackle is built in the tab with the Web Audio API, so there is nothing to download and nothing to license. The crackle is one noise source through a gain following a curve of random spikes, which is all a crackle is, and costs four nodes instead of the forty separate grains the first version fired per shell.

faq.q: How do I flap?
faq.a: Space, the up arrow, or a tap anywhere on the playfield. That is the whole control scheme — nothing else does anything.

faq.q: Does it get harder?
faq.a: Slightly. The gap opens at 168 units and loses one and a half for every gap you clear, down to a floor of 132. At ten gaps it has shrunk by about nine per cent, which you feel rather than see. The scroll speed never changes.

faq.q: Why does nothing move until I flap?
faq.a: The pipes hold still until your first flap, so a run never starts while you are still reading the screen. The score starts with that flap.

faq.q: Can it generate a gap I cannot reach?
faq.a: No. Each gap centre is at most 110 units from the last, and a good flap cadence climbs around 270 units in the time between two pipes, so there is always slack.

faq.q: Is my score sent anywhere?
faq.a: No. It is written to this browser and stays there. Clearing site data clears it, and there is no leaderboard to compare it against.

faq.q: Is the music real?
faq.a: It is generated in the tab with the Web Audio API rather than streamed, so there is nothing to download and nothing to license.
