faq.q: Why does the spray blow one way?
faq.a: The wind slider adds a horizontal acceleration to every droplet in flight. Heavier droplets are pushed less than fine spray, which is why the top of each arc bends further than its base.

faq.q: Can I make it bigger?
faq.a: Use the full-screen control. The canvas is drawn in logical units and scaled, so nothing pixelates.

faq.q: What is the glider gun?
faq.a: Bill Gosper's pattern from 1970 — the first arrangement found that grows without limit, firing a glider every thirty generations. It won a fifty-dollar prize.

faq.q: Is there a way to win?
faq.a: No. It is a zero-player automaton: you set the starting cells and the rules do the rest. That is why it is filed under toys rather than games.

faq.q: Why does my random soup settle down?
faq.a: Almost all random starts collapse into a mixture of still lifes and small oscillators within a few hundred generations. The interesting patterns are the rare ones that do not.

faq.q: Is this real git?
faq.a: No. Eighteen commands are reimplemented in JavaScript over an in-memory object store, and the hashes are pretend. The model — snapshots, parents, labels, the index, the reflog — matches the real thing, which is what the game is for.

faq.q: Do I need to know git already?
faq.a: No. The first mission is git init and each one introduces the next idea. If you want the theory in prose first, read Git, explained from the object up on the blog — the game and the article were written together.

faq.q: Why is there no push or pull?
faq.a: This page makes no network calls, by design, and a simulated server would hand out simulated lessons. Remotes, force-with-lease and the collaboration model are covered in the companion article instead.

faq.q: Can I get stuck?
faq.a: Not permanently. retry rebuilds the current mission’s scene from scratch, hint nudges, and Restart begins a fresh run. Exploring beyond the brief cannot wedge a later mission, because every mission builds its own scene.

faq.q: What counts towards the best score?
faq.a: Every command you run, including help, hint and the ones git refuses. Lower is better, and somewhere around seventy on a first pass is a respectable showing.

faq.q: Does anything I type leave the page?
faq.a: No. There are no network calls anywhere in this game. The only thing stored is the command count of your best run, in this browser.

faq.q: Do I always go first?
faq.a: Yes, you play X and open. That is a real advantage — free-style gomoku is a first-player win with perfect play. Nothing here plays perfectly, so it is an advantage rather than a result.

faq.q: Does six in a row count?
faq.a: Yes. These are free-style rules: five or more wins, and there are no forbidden openings. That is the version people play away from a tournament table.

faq.q: What actually changes between the three strengths?
faq.a: How heavily it weighs your threats against its own, and how much noise goes into the choice. Casual under-defends and wanders; Sharp defends almost as hard as it attacks; Ruthless defends fully and checks your best reply to its six best moves before committing.

faq.q: Can two of us play on one device?
faq.a: Yes — switch the first dropdown to pass and play. The cursor is shared and the side panel says whose turn it is.

faq.q: Does it work on a phone?
faq.a: Yes. Tap the point you want and the stone goes there, or use the pad if you would rather nudge the cursor a square at a time. It is turn-based, so a touchscreen costs you nothing.

faq.q: How do I win?
faq.a: You do not, exactly. You clear as much of the board as you can before no legal move remains. Ninety per cent is an excellent result; nobody clears it all.

faq.q: Is there any luck involved?
faq.a: Only the deal. After that the board is fixed and fully visible, so every outcome is a consequence of your choices. That is unusual and it is why the game holds up.

faq.q: Why does a direction sometimes show a dot?
faq.a: Because that move is illegal: either it runs off the board or it crosses a square you have already eaten.

faq.q: Does it work on a phone?
faq.a: Yes, with the pad. It is a turn-based game, so a touchscreen costs you nothing.

faq.q: Are these real implementations?
faq.a: Yes. Bubble, selection, insertion, merge, quicksort and heapsort are written as they are normally written, and every run is checked to produce a sorted array. Nothing is faked for the animation.

faq.q: Does the speed give it away?
faq.a: The duration does not — every run is stretched or squeezed to the same twelve seconds. The number of steps still differs, so quicksort changes the picture less often than bubble sort does, and you are welcome to use that. It is real information about the cost.

faq.q: Why only twenty-four bars?
faq.a: Enough for the patterns to be distinguishable, few enough that individual bars are visible on a phone. At two hundred bars everything looks like static and the only thing you can read is the overall shape.

faq.q: How is the score worked out?
faq.a: A correct answer is worth a hundred points at the start of a run, falling to five as it finishes. A wrong answer or running out of time scores nothing, and you get one guess per round. Five rounds, so five hundred is the maximum.

faq.q: Are these real outputs?
faq.a: Yes. Every JavaScript and Python snippet was run before it went in, and the C claims about sizes and conversions were checked with static assertions on an x86-64 build. Where the output depends on the compiler or the implementation, the option says so.

faq.q: Do I need to know all three languages?
faq.a: No. Each snippet is short enough to read cold, and the filter in the toolbar narrows the run to one language if you would rather. The C questions are the ones people who do not write C find hardest, and also the ones the explanations do the most work on.

faq.q: Is the order the same every time?
faq.a: No. The questions shuffle, and so do the four options under each one, so a second run is not a test of where the buttons were last time.

faq.q: What does Best mean?
faq.a: The most you have got right in a single run on this device, kept in local storage and nowhere else. Filtering to one language leaves fewer questions in the run, so those scores will not usually beat a full one.

faq.q: Where do the words come from?
faq.a: A hand-written list of sixty terms from security and computing, each with a one-line definition. The definitions are why the list is not pulled from a dictionary: you see one every time you solve a word.

faq.q: Can I just type?
faq.a: Yes. Click the board once so it has focus and then type letters normally. The on-screen grid is there because a touchscreen has no other way in, not as a fallback.

faq.q: Do the misses carry over to the next word?
faq.a: No. Each word starts with a fresh gallows. The run ends the first time a word beats you.

faq.q: How is the score worked out?
faq.a: Five points per letter in the word plus ten for every guess you had left, so a long word solved cleanly is worth a great deal more than a short one scraped through.

faq.q: Is there a hint?
faq.a: Only the two you would get on paper: how many letters the word has, and the list of letters you have already missed. Nothing else is revealed until you solve it.

faq.q: Is any of this legal advice?
faq.a: No. It is a training exercise. Two real obligations are referenced as context: CERT-In’s April 2022 direction under section 70B(6) of the IT Act asks for certain cyber incidents to be reported within six hours of noticing them, and GDPR Article 33 gives 72 hours from becoming aware of a personal-data breach to notify the supervisory authority. Which duties apply to a real organisation depends on where it operates and what data it holds.

faq.q: Does a replay actually differ?
faq.a: Yes. There are two scenarios, and inside each one your earlier choices remove and add later options — ask the bank for a wire recall in the first five minutes and the beat that offers it later never appears at all; keep watching the encrypting host and a chance to isolate it opens up that a contained run never sees. Surprise me picks a scenario for you.

faq.q: Why does the clock move while I am reading?
faq.a: Because it does on a real incident, and a tabletop where time only passes when you click teaches the opposite of the thing worth teaching. It is capped at fifteen simulated minutes per decision so careful reading is never punished for long, and the Measured setting switches it off completely.

faq.q: Are these really free, with no ads?
faq.a: Yes. There is no advertising, no analytics on the games themselves beyond the same page-view counter the rest of the site uses, and nothing to buy. They cost nothing to run because there is no server behind them.
faq.t: Games that run on your machine, not mine

faq.q: Do I need an account?
faq.a: No, and there is no way to make one. Your best scores are written to your own browser storage on your own device.
faq.t: Games that run on your machine, not mine

faq.q: Where are my high scores kept?
faq.a: In localStorage in the browser you played in. They do not follow you to another device or another browser, and clearing your site data removes them. There is no leaderboard, because a leaderboard would need a server and this has none.
faq.t: Games that run on your machine, not mine

faq.q: Do they work on a phone?
faq.a: Yes. Every game that needs directions ships an on-screen pad, which appears automatically on a touchscreen and stays hidden on a machine with a keyboard.
faq.t: Games that run on your machine, not mine

faq.q: Do they work offline?
faq.a: Once a game page has been visited, the service worker keeps it, so it will open again with no connection. The first visit needs the network like any other page.
faq.t: Games that run on your machine, not mine

faq.q: Is anything uploaded when I play?
faq.a: No. Nothing you do in a game leaves your browser. There is no score submission and no telemetry from the games; the only third-party script on the page is the same analytics tag the rest of the site loads, and it runs whether you play or not. Your network tab will show you exactly that.
faq.t: Games that run on your machine, not mine

faq.q: Where does the picture go when I save it?
faq.a: Into your downloads, built in the tab. The page composes the ground, the current rotation and the ink onto one 1280-pixel canvas and hands the browser a PNG. Nothing is uploaded, and no server ever sees the figure.

faq.q: Why does my line change colour as I draw?
faq.a: The palette advances with the pen rather than being picked per stroke. A slow base drift keeps it moving even when you hold still, and a term in your speed means a fast stroke sweeps a third of the wheel while a slow one stays in one family of colours.

faq.q: Does it flash?
faq.a: No. Ink accumulates gradually, the auto-mode fade removes about one per cent of it twice a second, and the only instantaneous change to the whole disc is the Clear button, which is a thing you pressed. If your system asks for reduced motion the rotation slider starts at zero, so nothing turns until you ask it to.

faq.q: Is this real?
faq.a: No, and it is not pretending to be. It is a hash function: a deterministic way of turning text into a number. It knows nothing about either person and could not, since two names are not information about a relationship.

faq.q: Why do I get the same number every time?
faq.a: Because a hash always maps the same input to the same output. That is the point of one. A calculator that gave a different answer each time would be using randomness and calling it insight.

faq.q: Does the order of the names matter?
faq.a: No. The two names are sorted before hashing, so "Asha and Ravi" and "Ravi and Asha" give the same result. It seemed the least defensible asymmetry to leave in.

faq.q: Are the names sent anywhere?
faq.a: No. Everything happens in your browser and nothing is stored, not even locally. Close the tab and it is gone.

faq.q: So what does predict whether a relationship works?
faq.a: Not letters in a name. Shared values, how you argue, whether you are both willing to change, and what each of you does under stress. There is a long piece about it on the blog, linked above.

faq.q: Can I play against another person?
faq.a: Yes, on the same device — choose Pass & play and hand it round. There is no online play: it would need a server to hold the game, and this site has none.

faq.q: How good is the computer?
faq.a: Decent, not brilliant. It prefers leaving the yard, then capturing, then getting a token home, then advancing whichever token is furthest along. It will beat you if you play carelessly and it will not out-think you.

faq.q: What are the star squares?
faq.a: Safe squares. A token standing on one cannot be captured, which makes them worth racing for when somebody is closing in behind you.

faq.q: Do I need an exact roll to get home?
faq.a: Yes. A token has to land exactly on the final home square, so an over-roll simply is not a legal move for it. That is the standard rule and it is what makes the last few squares tense.

faq.q: What happens on three sixes?
faq.a: The turn is forfeited. A six normally earns another roll, so without that rule a lucky streak could run indefinitely.

faq.q: Does it work on a phone?
faq.a: Yes. Tap Roll, then tap the token you want to move — the legal ones are ringed in white.

faq.q: What is a normal score?
faq.a: Most adults land between six and eight. Nine or more is well above the usual range, and it is very sensitive to distraction — a noisy room costs most people a full digit.

faq.q: Is chunking cheating?
faq.a: No, it is the skill. Reading 4 7 1 9 as "forty-seven, nineteen" is how people get past seven, and it is exactly what memory training teaches.

faq.q: Why does it feel harder than remembering a phone number?
faq.a: Because a phone number has structure and rhythm you already know. These are random, which is the point.

faq.q: How do I know which cards make a pair?
faq.a: By shape. Two cards match when they carry the same symbol — two stars, two hexagons. Colour follows the shape around and is there to help you scan, but it is never what decides a match.

faq.q: Why do two different shapes sometimes share a colour?
faq.a: Only on the 6×5 board, which has fifteen pairs and eight colours. There is no honest way to make fifteen colours distinguishable to everyone, so the shapes carry the identity and the colours are allowed to repeat.

faq.q: How is the score worked out?
faq.a: Your moves, plus one point for every five seconds. Lower is better. A perfect 4×4 run is eight moves, so eight points plus whatever the clock added.

faq.q: Are best scores kept for each size?
faq.a: Yes. Each of the three boards keeps its own record, in this browser only. Clearing site data clears them, and nothing is ever sent anywhere.

faq.q: Can I play it with a keyboard?
faq.a: Yes. Every card is a real button: Tab or the arrow keys move between them and Enter or Space turns one over. Matched cards drop out of the tab order so you are not stepping through dead ones.

faq.q: Can I lose on the first click?
faq.a: No. The mines are laid out after you click, avoiding that cell and everything touching it, so your opening move always reveals an area.

faq.q: How do I flag on a phone?
faq.a: Long-press a cell, or switch on flag mode with the flag button in the toolbar and tap normally.

faq.q: What is chording?
faq.a: Clicking a number that already has the right count of flags next to it opens all its unflagged neighbours in one go. On a mouse it is both buttons together; on a touchscreen, tap an already-revealed number.

faq.q: Are best times kept per difficulty?
faq.a: Yes. Beginner, intermediate and expert each keep their own best time on this device.

faq.q: Is this the real moon-buggy?
faq.a: It is a faithful rebuild, not the original binary. Same idea, same shape, same eighty-column screen — written in JavaScript so it runs in a browser tab instead of needing a terminal and a package manager.

faq.q: Why does it get faster?
faq.a: Speed climbs slowly with distance and caps out, so an expert run stays playable rather than becoming a reaction-time lottery.

faq.q: Can I shoot the craters?
faq.a: No — craters are holes, and a laser does not fill a hole. Rocks can be shot or jumped; craters can only be jumped.

faq.q: Does it work on a phone?
faq.a: Yes. The pad gives you an action button, and tapping the screen jumps.

faq.q: Is what I type sent anywhere?
faq.a: No. The conversion happens in the page and there is no request of any kind. Close the tab and it is gone; nothing is stored either.

faq.q: Can I turn the binary back into text?
faq.a: Yes, and so can anyone else — that is the point being made. Paste any row into the encoder and decoder at /labs/encoding and it comes straight back.

faq.q: Why does one emoji count as four bytes?
faq.a: UTF-8 uses one byte for ASCII and up to four for everything else. An emoji sits far outside ASCII, so it needs all four, even though it is a single character and a single code point.

faq.q: Why are some characters missing from the Morse row?
faq.a: Morse only defines codes for A to Z, the digits and a handful of punctuation marks. There is no Morse for an emoji, an accented letter or a non-Latin script, so those characters are left out and counted underneath rather than quietly mangled.

faq.q: Is ROT13 or leetspeak any use in a password?
faq.a: No. Both are fixed, public substitutions, and every cracking tool applies them automatically to its wordlists. Substituting digits for letters in a dictionary word leaves you with a dictionary word.

faq.q: Why can I only have two shots on screen?
faq.a: That is the original limit and it is what stops the game becoming a hold-to-win. Missing costs you the time until the shot leaves the top of the screen.

faq.q: Do the bunkers come back?
faq.a: No. They erode from both sides — your own shots damage them too — so by wave three you are usually out in the open.

faq.q: What happens if they reach the bottom?
faq.a: The run ends immediately, regardless of how many lives you have left. Letting them land is not survivable.

faq.q: Is this x86 or ARM?
faq.a: Neither, and not any other real instruction set. The machine is invented so that the whole of it fits beside the stack it is scribbling on: thirty-two cells, a couple of registers, and about a dozen instruction names that exist nowhere else. The shape of the frame is the honest part; the syntax is not meant to be.

faq.q: Will anything here work on a real program?
faq.a: No, and it is not built so that it could. There is no shellcode in the game and no way to author any, the addresses are fictional, and the machine only ever enters a routine at its first instruction. What you take away is the mental model — where the return address sits, why a canary stops one case and not another, what NX changed about the shape of an exploit — and that model is worth having whichever side of it you are on.

faq.q: Why can I not put a zero byte in the message?
faq.a: Because the copy stops at one, the way a C string copy does. It is a real constraint rather than a rule invented for the puzzle: an address containing a zero byte cannot be carried through a copy that terminates on zero, and that single fact has decided real exploits. The stack here sits on page 0x0100 so that the addresses you need do not contain one.

faq.q: Do I have to do the levels in order?
faq.a: No. The dropdown opens any of the four whenever you like, and each is a self-contained program with its own listing. They are written to be read in order, because level two only makes sense once level one has worked and level four is level three with the address taken away.

faq.q: Is anything stored or sent?
faq.a: Nothing is sent anywhere — there is no network call in the game at all. The only thing kept is your best total, in local storage in this browser on this device, and the reset strip under the board clears it.

faq.q: Which protocol should I pick to pass a scenario?
faq.a: Link state, on every one of them, and the reason is worth watching rather than being told: it converges in a flood plus one computation, where distance vector has to pass a metric round the network a round at a time. Static routing passes the first scenario and fails the link cut outright, because it cannot heal — it will keep posting packets into the hole until you move the next hop yourself, which you can, one router at a time.

faq.q: Why does the metric stop at 16?
faq.a: Because the count has to terminate, and it terminates by arriving at a number both ends agree means unreachable. RIP picked 16, and the price of that choice is that no network more than fifteen hops across can be served by the protocol at all. It is a ceiling on the diameter bought to put a floor under the failure.

faq.q: I turned split horizon on and it still counted. Why?
faq.a: You repaired the ring. Split horizon stops a router advertising a route back to the neighbour it learned that route from, which removes the loop between two adjacent routers and nothing larger. With a ring in the map the stale route simply travels the long way round, and every router on the way adds a link cost to it. That is true of the real technique, not a shortcut here, and it is why the demonstration scenario starts by cutting the two links that close the ring.

faq.q: Is this how RIP and OSPF actually work?
faq.a: The algorithms are, the plumbing is not. Bellman-Ford with a periodic exchange, an infinity of 16, split horizon, poison reverse and a route expiry counter are all here and all doing the work. Flooding with sequence numbers, a two-way check on every edge and a per-router shortest path first computation are here too. What is missing is everything below that: packet formats, hello and adjacency, areas, authentication, triggered updates and holddown. This will teach you why a protocol behaves the way it does. It will not teach you to configure one.

faq.q: How is the score worked out?
faq.a: Delivered minus dropped, with a priority packet counted five times if you lose one, all multiplied by ten — then up to nine points for low mean latency on top. The multiplication is so that latency can only ever separate two runs that moved the same traffic, rather than quietly becoming the thing being measured. The panel also keeps a best for each scenario separately, because the six of them do not offer the same load and one number covering all of them would be a comparison nobody could act on.

faq.q: Does anything leave my browser?
faq.a: No. There is no network call in the game, which is a slightly funny thing to be able to say about a game named after routing. The only thing stored is your best score, in this browser, under keys the reset strip under the game will list and clear for you.

faq.q: Is this the arcade maze?
faq.a: No. The arcade board is 28 by 31, which will not fit a 30 by 24 character grid with room left for a status line, so this maze is hand-drawn at 28 by 21. It keeps what matters: four corner pellets, wrapping side tunnels, a central ghost house with one door, and no dead ends.

faq.q: Why do the ghosts suddenly all turn round?
faq.a: Eating a power pellet reverses every ghost on the spot. Without that, a ghost already sitting on top of you simply eats you during the frightened window, which reads as a bug rather than a rule. The cyan one also turns round on its own every six seconds, when it switches between hunting and retreating.

faq.q: How long are they edible, and what are they worth?
faq.a: Six and a half seconds, and they flash white for the last two. The first ghost in a chain is 200 points, then 400, 800 and 1,600. Clearing all four on one pellet is worth 3,000, which is more than three hundred dots.

faq.q: What happens when I clear the board?
faq.a: You win the run and the score is final. There are no faster repeat levels — if you want more pressure, the ghost speed dropdown above the board changes it mid-run, and it takes effect on the next tick rather than the next game.

faq.q: Can I go inside the ghost house?
faq.a: No, the door is solid for you. The corridor that loops around the outside of the house is open, though, and it is one of the few stretches of the board with no dots in it at all.

faq.q: Is it safe to type my real password?
faq.a: It never leaves your browser and is not stored, so technically yes — but as a habit, typing a live password into any web page is a bad one. Type something structurally identical instead.

faq.q: It said "not cracked" — am I safe?
faq.a: Not necessarily. The browser gives up after a few seconds; real hardware does not. The estimate below the result is the number that matters.

faq.q: Why does adding ! at the end barely help?
faq.a: Because the rule engine tries it. Suffixes and substitutions are the first thing a cracker applies to a wordlist, so they cost an attacker almost nothing.

faq.q: Is there a tool version of this?
faq.a: Yes — the password lab and the live hash cracker in Labs do the same work without a score attached.

faq.q: Is this scientifically valid?
faq.a: The model is — the five-factor structure is the most replicated finding in personality psychology. This particular thirty-item questionnaire is a short informal version, not a validated instrument, and the result page says so.

faq.q: Why are some questions the opposite of others?
faq.a: To catch acquiescence — the tendency to agree with whatever is put in front of you. Reverse-keyed items score backwards, so agreeing with everything cancels out instead of producing a profile.

faq.q: What is "emotional volatility"?
faq.a: It is the trait usually called neuroticism, renamed because the clinical word carries baggage it does not deserve. High is not bad: it tends to come with noticing things other people miss.

faq.q: Is my data sent anywhere?
faq.a: No. Everything is computed in the page and nothing is stored, not even locally. Reloading loses it.

faq.q: Are any of these real companies?
faq.a: None of them. Every brand, person, domain, address and phone number in the deck is invented: the domains all sit under .example, which is reserved and can never be registered by anyone, and the IP addresses come from the ranges set aside for documentation. Nothing here links anywhere, and no real campaign or company's mail is reproduced — the lesson is in the shape of the thing, and the shape is what has been kept.

faq.q: I keep failing the genuine ones. Is that bad?
faq.a: It is the most common result and the most useful thing the game can tell you. Calling everything phishing is not caution: it means the real password expiry, the real revoked access and the real fraud alert all get treated as noise. The panel names it explicitly at the end of a run, and it names it far more often than any of the attack types.

faq.q: Can I turn the clock off?
faq.a: Yes — the dropdown has a no-clock setting, and it applies from the next message rather than the one you are halfway through reading. Speed points go with it; the base score and the streak bonus stay, so a slow careful run still scores and simply will not top a fast one.

faq.q: Are these real messages?
faq.a: They are faithful reconstructions of both real attacks and real service emails, with names and numbers changed. Nothing here links anywhere.

faq.q: I got the genuine ones wrong. Is that bad?
faq.a: It is the most common result and the most useful one. Calling everything phishing is not security — it means ignoring the alerts that matter, which is its own risk.

faq.q: What should I actually do with a suspicious message?
faq.a: Do not click, and do not use any phone number it gives you. Open the site or app yourself and check from there. It reaches the same place and cannot be faked.

faq.q: Why do pipes change colour at the edges?
faq.a: A pipe that wraps takes a new colour, so its reappearance on the far side reads as a new pipe rather than as a rendering glitch.

faq.q: What are the bright dots?
faq.a: The head of each pipe, so you can follow one if you want to.

faq.q: Is this a real plasma?
faq.a: No, and nothing here simulates one. It is interference between periodic functions — sines added up and read through a colour table. The name is inherited from the demoscene, where it described the look rather than the physics.

faq.q: Why a sine table when Math.sin exists?
faq.a: Because of how many times it is called. Four terms over 281,600 pixels is 1.1 million evaluations a frame, and a table lookup is an integer add, a mask and an array read where a trigonometric call is a great deal more than that. The frame counter in the HUD is there so you can watch the effect of the resolution control on your own machine rather than take my word for the arithmetic.

faq.q: Why does it look soft at low resolution?
faq.a: Because the small buffer is scaled up with the browser’s own smoothing rather than as hard squares. A plasma has no edges in it to preserve, so the blur costs nothing and is close to what a CRT did to a 320 by 200 mode anyway. The HUD says which size is really being filled.

faq.q: Does it flash, and does it store anything?
faq.a: The palette cycle is a continuous gradient rather than a switch between states, and if your system asks for reduced motion the toy opens on a still frame and starts the cycle slow, saying so on the screen. Nothing is stored for this page: there is no score to keep. The sound toggle is shared with the rest of the games and is the one setting that survives a reload.

faq.q: Why does holding the button jump higher?
faq.a: Letting go part-way up clips your upward speed rather than ignoring you, so a tap is a short hop and a held press is the full 109 units. Every gap in the three levels can be crossed with a full jump, and a few of the coins need one.

faq.q: How am I supposed to deal with the enemies?
faq.a: Land on top of one and it is flattened, worth a hundred points, and you bounce off it. Touch one from the side and you lose a life. Both kinds move a good deal slower than you run, so backing off and coming again is always an option.

faq.q: Do I keep my score when I lose a life?
faq.a: Yes. A life costs you the level you are on, not your points. You get three across all three levels, and the run ends when they are gone.

faq.q: Does it work on a phone?
faq.a: Yes. Tapping anywhere on the playfield jumps, and the pad gives you left, right and two jump buttons. Tapping is a full jump, since a tap has no length to read.

faq.q: Do I need to know threads to play this?
faq.a: No. Every step is one line of ordinary-looking code and the shared state is drawn above the columns as it changes, so you can work out what a level does by pressing things. What you will need by level six is the idea that a lock is a period of time rather than a spell cast over a variable, and the levels teach that by breaking four of them.

faq.q: Is the model a real CPU?
faq.a: No, and the page would rather say so than pretend. One step here is atomic; on a real processor an increment is several instructions and a store can be torn. Memory reordering is not simulated either — it appears exactly once, in the double-checked locking level, drawn openly as the order the compiler emitted, because inventing a plausible-looking memory model would be making something up. What is real is the interleaving, which is where these bugs actually live.

faq.q: Where do the ordering counts come from?
faq.a: A depth-first walk of the whole state space, memoised on the state, run in your browser at the moment you solve the level. Nothing is stored in the page as a lookup table. The three-request level has 33,078 legal orderings and 32,100 of them charge the card three times; the last level has two orderings and neither one is wrong.

faq.q: Can I get stuck?
faq.a: A run can reach a point where the bug is no longer reachable — that is not a bug in the game, it is the same thing as a scheduler having already made the decision for you. Step back undoes one step at a time, Run it again resets the level, and Hint will tell you either which thread to run next or that this particular run is already lost. Using a hint costs the fifty-point first-try bonus and nothing else.

faq.q: How is the score worked out?
faq.a: A hundred points a level, plus fifty if you produce the bug on your first complete run without a hint. The last level pays a hundred and fifty for correctly claiming it is impossible, which you can only do after running both of its orderings. Fifteen hundred is the maximum, and your best is kept in this browser on this device — there is no server here to keep it anywhere else.

faq.q: Does anything leave the browser?
faq.a: No. There are no network calls in the game at all, and the only thing written to storage is your best score, which the reset strip under the board will clear.

faq.q: Is this the same rain that comes with Linux?
faq.a: It is the same idea. The BSD games version animates three characters in place; this adds the spreading rings, a landing drop, and controls for how hard it rains.

faq.q: Why is it silent?
faq.a: At the Downpour setting there are forty landings a second. A plink on each one stops being rain and starts being a fault alarm.

faq.q: Is there anything to do?
faq.a: No. It is a screensaver, which is why it sits under toys rather than games. There is no score and nothing is saved.

faq.q: Why 78 columns and not 80?
faq.a: Ripples near the edge get clipped, and two columns of margin means the widest of them still reads as a ring rather than as a stray bracket.

faq.q: What is a good time?
faq.a: Around 250 ms is typical for an adult on a normal setup. Under 200 is genuinely quick. Under 150 usually means the click landed early and got lucky.

faq.q: Why did my early click not count?
faq.a: Because otherwise guessing beats reacting. An early click voids that attempt and you get another go at the same round.

faq.q: Does my phone score worse?
faq.a: Usually slightly, yes — touch panels add latency that a wired mouse does not. Compare yourself against yourself.

faq.q: Which flavour of regular expression is this?
faq.a: Your browser's own. Patterns are built with new RegExp and no flags, so matching is case sensitive and a pattern with no anchors can match anywhere in the string.

faq.q: Can I use lookahead, backreferences or named groups?
faq.a: Yes. Anything your browser's engine accepts, it will accept here. Whether it is shorter than the boring answer is another matter.

faq.q: Why was my pattern refused?
faq.a: Either it has an unbounded repeat nested inside another one, which is the shape that causes catastrophic backtracking, or it took longer than 40 milliseconds against eight short strings, which means it was already doing it.

faq.q: Is par really the shortest possible?
faq.a: No, and no claim is made that it is. It is the shortest the author found. Several of these lists almost certainly have shorter answers.

faq.q: Does anything leave the browser?
faq.a: No. There is no network call in the game at all. The only thing stored is your best total, in this browser, under a key you can clear with your site data.

faq.q: What is the difference between the two teleports?
faq.a: A safe teleport puts you somewhere no robot can reach next turn, and you only get a few. A risky one drops you anywhere at all, including next to something. Space uses a safe one if you have any and a risky one otherwise.

faq.q: Do wrecks kill me too?
faq.a: Yes. Walking into a wreck ends the run just as surely as being caught, so the piles you build are obstacles for you as well.

faq.q: How many levels are there?
faq.a: It keeps going, adding four robots a level up to sixty. Nobody clears it; the score is how far you got.

faq.q: Where does this come from?
faq.a: The BSD games collection, where it has been shipping since the 1980s. It is still one of the best small games ever written.

faq.q: Can I beat it?
faq.a: Yes, but only by being genuinely unpredictable, which is much harder than it sounds. Most people drift back to a pattern within a dozen rounds.

faq.q: Is it cheating — does it see my move first?
faq.a: No. It commits to a throw from the table before your click is scored. That is the whole reason it is beatable at all.

faq.q: How could I actually be random?
faq.a: Use something outside your head: the second hand on a clock, digits of a phone number, a coin. Any external source beats intuition.

faq.q: Can I save a run?
faq.a: No, and there is no undo either. That is what permadeath means: the run ends when you die, and the only thing that survives it is the score.

faq.q: How is the score worked out?
faq.a: Twenty-five for every level you reached, plus every piece of gold you picked up. Going deeper is worth more than clearing a level, which is the right way round.

faq.q: How do I go down a level?
faq.a: Find the % and press Space while you are standing on it. On a phone, the Action button does the same thing.

faq.q: Is there a way to win?
faq.a: Yes. The Amulet of Yendor lies on level ten and on every level below it, so it cannot be permanently missed. Pick it up and the run ends there, which is a good deal shorter than the original's twenty-six floors and a climb back out.

faq.q: What do the letters mean?
faq.a: Each one is a monster, roughly in order of how much trouble it is: r for a rat, k for a kobold, o for an orc, T for a troll, D for a dragon. ! is a potion, ) a weapon, * gold and % the stairs down.

faq.q: Is this a real Linux shell?
faq.a: No. Thirteen commands are reimplemented in JavaScript over a filesystem held in memory. For a real kernel and a real shell, both running in the browser, use the Linux terminal in Labs.

faq.q: Are there pipes and redirection?
faq.a: No. No |, no >, no variables and no command substitution. Every quest is solvable with one command at a time, and several are easier that way.

faq.q: Why does wc -c disagree with a real machine?
faq.a: Files here are JavaScript strings, so wc counts characters. A real wc counts bytes, and any character outside ASCII is more than one byte. Everything in this filesystem is ASCII, so for these files the two happen to agree.

faq.q: Is the filesystem the same every time?
faq.a: Yes. One fixed seed builds it, so the logs, the addresses and the answers are identical on every run and on every device. Restarting resets the permissions you changed.

faq.q: What counts towards the best score?
faq.a: Every command you run, including help, hint, clear and wrong answers. Lower is better, and a first pass of around thirty is a reasonable showing.

faq.q: Does anything I type leave the page?
faq.a: No. There are no network calls anywhere in this game. The only thing stored is the number of commands your best run took, in this browser.

faq.q: Can I play with the walls off?
faq.a: Yes. The arrows button in the toolbar switches between walls that kill you and edges that wrap around to the other side. It changes the game a lot — wrap-around is easier to survive and much harder to score well on.

faq.q: Does the speed setting change my score?
faq.a: No. A point is a point at any speed. The speed only changes how much time you get to think, and your best score is kept as a single number across all three.

faq.q: Where is my high score stored?
faq.a: In your own browser, on this device. There is no server and no leaderboard. Clearing your site data clears it.

faq.q: Does it work on a phone?
faq.a: Yes. A thumb pad appears automatically on a touchscreen, and swiping on the board works too.

faq.q: Is there any skill in snakes and ladders?
faq.a: None. Every outcome is decided by the dice, and no choice you make changes anything, because there is no choice to make. That is not a shortcoming of this version — it is the game.

faq.q: Do I need a six to start?
faq.a: Not here. You enter the board on your first roll, whatever it is. Requiring a six is a common house rule and it mostly adds waiting.

faq.q: What happens if I roll more than I need at the end?
faq.a: You stay where you are and the turn passes, because an over-roll is not a legal move. The board shows the number you still need.

faq.q: Does a six do anything?
faq.a: It earns you another roll, even when the six itself could not be used. There is no three-sixes forfeit here, though plenty of households play one.

faq.q: Is the board different every game?
faq.a: No. It is the same fixed layout every time — nine ladders and ten snakes in the positions most printed boards use — so a square you have learned stays learned.

faq.q: Can two of us play on one device?
faq.a: Yes. Choose pass and play, and set two, three or four players. There is no online play: that would need a server to hold the game, and this site has none.

faq.q: Is this teaching me to be suspicious of everybody?
faq.a: The opposite, and the scoring enforces it. Three of the eight conversations are genuine callers and every run contains at least one, without saying which. Refusing them outright costs you on both meters, because it is not actually safe: turn a new starter away with no route and somebody lends them a login by Thursday, and now an account in the audit trail is two people. A defender who blocks everything has moved the risk somewhere nobody can see it rather than removing it.

faq.q: Are any of these real companies, people or scripts?
faq.a: None of them. Every name, company, building, purchase order and job reference is invented, and where a phone number is printed it comes from the block Ofcom reserves for drama and never allocates. No real campaign is reproduced. The attacker's side of each conversation is deliberately thin — a name, a hurry, a deadline, a reference you cannot reach — because the shape is the part worth recognising and nothing here should be liftable.

faq.q: Why is there no attacker mode?
faq.a: Because a game that had you writing the pretext would be publishing a working one, and there is no version of that which teaches a defender something they could not learn from the defender's chair. The depth in this game is all on your side of the conversation, which is where it is useful.

faq.q: How is the score worked out?
faq.a: Each reply is rated out of ten on two axes: whether the asset stayed protected, and whether the answer was professionally acceptable. Each meter is the mean of every reply so far, out of a hundred, and the score is the mean of the two. A run that is strong on one and weak on the other is the interesting result rather than a mistake, and the debrief says which.

faq.q: Does it work on a phone?
faq.a: Yes. Every reply is a full-width button you tap, there is no pad and no gesture to learn, and nothing is timed, so a slow read costs nothing. The two meters carry their figures as text and a word — strong, holding, slipping, poor — so colour is never the only signal.

faq.q: Is anything uploaded?
faq.a: No. There are no network calls in the game at all. The only things stored are your best score and the two toggles, in this browser on this device, and the reset strip under the game clears them.

faq.q: Is this real SQL?
faq.a: No — it is a small SQL engine reimplemented in JavaScript over five tables held in memory. It understands SELECT, WHERE, AND/OR, comparisons, LIKE, UNION SELECT, ORDER BY, LIMIT, scalar subqueries, both comment forms and a few string functions. The model matches the real thing closely enough that the techniques transfer, which is the point of the toy.

faq.q: Does anything I type reach a real database?
faq.a: No. There are no network calls anywhere in this game, and the tables live in the page. The passwords you are trying to get around are sitting in that in-memory data, which is safe because a query cannot leave the tab it runs in.

faq.q: Do I need to know SQL already?
faq.a: It helps, but the Schema button shows every table and the SQL the engine understands, and each room has a hint that spells out the technique. If you want the theory in a tool rather than a game, the SQL playground and the SQLite browser in Labs cover it without a score attached.

faq.q: The blind rooms are slow. Is that the point?
faq.a: Yes. A blind injection leaks one bit at a time, so you extract a value character by character — and a binary search using the comparisons gets there in a handful of queries where marching the alphabet takes dozens. In the time-based room the only signal is a delay, and that delay is simulated in your tab; nothing is holding a server open.

faq.q: What counts towards the best score?
faq.a: Every query you send, in every room, whether it works or errors — an attacker pays for each request. Lower is better, so a clean run is a small number of well-chosen queries, and a binary search on the two blind rooms is most of the difference between a tidy score and a slog.

faq.q: Is this teaching me to attack websites?
faq.a: It is teaching you to recognise and close the bug. Every payload targets only the toy tables in this page, there is nothing here aimed at a real product, and each room ends on the one thing that actually stops the attack: a parameterised query. That is the whole takeaway.

faq.q: What format should answers be in?
faq.a: Dotted decimal for addresses and masks, a plain number for host counts, yes or no for the same-subnet questions, and either /26 or 26 for a prefix.

faq.q: Why is a /31 not two usable hosts?
faq.a: It is, by RFC 3021, for point-to-point links — but the question uses the classic formula everywhere else, so the range here stops at /29 to avoid teaching an edge case as a rule.

faq.q: Is there a calculator version?
faq.a: Yes, in Labs. This is the same maths with a timer on it.

faq.q: Are the puzzles always solvable by logic?
faq.a: They always have exactly one answer, which is the guarantee that matters. On Expert some positions may need a fairly advanced technique, but no puzzle here requires guessing between two valid grids, because no puzzle here has two.

faq.q: What are pencil marks?
faq.a: Small candidate numbers you jot into an empty cell. Press the pencil button, then tap numbers — they toggle rather than replace.

faq.q: Does Check tell me the answers?
faq.a: No. It highlights entries that are wrong, in red, for a couple of seconds. It will not fill anything in.

faq.q: Is my progress saved?
faq.a: No — each run generates a fresh puzzle. Your best completion time per device is kept.

faq.q: How does scoring work?
faq.a: One line is 100 points times the level, two is 300, three is 500, and four at once is 800. Soft dropping adds one point a row and hard dropping adds two, so pushing pieces down quickly is worth a little on its own.

faq.q: What does hold do?
faq.a: It parks the current piece and gives you the one you held before, or the next one if the hold is empty. You can only do it once per piece, which is what stops it being an undo button.

faq.q: Does it get faster?
faq.a: Yes. Every ten lines raises the level and shortens the drop interval. The top level is reached at a hundred and forty lines, at which point the pieces are falling faster than you can read them.

faq.q: Can I play it on my phone?
faq.a: Yes. The pad gives you left, right, rotate, soft drop and a hard-drop button.

faq.q: What are the four Coffman conditions?
faq.a: Mutual exclusion, hold and wait, no preemption, and circular wait. All four have to hold at the same instant for a deadlock, which is why the panel shows them as four separate lights rather than as one warning — deny any single one and the entire failure becomes impossible. The Deny hold-and-wait button does that to the second one, and Clear the jam does it to the third.

faq.q: How do I make it deadlock on purpose?
faq.a: Leave it on Uncontrolled and tap each of the four arms in turn, which sends a car down all four at once. Otherwise just wait: at the default arrival rates the junction locks itself somewhere inside the first minute, every time, and each jam is counted.

faq.q: Which strategy is actually best?
faq.a: None of them, which is the point. The four-way stop is perfectly fair and pushes about half the traffic of the others, because it serialises the whole box to one car. The lights and the roundabout are close at an even load; the lights lose when the load is uneven, because they keep giving green to an empty arm, and the roundabout loses when contention is heavy, because a rolled-back car did work that produced nothing. Uncontrolled looks quickest for about a minute and then spends a third to a half of its time gridlocked — deny hold-and-wait and it becomes as fast as anything here, which is the real lesson.

faq.q: What do the three digits in a galaxy chart cell mean?
faq.a: Klingons, starbases and stars in that quadrant, in that order. Three dots mean you have not scanned it yet. A long range scan reads the eight quadrants around you onto the chart, and it costs neither energy nor time.

faq.q: How do I refuel?
faq.a: Move next to a starbase under impulse power. Docking happens by itself once you are in one of the eight squares around it, and it fills both the energy and the torpedo racks. It also drops your shields to zero, so leave carefully.

faq.q: Can I run out of energy?
faq.a: Yes, and it ends the run there and then. Below twenty units you cannot move a single sector, which means you cannot reach a starbase, so the game says so rather than leaving you to press buttons at a ship that can no longer do anything.

faq.q: Is the stardate a real clock?
faq.a: No. It moves only when you do: roughly one stardate for each quadrant of warp, a twentieth for a sector of impulse, a tenth for firing. Sitting and reading the chart is free.

faq.q: Is this draw one or draw three?
faq.a: Draw one, and you can turn the deck over as often as you like. It is the kinder version, and it is the one that makes a deal winnable often enough to be worth starting.

faq.q: Can I take a card back off a foundation?
faq.a: Yes. Point at the foundation, press action, and the top card comes back into your hand for a tableau column. It costs fifteen points, which is roughly what it costs you in the paper game too.

faq.q: Is every deal winnable?
faq.a: No, and nothing checks the deal before it hands it to you. Most draw-one deals can be solved by somebody who can see every card; rather fewer by somebody who cannot, which is the game.

faq.q: Is there an undo?
faq.a: No. Restart deals a fresh game, but a move you have made is made. That is the same bargain the physical game makes, and it is what makes the choice of which card to turn matter.

faq.q: What is the score counting?
faq.a: Ten for a card sent home, five for turning a face-down card, five for a card played out of the waste, and fifteen off for taking one back down from a foundation. It measures progress rather than speed; the move counter beside it is there if you would rather judge yourself on that.

faq.q: What happens when I hit a tree?
faq.a: You lose most of your speed and the screen flashes, but the run carries on. A downhill you can lose four seconds in is not one anybody plays twice.

faq.q: How do I win?
faq.a: Get to the finish. The course is 1,200 metres and the banner appears across the piste as you approach it. Your score is the TIME, so a faster run is a better one — and your best is a lap record rather than a high score.

faq.q: Why can I barely steer sometimes?
faq.a: You are tucked. Let go of down and the steering comes back immediately.

faq.q: Do I press Enter?
faq.a: No. The word dies the instant what you have typed matches it. Space and Enter both just clear the buffer if you want to start a different word.

faq.q: What happens when a word reaches the wall?
faq.a: You lose a life. Five lives, then the run ends and you get your words-per-minute for the session.

faq.q: How is this different from the typing trainer?
faq.a: The trainer gives you long passages and measures sustained accuracy. This is a panic: short words, rising speed, and it measures how fast you recognise and fire.

faq.q: Can I play it on a phone?
faq.a: Tapping the playfield opens the keyboard, so yes — though this is one of the few here that genuinely wants a real keyboard.

faq.q: How is WPM calculated?
faq.a: Characters typed divided by five, scaled to a minute. The headline figure is net WPM, which subtracts characters left wrong at the end, so accuracy and speed are one number rather than two.

faq.q: What counts as an error?
faq.a: Any character that does not match the target at the moment you type it. Fixing it with backspace removes it from the net score but it is still counted in the per-key breakdown, because it is still a key you struggle with.

faq.q: Can I practise code and symbols specifically?
faq.a: Yes. The text picker has real code, a punctuation drill and a numbers-and-symbols mode. Those are the three that actually slow programmers down.

faq.q: Is my typing sent anywhere?
faq.a: No. Everything is computed in the page, and your results are stored in your own browser. There is no server involved at any point.

faq.q: How is this different from the typing test in Labs?
faq.a: The lab is a quick benchmark — one short passage, a number at the end. This is for practice: longer texts, several durations, a per-key breakdown and a history you can watch improve.

faq.q: Does this tell me anything about myself?
faq.a: No. Not a thing. Fourteen questions about imaginary parties cannot measure a person, and there is no sense in which somebody resembles a denial-of-service attack. It is a way of reading eight attack summaries without noticing you are doing it.

faq.q: Are the descriptions in the results accurate?
faq.a: Yes. Each one says how the attack works and what actually defends against it, and none of them recommend the folk remedies — filtering rude words does not stop SQL injection, and antivirus does not stop credential stuffing. There is a fuller map in the post on types of cyberattacks.

faq.q: Why is brute force described as credential stuffing?
faq.a: Because most of what gets logged as a brute-force attack is a replay of username and password pairs leaked from some other breach. Genuinely guessing a long password is impractical; reusing one you have already had leaked is not.

faq.q: Do you store my answers?
faq.a: No. Nothing is sent anywhere and nothing is saved — reloading the page loses the lot.

faq.q: Is this Wordle?
faq.a: It is the same rules, which are not anybody’s to own, with a different dictionary and no connection to the New York Times. The word list here is development and security vocabulary rather than general English.

faq.q: Does everybody get the same word?
faq.a: Yes, on the same calendar date. It is picked from your local year, month and day, so somebody in Sydney gets it before somebody in London does — but they get the same word, on the date they both call today.

faq.q: Why was my guess rejected?
faq.a: Only the 232 words on the list are accepted, and they are the same 232 the answer is drawn from. If it was refused it could not have been the answer, which is worth knowing.

faq.q: Can I play more than once a day?
faq.a: Yes. The practice button deals a random word from the same list, as often as you like. Practice rounds do not count towards the streak, which is the point of keeping them separate.

faq.q: What happens if I close the tab halfway through?
faq.a: The guesses you have already submitted are saved on this device and come back when you return, as long as it is still the same day where you are.

faq.q: I am colour-blind. Can I tell the tiles apart?
faq.a: Amber tiles carry a diagonal stripe as well as the colour, and every tile is announced with its state — "T, wrong place" — so a screen reader gives the full result without any colour at all.

faq.q: What do the warnings mean?
faq.a: A smell means the wumpus is in one of the three rooms next to you. A draught means a bottomless pit. Wings mean giant bats, which will pick you up and drop you somewhere random.

faq.q: Can I map the cave?
faq.a: Yes, and that is how the game is meant to be played — with a pen. The room numbers are stable for the whole run.

faq.q: What happens if I miss?
faq.a: The noise usually wakes the wumpus and it moves to a neighbouring room, so a miss does not just cost an arrow, it invalidates your map.

faq.q: Is the internship really free?
faq.a: Yes — ₹0, always. No application fee, no training fee, no hidden charges. Seats are earned through selection, 2–3 per cohort. If anyone asks you to pay for an internship in my name, it is a scam — please report it to me directly.
faq.t: Two ways to work with me. Both end with real projects shipped.

faq.q: Can I pay my way into the internship instead?
faq.a: No. Joining the paid mentorship never converts into an internship title — the two tracks stay separate on purpose. That separation is what keeps both certificates worth something.
faq.t: Two ways to work with me. Both end with real projects shipped.

faq.q: How does selection work?
faq.a: A short application through the form below, then an interview. Commitment and curiosity matter more than what is already on your resume.
faq.t: Two ways to work with me. Both end with real projects shipped.

faq.q: What will my certificate actually say?
faq.a: Interns receive a certificate describing the real project work they shipped. Mentees receive a certificate stating they completed the mentorship program. Neither claims employment or a title that didn’t happen.
faq.t: Two ways to work with me. Both end with real projects shipped.

faq.q: Will my college accept this internship for credit?
faq.a: That is your college’s decision — every institution applies its own internship policy. I provide an offer letter, a completion certificate describing your actual project work, and I am available if your college wants to verify anything. Completion certificates can be checked instantly on the verification page; offer letters I confirm personally by email. To be safe, get approval from your training & placement cell or internship coordinator before you start.
faq.t: Two ways to work with me. Both end with real projects shipped.

faq.q: What does the ₹4,999/month mentorship include?
faq.a: Weekly 1:1 sessions, a personal learning roadmap, portfolio projects we scope together, code review, and interview preparation. Billing is month to month and you can cancel anytime.
faq.t: Two ways to work with me. Both end with real projects shipped.

faq.q: How do payments work?
faq.a: Month to month. Students in India pay ₹4,999/month via UPI; international students pay $120/month via Wise. Once we confirm your plan on WhatsApp, I share the payment QR or account details with you personally. I never post payment links, QR codes, or account details publicly — if you see one claiming to be me, it is fake; please report it to me directly.
faq.t: Two ways to work with me. Both end with real projects shipped.

faq.q: What if the first session isn’t what I expected?
faq.a: Say so within the first seven days of your first month and that month’s fee is refunded in full — no forms, no argument. The details are in the Refund Policy.
faq.t: Two ways to work with me. Both end with real projects shipped.

faq.q: Are scholarships available?
faq.a: Yes — a limited number each month, up to 50% off, based on need and merit. Request one in your application and we’ll discuss it in the interview.
faq.t: Two ways to work with me. Both end with real projects shipped.

faq.q: Can I bring my own project idea?
faq.a: Absolutely. The tracks are open — pick the area that excites you most or bring your own idea, and we will shape the work around where you want to go.
faq.t: Two ways to work with me. Both end with real projects shipped.

faq.q: I’m from a company — do you train teams?
faq.a: Yes, but not through this page. Both tracks here are for individuals; training a company team is a separate paid service with its own scope and pricing. See corporate training on the services page.
faq.t: Two ways to work with me. Both end with real projects shipped.

faq.q: Which algorithms are included?
faq.a: Twenty-one in total. Thirteen sorts: quicksort, merge sort, heap sort, shell sort, comb sort, cocktail shaker sort, gnome sort, odd-even sort, insertion sort, selection sort, bubble sort, counting sort and radix sort (LSD). Two array searches: linear and binary. Six pathfinders: breadth-first search, depth-first search, Dijkstra, A*, greedy best-first and bidirectional BFS.

faq.q: How do I run two algorithms side by side?
faq.a: Set Compare to two. Two more dropdowns appear, one for each side, and Play then runs both in their own panel on exactly the same input - the same array, the same search target, the same board - stepping in lockstep, so the counters are the only thing that differs. Leave Compare on none and it visualises the single chosen algorithm across the full width. All three modes have the control, and picking the same algorithm on both sides is allowed: two identical panels finishing together is the cheapest demonstration there is that these runs are deterministic.

faq.q: Why is the array in searching mode always sorted?
faq.a: Because binary search needs it to be. Halving the range you still have to consider is only sound if the values are in order; on unsorted data binary search is not slow, it is wrong. Linear search does not care, and that is the trade the side-by-side puts on screen: on 300 sorted values with the target in the last slot, linear needs all 300 probes and binary needs 9 - but binary only gets to do that because someone sorted the array first.

faq.q: Why are counting sort and radix sort so much faster to watch?
faq.a: Because they are not comparison sorts. Instead of comparing pairs of values they bucket by the value itself, which is why they can beat the O(n log n) barrier - at the cost of only working on integer keys in a known range, which is exactly what the bars here are.

faq.q: Can I draw my own maze?
faq.a: Yes. In pathfinding mode, drag on the grid to paint or erase walls, and drag the start and end cells to reposition them. There are also generators for random walls and a perfect maze.

faq.q: Can I step through one operation at a time?
faq.a: Yes. Pause, then use the arrow keys to move one operation forward or back - the whole run is recorded, so stepping in either direction is instant.

faq.q: Is it accurate to the real algorithms?
faq.a: Yes. Each animation is driven by the real algorithm running on the data and recording its actual comparisons and swaps; the visualisation replays those exact operations.

faq.q: Does it run on my machine?
faq.a: Entirely. It is canvas and JavaScript in your browser, with no server and no network call.

faq.q: Why does ls lose its colours when I pipe it into cat?
faq.a: Because ls checks isatty on standard output before it emits any colour. Piped or redirected, stdout is a pipe or a file rather than a terminal, so a well-behaved program turns colour off. Nothing swallowed it — the escape sequences were never written. Passing --color=always overrides the check and writes them anyway.

faq.q: I used --color=always and now my file is full of [01;34m. What is that?
faq.a: Those are the escape sequences themselves, sitting in the file as literal bytes. Each starts with a real 0x1B byte, which is invisible in most viewers, so you see the [01;34m and not the ESC in front of it. Paste a line into the decoder here and it will name every one, with its standard and its effect.

faq.q: How do I turn colour off for everything?
faq.a: Set NO_COLOR. The rule from no-color.org is that the variable's presence disables colour whatever its value is, so even an empty NO_COLOR= counts as set. The neighbouring conventions are older and less consistent: CLICOLOR=0 disables, CLICOLOR_FORCE=1 forces colour on even when output is not a terminal, TERM=dumb tells a program the terminal can do nothing, and FORCE_COLOR is honoured by a lot of Node tooling. Support for each is per-program.

faq.q: Is running cat on an untrusted log file actually dangerous?
faq.a: It is a real risk rather than a theoretical one. Cursor movement and erase let bytes in the file rewrite lines already on your screen, so a log entry can be made to lie about what happened. OSC can change the window title, and OSC 52 can write your clipboard, so the next thing you paste into a root shell is the attacker's. Several terminal emulators have also had memory-safety bugs in their OSC and DCS handlers. The sanitiser here shows you what is in a file before you let a terminal act on it.

faq.q: Does less -R make it safe?
faq.a: No. The whole point of -R is to pass colour sequences through to the terminal, which means it passes the sequence through, and -r passes everything. Plain less with no flags is reasonable because it displays ESC[ instead of obeying it, and cat -v is closer to a safety measure because it makes every control byte visible. Neither is a security boundary. The durable fix is to strip control characters where the log is written, not where it is read.

faq.q: Why does my escape sequence work in bash but not in sh?
faq.a: Usually two separate reasons. echo -e is not POSIX: bash and zsh builtins honour it, dash prints a literal -e, and /bin/echo differs again, so printf is the portable choice. And the backslash-e shorthand is a GNU extension, while backslash-033, the octal form, works everywhere. The builder here prints both command lines side by side so you can see the difference.

faq.q: Why do some requests fail here but work in Postman?
faq.a: Because a browser enforces CORS and Postman is not a browser. A browser will only hand a cross-origin response back to a page when the server sends an Access-Control-Allow-Origin header permitting it. curl and Postman have no such rule. So a failure here usually means the API has not opted in to browser access - not that the API is down.

faq.q: Does my request go through your server?
faq.a: No. The request goes from your browser straight to the address you typed. There is no proxy and no relay here, which is also why CORS applies - a proxy is exactly how other online API testers work around it, and running one would mean your requests, headers and tokens passing through someone else's machine.

faq.q: Is it safe to paste an API key?
faq.a: Your key is used only to build the request your browser sends, and it is never stored or transmitted anywhere else. That said, treat any key you paste into any web page as one that could be exposed - use a test key where you can, and revoke anything you would not want in a browser's memory.

faq.q: Which methods are supported?
faq.a: GET, POST, PUT, PATCH, DELETE, HEAD and OPTIONS. Bodies are sent for everything except GET and HEAD, which is what the HTTP spec expects.

faq.q: Why can I only see a few response headers?
faq.a: Another CORS rule: a cross-origin response exposes only a small safelist of headers unless the server names more in Access-Control-Expose-Headers. Same-origin requests show everything.

faq.q: Can I test an http:// endpoint?
faq.a: Not from here. This page is served over HTTPS, and browsers block mixed content, so a plain-HTTP request is refused before it is sent. Local development over http://localhost is the usual exception, but only from a page that is itself on localhost.

faq.q: Does it extract or run the archive?
faq.a: No. It reads the ZIP index structures only - never decompressing a byte and never executing anything - which is what makes it safe for a file you do not trust.

faq.q: What is zip slip?
faq.a: A path-traversal vulnerability where an archive entry uses ../ to write outside the intended directory during extraction. This tool flags any such entry so you know before you extract.

faq.q: How does it detect a zip bomb?
faq.a: By comparing declared uncompressed sizes to the compressed size. A ratio over about 100:1 is suspicious and over 1000:1 is almost certainly a bomb; the tool reports both the per-entry and whole-archive figures.

faq.q: Is my archive uploaded?
faq.a: No. It is parsed in your browser with no server involved.

faq.q: Does it work on .docx or .jar files?
faq.a: Yes. Those are ZIP archives, so the listing works, and it notes Office documents and flags macro files (vbaProject.bin) inside them.

faq.q: Are these numbers real, or a canned animation?
faq.a: They are real. Every point on the chart is a timing taken on this device, in this tab, seconds ago: the algorithm runs over a ladder of growing input sizes, each size is measured several times, and the median is plotted. Nothing is precomputed and nothing is fetched. Close the page and the numbers are gone.

faq.q: Why does the slope of the line matter so much?
faq.a: Because on log-log axes a power law is a straight line whose slope is the exponent. A curve that measures slope 1 is linear, slope 2 is quadratic, and slope 1.1 is n log n wearing a disguise. It turns a question about asymptotics into something you read off a picture with a ruler, which is the one thing a table of complexity classes cannot do for you.

faq.q: Why does it sometimes disagree with the textbook?
faq.a: Usually because the range is too short to prove what the textbook is claiming. Between five hundred and a hundred thousand elements the log in n log n only grows by about half, and if the algorithm is fast that difference sits under the measurement noise, so O(n) and O(n log n) both fit. The verdict says so rather than picking a winner. The other common reason is the memory hierarchy: a genuinely constant-time array index gets slower as the array outgrows cache, and that curve is real even though the operation count never changed.

faq.q: What are the warm-up runs and the median for?
faq.a: A JavaScript engine runs new code in a slow tier and only optimises it once it has seen it run hot, so the first few executions are not representative and are thrown away. The median is there because a garbage collection or another tab waking up can triple a single sample, and one bad sample would drag an average. The chart draws a whisker from the fastest to the slowest run of each cell, so you can see the noise instead of taking my word for it.

faq.q: Does insertion sort really beat merge sort?
faq.a: Below a threshold, yes, and you can measure where. Insertion sort is one tight loop with no allocation and no recursion, and for a small array that beats an algorithm doing asymptotically less work. This is not trivia: V8 sorts short runs with binary insertion sort inside its TimSort, and libstdc++ stops recursing at sixteen elements and finishes with a single insertion-sort pass. The thresholds in those libraries are the crossover you just measured, decided once by somebody running this same experiment.

faq.q: Why does the page not freeze while it is measuring?
faq.a: Because the unit of work is one timed repetition, not one algorithm. Each repetition is scheduled as its own task, so between any two of them the browser gets to paint, scroll and notice that you pressed Stop. A single run that passes a 140 millisecond budget also stops its ladder climbing any further, which is why bubble sort gives up earlier than insertion sort on a slower machine, and the panel says when that has happened.

faq.q: Will I get the same numbers you did?
faq.a: No, and you will not get the same numbers twice in a row either. The absolute times depend on your CPU, your browser, your battery state and whatever else is running. What should survive all of that is the shape: the slopes, the ordering of the curves and roughly where two of them cross. If the shape comes out different on your machine I would genuinely like to hear about it.

faq.q: Is it really free, with no watermark?
faq.a: Yes. No account, no watermark, no paid templates, no export limit. The page does the whole job in your browser and the print dialog is the export.

faq.q: Is my data uploaded anywhere?
faq.a: No. There is no server behind this page, so there is nothing to upload to. That matters more here than on most tools: a biodata carries a date and time of birth, a home address, an income figure and a photograph on one sheet - exactly the set of details used for identity theft and fake matrimonial profiles. Here they go from the form to the sheet inside your own browser, and nothing leaves it.

faq.q: How do I get a PDF?
faq.a: Press Print / Save as PDF, and in the browser's print dialog choose "Save as PDF" as the destination. The page prints only the biodata sheet - no site header, no buttons - sized to A4. A paper printer works the same way.

faq.q: Will my data still be here tomorrow?
faq.a: No - and on this form that is exactly the point. A biodata carries a date and time of birth, an income figure, a home address and a photograph on one sheet, and none of it is written to this device. The draft lives in the page's memory for that one session, so closing or reloading the tab clears it, and the shared computer at the print shop keeps nothing after you walk away. The trade is that you have to keep a copy on purpose: press "Download data" before you leave and you get a biodata-data.json file you own, and "Load data" brings it back here or on any other device. "Clear everything" empties the form and the sheet on the spot.

faq.q: Can I use my own photo?
faq.a: Yes. The photo is read from your device, resized in the browser to a sensible size, and placed on the sheet. It is never uploaded - it goes from your file picker to the page and nowhere else, and every template is designed to look right with or without one.

faq.q: Can the biodata be in Hindi or Gujarati?
faq.a: Yes. The Labels toggle in the toolbar switches every heading and field label printed on the sheet - जन्म तिथि instead of Date of birth - between English, Hindi and Gujarati, while the form you fill stays in English. And whatever you type prints exactly as you typed it, so values written in any language appear on the sheet in that language.

faq.q: Can I move my biodata to another device?
faq.a: Yes. Download data (.json) saves everything - every field, the photo, the template and the label language - into one file on your device, and Load data brings it back in any other browser or on any other computer. The file travels however you choose to carry it; the tool itself still sends nothing anywhere.

faq.q: Does it work offline?
faq.a: Yes, after the first visit. A small service worker keeps a copy in your browser, so the maker opens, renders and prints without a connection. Fitting, for a tool whose whole point is that no connection is ever used.

faq.q: Why does a biodata maker need a privacy story?
faq.a: Because this one page carries a date of birth, a birth time, a home address, an income and a photo: everything an identity thief or a scam matrimonial profile needs, assembled and formatted. Most free biodata sites receive all of it on their servers before showing a watermarked preview. A tool with no server is the only kind that cannot leak it. I have written up exactly what a marriage biodata leaks, field by field, in a separate post.

faq.q: Is my password sent to the server?
faq.a: No. Your password is hashed in your browser and only the first five characters of that hash are transmitted. The full hash and the password itself never leave the tab, and the comparison is done locally after the response arrives.

faq.q: Why SHA-1, which is broken?
faq.a: Because that is the protocol Have I Been Pwned defines, and it is not being relied on for security here - it is an index into a public dataset. Nothing is being protected by the hash; the privacy comes from only sending part of it.

faq.q: What does the padding option do?
faq.a: It asks the server to pad the response with decoy entries so every reply is a similar size. Without it, someone watching your encrypted traffic could infer which prefix you asked for from the response length alone.

faq.q: Should I type my real password in?
faq.a: That is your call, and the design is what makes it defensible rather than any assurance from me. If you would rather not, check an old password you have stopped using - the result is usually instructive.

faq.q: It says my password was found thousands of times. What do I do?
faq.a: Stop using it everywhere, starting with any account that matters, and turn on two-factor authentication. If you reused it across sites, change it on all of them.

faq.q: Is this macOS?
faq.a: No, and nothing in a browser can be. macOS is licensed to Apple hardware and cannot be redistributed, and this emulator is a 32-bit PC that could not boot it regardless. What this is instead is real BSD - and the macOS command line is BSD underneath, which is why the same commands behave subtly differently on a Mac than on Linux.
faq.t: A real BSD shell, running in your browser

faq.q: So what is actually running?
faq.a: OpenBSD, booted from its 1.4 MB install floppy. A genuine OpenBSD kernel probes the hardware and hands you a real ksh. It is the installer’s rescue environment, not a full system - see the next answer before you plan anything around it.
faq.t: A real BSD shell, running in your browser

faq.q: Which commands are available?
faq.a: Nineteen, and that is the honest number: cat, chgrp, chmod, cp, cpio, dd, df, ed, ksh, ln, ls, mkdir, mv, pax, rm, sh, sleep, stty and tar. There is no grep, no sed, no awk, and no uname - an install ramdisk carries only what the installer itself needs. If you want a full command line, the Linux terminal has 227 BusyBox applets.
faq.t: A real BSD shell, running in your browser

faq.q: Then why is it here at all?
faq.a: Because ls, ksh, pax and ed here are the BSD implementations, not the GNU ones, and the differences are real: BSD ls takes -G for colour where GNU takes --color, BSD ed and pax predate their GNU counterparts entirely. If you have ever hit a shell script that works on Linux and fails on a Mac, this is the family of reasons why.
faq.t: A real BSD shell, running in your browser

faq.q: Why does it drop me straight into a shell?
faq.a: The installer asks “(I)nstall, (U)pgrade or (S)hell?” and waits. S is chosen for you, because the other two would start partitioning a disk, which is not what anyone came here for.
faq.t: A real BSD shell, running in your browser

faq.q: Does it have internet access?
faq.a: No. No network device is attached, so nothing inside can reach anything outside.
faq.t: A real BSD shell, running in your browser

faq.q: Do my files survive a reload?
faq.a: No. The ramdisk lives in memory and is gone when the page unloads. Every boot is identical.
faq.t: A real BSD shell, running in your browser

faq.q: Does any of this touch a server?
faq.a: Only to download the 1.4 MB floppy image the first time. After that it is cached and the machine runs entirely on your own processor.
faq.t: A real BSD shell, running in your browser

faq.q: Is this a real exploit?
faq.a: No. It is a diagram of one. The stack is an array of bytes at pretend addresses, the overflow is a write past the end of that array, and “jump to shellcode” moves a number that represents the instruction pointer. Nothing is compiled and nothing is executed — it could not be, running as arithmetic in a sandboxed browser tab.
faq.t: Stack buffer overflow, byte by byte

faq.q: Why does the copy write upward into the return address?
faq.a: Because that is the real memory layout. The stack grows toward lower addresses, so a local buffer is at the lowest addresses of the frame and the saved return address is above it. A C string is laid out from low address to high, so copying into the buffer writes toward — and eventually over — the return address.
faq.t: Stack buffer overflow, byte by byte

faq.q: Do buffer overflows still matter in 2026?
faq.a: Yes.
