They are less common in memory-safe languages, but C and C++ still run most operating systems, browsers and embedded devices, and memory-safety bugs remain among the most exploited vulnerability classes every year. The mitigations shown here are why they are harder to exploit than they were, not why they have gone away.
faq.t: Stack buffer overflow, byte by byte

faq.q: What actually stops these?
faq.a: Layered mitigations raise the cost: stack canaries, non-executable memory (NX/DEP) and address randomisation (ASLR), plus compiler and hardware features beyond this lab. The complete fix is a memory-safe language - Rust, Go, Java, Python - which makes the out-of-bounds write impossible rather than merely survivable.
faq.t: Stack buffer overflow, byte by byte

faq.q: Is anything uploaded?
faq.a: No. The whole model runs in your tab and there is no network request. It is a teaching diagram of a vulnerability class, built for defenders and students, not an attack tool.
faq.t: Stack buffer overflow, byte by byte

faq.q: Is this a real C compiler?
faq.a: Yes. It is clang, compiled to WebAssembly, with lld doing the linking against a real libc. Your code is genuinely compiled to a binary and executed — not interpreted, and not approximated.

faq.q: Why is the first run so much slower?
faq.a: The download is about 19 MB compressed, once. It unpacks to roughly 58 MB in the browser cache, so later runs compile in about a second and a half, and it then works with no connection.

faq.q: Do structs, malloc and pointers work?
faq.a: All of them, exactly as they do locally — that is the point of using a real compiler rather than an interpreter.

faq.q: How do I give input to scanf?
faq.a: Put each value on its own line in the Input panel below the output, before pressing Run. The program reads them in order.

faq.q: Can I split my program across several files?
faq.a: Not currently — a single source file is compiled and linked. Everything has to be in the one editor.

faq.q: Does my C code get uploaded anywhere?
faq.a: No. The compiler, the linker and your program all run inside your browser tab. There is no build server, so there is nothing to send anything to.

faq.q: Is this talking to a real database?
faq.a: No. There is no cluster and no network request of any kind. The five replicas, the ten links and the round-trip times are a model running in your tab. What is real is the arithmetic: components come from a traversal, quorum verdicts from counting replicas, and the R + W > N verdict from enumerating every read set and every write set and testing whether all the pairs intersect.

faq.q: So is pick two of three simply wrong?
faq.a: It is a slogan rather than the theorem. Partition tolerance is not optional on a real network, so there is no meaningful CA choice to make. What Gilbert and Lynch proved is that when messages can be lost, you cannot have both linearizable consistency and a non-error response from every non-failing node. That is a statement about behaviour during a partition, and it says nothing about the rest of the time.

faq.q: Does choosing CP mean my database goes down?
faq.a: No. It means the minority side of a partition returns an error for the affected keys, for the duration of that partition. The processes stay up. Spanner is a CP system and its own authors argue its availability is high enough in practice that users treat it as always up. Read CP as refuses rather than as down.

faq.q: What does R + W > N actually promise?
faq.a: That any read set and any write set of those sizes share at least one replica, so a read cannot miss a write that has already completed. The sandbox proves it by enumeration rather than asserting it. It is weaker than it looks: it says nothing about writes still in flight, a partly failed write is not rolled back, sloppy quorums count acknowledgements from outside the preference list, and concurrent writes still need resolving. Quorums buy staleness bounds, not linearizability.

faq.q: Why is last write wins a problem?
faq.a: Because last is decided by a clock, and the nodes do not share one. Set the clock skew slider, make two concurrent writes on either side of a partition, and watch the rule hand the key to the older one. Nothing raises an error: the losing write returned success to its client and then vanished. Version vectors can tell you the writes were concurrent; they cannot tell you which came first, because nothing can.

faq.q: What is PACELC and why does it matter more?
faq.a: PACELC adds the half CAP leaves out: if Partitioned, choose Availability or Consistency, Else choose Latency or Consistency. With no partition at all a replicated store still has to decide whether to wait for more acknowledgements or reply early. That decision is made on every single request, and partitions happen a handful of times a year, so for most systems the else half is the one that shapes the design.

faq.q: Do I need OpenSSL to use this?
faq.a: No, that is the point. Paste the PEM block and it is parsed in your browser. OpenSSL is still the better tool when you have it - this is for when you do not.

faq.q: Is my certificate uploaded?
faq.a: No. It is base64-decoded and parsed in the page. A public certificate is not secret, but a certificate from an internal PKI leaks your internal hostnames, and those go in the same paste box.

faq.q: Can it check whether the certificate is trusted?
faq.a: No. Chain validation and revocation checking both need network lookups. This reads what the certificate contains and whether it is currently within its validity window.

faq.q: What if I paste a private key by mistake?
faq.a: The tool detects it, refuses to parse it, and says so. Nothing is transmitted either way - this page has no network code - but treat any private key that has been in a clipboard as worth rotating.

faq.q: How do I get a certificate from a live site?
faq.a: Either export it from the padlock icon in your browser, or run: openssl s_client -connect example.com:443 </dev/null | openssl x509 -outform PEM

faq.q: Are these real certificates?
faq.a: Yes. The keypair is generated by WebCrypto in your browser, and the certificate is signed with it and encoded as genuine ASN.1/DER. Paste the PEM into openssl x509 -text -noout and it parses; the signature verifies against the public key. The build is even tested by handing its output to a real X.509 parser.
faq.t: Build a real certificate, byte by byte

faq.q: Is my private key safe?
faq.a: The key never leaves your browser - there is no upload and no network request. That said, this is a learning tool: for a certificate that protects something real, generate the key with tooling you can audit and manage the private key properly. The page says so where it matters.
faq.t: Build a real certificate, byte by byte

faq.q: Can I actually use a certificate from here?
faq.a: You can use it anywhere a self-signed certificate is appropriate - a local development server, a test environment, an internal tool - by adding it to the relevant trust store. For a public website you need a certificate authority to sign it, which is what the CSR tab is for.
faq.t: Build a real certificate, byte by byte

faq.q: RSA or ECDSA - which should I pick?
faq.a: ECDSA P-256 for anything new: the keys and signatures are far smaller for the same security, which is why modern deployments prefer it. RSA-2048 is still everywhere and worth seeing for comparison - notice how much larger its certificate is.
faq.t: Build a real certificate, byte by byte

faq.q: Is anything uploaded?
faq.a: No. Key generation, signing, verification and encoding all happen in your tab. WebCrypto is local computation, not a network service, and nothing here opens a connection.
faq.t: Build a real certificate, byte by byte

faq.q: Do my messages go through your server?
faq.a: No. There is no server here to go through — the two browsers hold the connection directly, and no message is written anywhere. The only outside contact the chat itself makes is to a STUN server, which answers what public address you appear to come from and never sees a message. The page also loads analytics, like every page on this site: it records that a connection happened and whether a call was voice or video, never anything you sent.
faq.t: Peer-to-peer chat, and why a browser cannot listen on a port

faq.q: Why is the code so long?
faq.a: Because it has to carry everything the other browser needs to reach you: the ICE credentials, the fingerprint of your certificate, and up to eight of the addresses you might be reachable at. The page already drops the boilerplate lines of the handshake that do not vary between connections, and sends only the parts that do. Most of what is left is cryptographic randomness, which no encoding compresses. A short code would have to be looked up somewhere, and there is nowhere to look it up.
faq.t: Peer-to-peer chat, and why a browser cannot listen on a port

faq.q: Why does it say “Could not connect”?
faq.a: Both sides gathered addresses and no pair of them could reach the other, which usually means a strict NAT on one of the two networks. The fix is a TURN server that forwards the traffic on your behalf, and running one costs real money, so this lab does not have one. Put both machines on the same wifi, or try one of them on a different network. The page says so rather than spinning, because there is nothing else it can honestly do.
faq.t: Peer-to-peer chat, and why a browser cannot listen on a port

faq.q: How big a file can I send?
faq.a: That is the receiver's decision, not yours. When they press Accept, Chrome and Edge open a save dialog and write each chunk straight to disk, so the ceiling is their free space rather than their memory. Firefox and Safari have no such dialog, so they hold the file in memory and decline anything over 512 MB the moment it is offered, instead of accepting it and dying halfway through. Accept is a button because the save dialog will only open from a real click.
faq.t: Peer-to-peer chat, and why a browser cannot listen on a port

faq.q: Can more than two people join?
faq.a: Yes, for text. Everyone connects to the host and the host repeats what it receives, so each extra person is one more code exchange with the host and none with anybody else. That also means the host sees every message, since it is the thing doing the repeating. Voice and video stay one to one, because a browser cannot forward someone else's stream without decoding and re-encoding it, and that is the job a media server exists to do.
faq.t: Peer-to-peer chat, and why a browser cannot listen on a port

faq.q: Are these ciphers safe to use for real?
faq.a: Absolutely not. Every one of them is broken by the buttons on this page, without a key, in milliseconds. They are here for learning, for puzzles and for CTF challenges.

faq.q: What is ROT13?
faq.a: A Caesar cipher with a shift of 13. Because the alphabet has 26 letters, applying it twice returns the original - it is its own inverse. It was used on old forums to hide spoilers, not secrets.

faq.q: How does it break a Vigenere cipher without the key?
faq.a: It finds the key length using the index of coincidence, then treats each column of the ciphertext as a separate Caesar cipher and solves each with frequency analysis. The key is derived from the ciphertext alone.

faq.q: How much text does the automatic break need?
faq.a: Caesar needs very little. Vigenere needs at least 40 letters, and works better with more - statistical attacks need enough text for the statistics to mean anything.

faq.q: Is my text uploaded?
faq.a: No. Everything runs in your browser with no server involved.

faq.q: Is this a real compiler?
faq.a: It is a real front end and a real back end for a small language: a hand-written lexer, a recursive descent parser, a single-pass emitter and a stack machine that executes the bytecode. Nothing is handed to the browser's own compiler, and nothing is eval'd. What it is not is an optimiser, and it does not target a real processor - the machine it compiles for is the one running in the pane beside it.
faq.t: A compiler, and the machine it feeds

faq.q: Which language is this?
faq.a: One I defined for this page. It has numbers, strings, booleans, variables, arithmetic with the usual precedence, comparisons, if and else, while, functions with parameters and recursion, and print. That is enough to write fibonacci and greatest common divisor, which is enough to make the call frames worth watching.
faq.t: A compiler, and the machine it feeds

faq.q: Why bytecode instead of walking the tree?
faq.a: A tree-walking interpreter would be shorter and would hide the two things most worth seeing. Bytecode makes control flow explicit: a while loop becomes a jump backwards, an if becomes a jump forwards over the branch you did not take, and the instruction pointer has something to point at.
faq.t: A compiler, and the machine it feeds

faq.q: What happens when a program is wrong?
faq.a: A syntax error stops the pipeline where it broke and shows the offending line with a caret under the exact column. A runtime error stops the machine and shows the call stack as it stood at that instant, innermost frame first. Both come out of the same code paths the working case uses; neither is a canned message. Two of the example programs are broken on purpose so you can see each.
faq.t: A compiler, and the machine it feeds

faq.q: What is deliberately missing?
faq.a: Closures, objects, arrays, garbage collection, and any optimisation at all. Functions are declared at the top level and see only their own parameters and locals, so there is no environment chain to draw and no function values to pass around. Each of those is a chapter of its own, and adding them would bury the pipeline this page exists to show.
faq.t: A compiler, and the machine it feeds

faq.q: Why does it stop after so many instructions?
faq.a: Every step is recorded so that stepping backwards is exact rather than a re-simulation, and that record has to fit in memory. The machine stops at 25,000 instructions, at 64 call frames and at 512 values on the stack, and says which. An endless loop therefore ends as a message with the stack still readable rather than as a frozen tab.
faq.t: A compiler, and the machine it feeds

faq.q: Are these real threads?
faq.a: No, and I would rather say so on the front page than in a footnote. JavaScript is single-threaded; there is one array of program counters and a switch statement, and you are the scheduler. The model is also sequentially consistent, meaning every step is atomic and every write is visible instantly. A real machine gives you neither: stores get reordered, a value can sit invisible in a store buffer, and the compiler will hoist your load out of the loop. All of that makes real concurrency worse than this simulation, never better, which is the point. A sequentially consistent model is already enough to lose an update.
faq.t: Concurrency primitives, one step at a time

faq.q: Why does a semaphore with two permits still lose updates?
faq.a: Because two permits means two threads are allowed inside at the same time, and that is not a bug in the semaphore, it is the entire feature. A semaphore counts a resource. A mutex enforces exclusion. A semaphore of one happens to enforce exclusion as a side effect, which is why the two get confused. Set the permits to one in the semaphore tab and the lost updates stop; set it back to two and they return immediately.
faq.t: Concurrency primitives, one step at a time

faq.q: Is the percentage of bad interleavings a probability?
faq.a: No, and treating it as one would be worse than not having it. Every schedule counted is legal, and the count says nothing about which ones your machine is likely to produce. Real hardware favours long uninterrupted runs, which is exactly why the losing schedules are rare enough to reach production and common enough to hurt once they are there. The number is an upper bound on how much luck you are relying on, not an estimate of how much you have.
faq.t: Concurrency primitives, one step at a time

faq.q: Why is a timeout not a fix for deadlock?
faq.a: Because it does not remove the cycle, it survives one instance of it. Give up on a lock after 200 ms and the hang becomes a retry; if both threads retry they can collide again, and again, in step, which is livelock — every thread busy, no thread progressing. It also turns a deterministic failure you can reproduce into an intermittent one you cannot, which is a straight downgrade for whoever debugs it next. Ordering the locks removes the cycle, costs nothing at runtime and is checkable by reading the code.
faq.t: Concurrency primitives, one step at a time

faq.q: Does any of this apply to JavaScript?
faq.a: More than people expect. Web Workers plus a SharedArrayBuffer give you genuine shared memory and genuine data races, and Atomics exists precisely because of them. Even on one thread, anywhere execution can suspend and resume is a place another task can run and change the state you were holding, which produces the same read-then-stale-write shape without any parallelism at all. What single-threaded JavaScript buys you is that each step is atomic, which is exactly the friendly assumption this model makes.
faq.t: Concurrency primitives, one step at a time

faq.q: How is the interleaving table computed?
faq.a: By walking the whole tree. At every point it tries every thread that could run next, and every complete run is counted where it lands. Nothing is sampled and nothing is estimated. A blocked thread is modelled as one that cannot be chosen, so what is counted is distinct orders of progress. The search runs in your tab and stops at 600,000 schedules; when it stops, the row says so and prints the arithmetic upper bound rather than a smaller number that would be a lie.
faq.t: Concurrency primitives, one step at a time

faq.q: Is this the number an auditor will use?
faq.a: For WCAG 2.1 and 2.2, yes. Success criteria 1.4.3, 1.4.6 and 1.4.11 are all defined against this exact formula, and the page computes it straight through with no rounding until the last line. Where two checkers disagree it is almost never the arithmetic - it is that one of them guessed at a background the CSS never actually resolves to.
faq.t: Colour contrast, with the arithmetic shown

faq.q: Why is APCA here at all if it does not count?
faq.a: Because it explains failures you can already see. WCAG 2.x scores light-on-dark and dark-on-light identically, and anyone who has built a dark theme knows they do not look identical. APCA computes a different curve for each polarity, which matches that experience much better. It is still a draft method inside a draft standard, so I show the number and refuse to turn it into a pass or a fail.
faq.t: Colour contrast, with the arithmetic shown

faq.q: Can I be failed for ignoring the APCA score?
faq.a: No, and you cannot claim conformance with it either. WCAG 3 is a working draft with no target date, and APCA inside it is a candidate method that has already changed several times. Use it to argue about a dark theme with your designer. Conform against WCAG 2.2, and put that in the contract.
faq.t: Colour contrast, with the arithmetic shown

faq.q: Does passing 4.5:1 mean the text is readable?
faq.a: No. The formula takes two colours and nothing else. It never sees the typeface, the weight, the size beyond the large-text cut-off, the anti-aliasing, the panel, or the light in the room. Thin 300-weight text at 4.6:1 can be meaningfully harder to read than 600-weight at 4.3:1, and no contrast ratio can tell you that.
faq.t: Colour contrast, with the arithmetic shown

faq.q: Are the colour-blindness simulations accurate?
faq.a: They are the Machado, Oliveira and Fernandes matrices at full severity, applied in linear light, which is the usual way to do this and is still a model of dichromacy rather than a window into anyone's eyes. Most colour vision deficiency is anomalous rather than absent, so real people generally see more than these panels show. Use them to find meaning that is carried by hue alone, not as a rendering of somebody's experience.
faq.t: Colour contrast, with the arithmetic shown

faq.q: Is anything I paste uploaded?
faq.a: No. The header is parsed in your browser and nothing is sent anywhere — there is no server here to send it to. That matters more than usual for this tool, because the thing being pasted is often a live session cookie from a system you are responsible for.

faq.q: Why would a browser reject a cookie without telling me?
faq.a: Because the specification says to ignore, not to warn. A __Host- cookie with a Domain attribute, a __Secure- cookie without Secure, SameSite=None without Secure, a Domain that does not match the host: every one of those is dropped on the floor. Some browsers log a note in devtools, most of the time nobody is looking at it, and the server never learns anything. The symptom is a session that does not persist.

faq.q: Does SameSite=Lax mean I can drop my CSRF token?
faq.a: No, and this is worth being precise about. Lax still permits top-level cross-site GET navigation, so any state-changing GET is still exposed. It is a browser behaviour, so an old or unusual client can ignore it. Site means registrable domain, so a compromised sibling subdomain is same-site and unaffected. And Chromium shipped a carve-out letting a cross-site top-level POST through for very new cookies, published as temporary. Keep the token.

faq.q: What does Partitioned do to an embedded widget?
faq.a: It gives the widget a separate cookie jar per embedding site. Anything the widget remembers about one site keeps working. Anything that depended on recognising the same visitor across different embedding sites stops, permanently, and there is no attribute that restores it. If a widget needs identity across sites, that now has to be an explicit sign-in rather than a cookie.

faq.q: Max-Age or Expires — which one wins?
faq.a: Max-Age, always. It wins regardless of which appeared first in the header and regardless of which date is later; Expires is only consulted when Max-Age is absent or is not a plain integer. Max-Age is also the better attribute, because it is a duration rather than a date and does not depend on the visitor’s clock being right.

faq.q: What can this tool not tell me?
faq.a: A great deal. It reads the text you paste, so it cannot know whether your server really sent that, or what a framework or CDN rewrote on the way out. It cannot judge the value — a predictable session id is the worst thing a cookie can carry and the header never shows it. Browser behaviour also moves, so where a rule is in flux the output says so rather than quoting a version. The score is mine, not a standard, which is why every deduction is printed with its reason.

faq.q: Is this really clang, with the real STL?
faq.a: Yes. clang and lld are compiled to WebAssembly and linked against a genuine libc++. That is why std::vector, std::map and <algorithm> behave the way they do locally.

faq.q: Which C++ standard does it support?
faq.a: The sysroot is a C++17-era libc++. Everyday modern C++ — auto, lambdas, range-for, smart pointers, structured use of the STL — all works. Concepts, ranges and coroutines from C++20 do not.

faq.q: Why is the first run slow?
faq.a: clang and lld together are about 19 MB compressed to download, once, and unpack to roughly 58 MB in the browser cache. Later compiles take roughly a second and a half.

faq.q: How do I provide input to cin?
faq.a: Type the values into the Input panel below the output, one per line, before pressing Run. Each extraction reads the next one.

faq.q: Can I use Boost, or split across headers?
faq.a: No — a single source file is compiled, and only the standard library is available. There is no package manager and no network access.

faq.q: Is my C++ code private?
faq.a: Entirely. Compilation, linking and execution all happen inside your browser tab. No build server exists, so your code is never transmitted.

faq.q: Do I need to know assembly already?
faq.a: No. The instruction set is small and documented on the page, and the example programs show the patterns. Stepping through them is a good way to learn what assembly is.

faq.q: Is this a real CPU architecture?
faq.a: It is a small, clean teaching instruction set rather than x86 or ARM - the concepts (registers, flags, jumps, a stack, load/store) are exactly the same, without the decades of real-world complication.

faq.q: How does it run the code without eval?
faq.a: A two-pass assembler parses your source into an internal representation, and an interpreter executes that. No eval or new Function is used anywhere, which also satisfies the site's strict Content-Security-Policy.

faq.q: Can I watch memory and the stack?
faq.a: Yes. Registers, flags, a memory grid and the stack are all shown live, and cells that change on a step are highlighted.

faq.q: Does it run on my machine?
faq.a: Entirely in your browser. Nothing is uploaded.

faq.q: Is the arithmetic actually correct?
faq.a: Yes, and it is checked rather than claimed. AES is verified against the FIPS-197 Appendix B and C.1 vectors and the all-zero known-answer test; SHA-256 against the FIPS-180-4 examples. Those tests run against the same file the page loads, not a copy of it, so an animation of the wrong arithmetic would fail the build.

faq.q: Can I use this to encrypt something for real?
faq.a: No, and please do not. These are teaching implementations: no constant-time guarantees, no mode of operation, no padding, no key management. Use the WebCrypto API, which the browser implements in audited native code.

faq.q: Why does AES only encrypt one 16-byte block?
faq.a: Because that is what the AES cipher is. Encrypting anything longer needs a mode of operation - CBC, CTR, GCM - which is a separate decision with its own failure modes, and mixing it in here would hide the round function behind it.

faq.q: Why are the primes so small?
faq.a: So you can verify every step by hand and watch the attacks succeed. A real 2048-bit modulus would make the exchange identical in structure and impossible to follow, and the brute-force panel would simply never finish - which is the point being made.

faq.q: Is anything uploaded?
faq.a: No. Every byte is computed in your tab and there is no network request. Keys you type stay in the page, though since these are teaching implementations you should not be typing a real one anywhere.

faq.q: Does my policy or my markup get uploaded anywhere?
faq.a: No. Both are read in this tab and nothing is sent. The tool makes no network request of any kind — not to check a URL, not to fetch a script, not to look anything up. That is also why the four built-in policies are copied into the module as text rather than read from the live site.

faq.q: Is the markup I paste actually parsed, or just pattern-matched?
faq.a: Parsed, with the browser's own HTML parser through DOMParser. That document has no browsing context, which means scripts in it never run and images in it are never requested — so pasting a hostile page here is safe. Inline CSS is scanned separately for url() and @import, and inline scripts are scanned for literal URLs passed to the network APIs.

faq.q: Why does it say a directive is unknown when I copied it from a blog post?
faq.a: Most likely it was removed from the specification, or it was a typo in the post. Either way the outcome is the point: a browser ignores a directive name it does not recognise, usually without a console error, so a misspelled object-src protects nothing and looks identical to a working one. The tool suggests the nearest real directive name when the spelling is close.

faq.q: Does it tell me what my browser would really do?
faq.a: It implements the source-matching rules from CSP Level 3 that decide real policies: scheme, host with a leading wildcard, port, path prefix, 'self', scheme sources, nonces, hashes, 'strict-dynamic' and the fallback chain. It is not a browser. It does not follow redirects, which drop path matching in practice, and it has no model of sandbox, trusted-types or report grouping. Check anything surprising against a real browser's console.

faq.q: Why is script-src 'self' not enough on its own?
faq.a: Because 'self' means your whole origin, not your intended files. One JSONP endpoint, one open redirect that reaches one, one user-writable path, and an injected script tag pointing at your own host executes attacker-chosen code. The stronger shape is a per-response nonce with 'strict-dynamic', which ignores host and scheme sources entirely and admits only what you nonced plus what those scripts load themselves.

faq.q: What are the four policies in the dropdown?
faq.a: The real Content-Security-Policy headers this site ships, one per path rule, copied out of its vercel.json. Loading one prints what it is protecting and why. The strictest is the one on the HackLab guestbook: it is the only policy here that allows inline script, because it is a deliberate stored-XSS target, and it is the only one where connect-src, form-action and base-uri are all 'none' so the payload runs and has nowhere to send what it finds.

faq.q: Is searching CT logs legal?
faq.a: Yes. Certificate Transparency logs are public infrastructure, published deliberately so that anyone can audit certificate issuance. Reading them is the intended use.

faq.q: Does this scan or probe the domain?
faq.a: No. Not a single packet is sent to the domain. Everything comes from the log, which is why this leaves no trace in the target’s server logs.

faq.q: Why does it use Cert Spotter rather than crt.sh?
faq.a: crt.sh is better known but was timing out on every request while this was built. Cert Spotter is reliable and sends the CORS headers a browser needs.

faq.q: I found a subdomain that should not be public. What now?
faq.a: It cannot be unpublished - the log is append-only. What you can do is make sure the host behind it is properly secured, and use a wildcard certificate in future so individual internal names are not printed.

faq.q: Why do I see certificates I never requested?
faq.a: Most likely your CDN or hosting provider issued them on your behalf. If genuinely unexplained, that is precisely the mis-issuance CT was designed to surface.

faq.q: Is this the official CVSS formula?
faq.a: Yes. It implements the CVSS v3.1 base score equations published by FIRST, including the specification Roundup function, which is why the results match the official calculator exactly rather than being off by a decimal.

faq.q: What is the difference between CVSS 3.0 and 3.1?
faq.a: The metrics are identical. 3.1 clarified definitions and fixed the rounding function, which is where 3.0 implementations occasionally disagreed by 0.1.

faq.q: What about CVSS v4.0?
faq.a: It exists. FIRST published v4.0 in 2023, and it is a restructuring rather than a tweak: it adds Attack Requirements alongside Attack Complexity, splits the single impact triad into Vulnerable System impact (VC, VI, VA) and Subsequent System impact (SC, SI, SA), and reorganises the optional metrics into a Threat group that replaces Temporal and a reworked Environmental group. This calculator implements v3.1, which is still the version most advisories and CVE records carry, so paste v3.1 vectors here. A v4.0 string shares only some of its metric names with v3.1 and will not score correctly.

faq.q: Should I patch everything above 7.0 first?
faq.a: Not necessarily. CVSS does not know your environment. A high-scoring flaw in software you do not expose can wait behind a medium-scoring flaw on your perimeter. Use CVSS to compare, and exposure and exploitation data to prioritise.

faq.q: Can I load an existing vector string?
faq.a: Yes. Paste a CVSS:3.1/... string into the field and press Load vector; the dropdowns update and the score recalculates.

faq.q: Does this look up CVEs?
faq.a: No. It makes no network requests. Enter the metrics yourself, or paste the vector string from an advisory.

faq.q: Are these page counts real, or a formula?
faq.a: Counted. There is a 100,000-row table in three typed arrays, laid out into 8 KB heap pages, and there are real indexes over it built by a counting sort and packed into leaves. When a panel says the index read 462 pages, the tool walked the matching rows, asked which heap page each one lives on, and counted the reads. That is why switching the table to clustered order changes the number: nothing was estimated from a correlation coefficient, so nothing has to be re-estimated.
faq.t: How a database index actually works

faq.q: Is this PostgreSQL?
faq.a: No, and the difference matters. The page counting is real. The cost model on top of it is a cut-down version of PostgreSQL costsize.c: seq_page_cost, random_page_cost, cpu_tuple_cost, and the same square-root interpolation a bitmap heap scan uses for its heap pages. Real planners have more terms, better statistics and parallelism. So read the chosen plan as what this model prefers, not as what your database will do. If you want the real thing, the Postgres lab runs an actual server in your browser.
faq.t: How a database index actually works

faq.q: Why does the planner stop using my index?
faq.a: Because past a certain number of matching rows the index costs more than it saves. Following an index one row at a time means a seek per row, and on a table that is not physically ordered by that column those seeks land all over the heap. Once the query is going to touch most of the pages anyway, reading all of them straight through is cheaper, and the index becomes pure overhead on top. The last tab plots exactly where that happens on this table and lets you move random_page_cost to see the crossover shift.
faq.t: How a database index actually works

faq.q: What is the difference between an index scan and a bitmap heap scan?
faq.a: An index scan walks the index in key order and fetches each row as it finds it, so it re-reads the same heap page every time two matching rows happen to share one. A bitmap heap scan collects every matching row pointer first, sorts them into physical page order, and then reads each page exactly once. That is why the plain index scan dies so early on this table and the bitmap plan keeps winning to a much higher selectivity. The folklore that an index stops being used above about five percent is really a statement about the first of those two plans.
faq.t: How a database index actually works

faq.q: Why is the B+tree in the first tab only three or four keys wide?
faq.a: So a split fits on your screen. A real index page is 8 KB and holds hundreds of entries, which is why the table under the tree shows what the height does at production fan-out: a billion rows is four levels deep. At a fan-out of four the same billion rows would be fifteen levels, and every one of those levels is a page read. Drag the fan-out slider and the whole argument for short, fat trees is on screen in one move.
faq.t: How a database index actually works

faq.q: Does adding an index ever make things worse?
faq.a: Always, for writes. Every index has to be descended and its leaf written on every insert, and roughly one insert per leaf-full also splits that leaf and writes two more nodes. The first tab counts the nodes each operation touches and shows the running average, and the table underneath turns that into pages written per INSERT for one, two, three and four indexes. An index that no query uses is not free and not neutral. It is a tax on every write you will ever do.
faq.t: How a database index actually works

faq.q: Why does SELECT * matter so much here?
faq.a: Because it decides whether the table has to be opened at all. If every column you ask for is already in the index, the leaves answer the query on their own and the heap is never touched. Add one column the index does not hold and every matching row has to be fetched from the table. The covering tab lets you tick columns on and off with the WHERE clause held fixed, so you can watch the plan change from Index Only Scan to Index Scan and the page count jump, with nothing else different.
faq.t: How a database index actually works

faq.q: Does anything leave my browser?
faq.a: No. There is no server, no upload and no network request of any kind. The table, the indexes and the tree are built in this tab and gone when you close it. That is not a privacy footnote so much as a design constraint: the point of the exercise is that the counting happens somewhere you can check it.
faq.t: How a database index actually works

faq.q: Why does my diff say every line changed?
faq.a: Almost always line endings. One copy of the file uses CRLF and the other uses LF, so every line differs by a character you cannot see. Paste both sides here: if the text is otherwise identical, the report says so in exactly those words and gives the CRLF and LF counts per side. The other common causes are trailing whitespace and a missing final newline, and both are counted too.

faq.q: Does the whitespace toggle change the exported patch?
faq.a: No, and that is deliberate. The toggle changes what the view shows and the hunk counts it compares. The patch and the merge are always computed with whitespace respected, because a patch generated from an ignore-whitespace diff writes the wrong indentation into its context lines and will not apply. The report repeats this whenever the toggle is not set to respect whitespace.

faq.q: What counts as a conflict?
faq.a: A region of the base changed on both sides, to different text. If only one side changed it, that side wins. If both sides changed it to the same text, that applies cleanly too. Insertions are the awkward case, because they cover no base lines at all: an insertion collides with another edit only when it lands strictly inside that edit’s range, or at exactly the same point as another insertion.

faq.q: Will the patch it exports really apply?
faq.a: That was the point of writing it, and the hunk arithmetic was checked against real git apply while building it — including the awkward cases: an insertion at the top of a file, a deletion of everything, a one-line file, and a missing final newline on either or both sides. It writes ordinary unified diff with three lines of context, so git apply or patch -p1 should take it. The file name in the headers is yours to set.

faq.q: Why does a reformatted file look like a rewrite?
faq.a: Because this is line-oriented, and after a reformat almost no line is the same line any more. Ignoring whitespace helps when only the indentation moved; it cannot help when a formatter rewrapped the text, because then the lines genuinely are different lines. No whitespace mode fixes that, and this one does not pretend to.

faq.q: Is anything uploaded?
faq.a: No. There is no server to upload to. The text is read from the boxes on the page, compared in this tab, and any file you download is built here and handed back through a blob URL. That matters more than usual for this tool, because what people want to diff is very often unreleased source or a config file with credentials in it.

faq.q: How is this different from the email security audit?
faq.a: That one checks, this one authors. The audit queries public DNS for a domain you name and grades what is already published there. This page never touches DNS: it builds the record text you are going to publish, and reads the aggregate reports that come back once you have. Build here, publish, then audit.

faq.q: Why do I have to type in the lookup cost of an include?
faq.a: Because working it out honestly needs DNS, and this page has none. An include pulls in another record whose own terms count against your ten, so the true cost of include:_spf.google.com is not one. Rather than print a comfortable number I cannot stand behind, I ask you for it, label the total an estimate everywhere it appears, and say what it was based on.

faq.q: Will it generate a DKIM key pair for me?
faq.a: No, and that is a refusal rather than an omission. A private key generated by a web page is a key that page has seen, and there is no way for you to check from the outside that it was not kept or derived from a predictable seed. Generate it on a machine you control, or let your mail provider generate it and hand you only the public half.

faq.q: Can I paste the .gz file an aggregate report arrives as?
faq.a: No. Decompress it first and paste the XML from inside. The parsing is the hard part and the decompression is one command you already have, so the tool draws the line there rather than adding a decompressor it would then have to defend against malformed archives.

faq.q: Is any of this uploaded?
faq.a: No. There is no fetch and no XMLHttpRequest in the file, and no server behind the page to receive anything. That matters most for the report parser: an aggregate report lists every IP address on the internet sending mail as your domain, which is precisely the thing not to hand to a stranger’s website.

faq.q: If I build a record here, is my domain protected?
faq.a: Not until you publish it, and not by the record alone. The tool checks syntax, counts lookups from what you told it, and lays out a rollout — it cannot tell you that a name resolves, that a vendor still sends for you, or that one real message would pass. Publish it, wait for the reports, and read them before you tighten the policy.

faq.q: Does this use a proxy or a server of yours?
faq.a: No. Your browser makes the request directly to Google or Cloudflare. Nothing is relayed through me and I never see the query.

faq.q: Why can a web page not do a normal DNS lookup?
faq.a: Because DNS runs over UDP port 53 and browsers have no raw socket access. DNS-over-HTTPS exists precisely to make DNS reachable from environments like this one.

faq.q: Which resolver should I pick?
faq.a: Either works. Cloudflare states it does not log the querying IP to disk and purges logs quickly; Google retains some data. If you have a preference, the picker is there so you can act on it.

faq.q: Is the result cached?
faq.a: The resolver serves from its cache, so a TTL you see may be counting down from a lookup somebody else caused. Values fresh from the authoritative server show the full TTL.

faq.q: Why does the same domain give different answers?
faq.a: Large sites use geographic and load-based routing, so the answer legitimately depends on which resolver asked and from where.

faq.q: Are these sizes real?
faq.a: They are modelled estimates, and I would rather say that loudly than have you quote one in a meeting. Nothing here builds anything. The numbers come from tables in the tool: measured uncompressed sizes for the common base images, and typical installed sizes for the packages, wheels and dependency trees people actually install. They are close enough to tell you which line is costing you a gigabyte, and wrong enough that the only number worth trusting is the one docker images prints on your machine.

faq.q: Why is the base image bigger here than on Docker Hub?
faq.a: Because these are uncompressed sizes and the registry page shows the compressed download. node:20-alpine is about 55 MB to pull and about 135 MB once it is on your disk. Both numbers are true and they answer different questions: the compressed one is what your network pays, the uncompressed one is what your disk pays and what docker images reports.

faq.q: I delete the file on the very next line. Is it really still in the image?
faq.a: Yes. A layer is a diff and a diff can only add. The earlier layer is already committed, immutable, and possibly shared with other images, so a later layer cannot reach into it — all it can write is a whiteout marker saying the file is no longer visible. The bytes ship with the image. Anyone holding it can run docker save, untar the result, and read the layer blob with nothing more exotic than tar. The Union filesystem tab prints the exact commands. If a credential has ever been in a pushed layer, rotate it: squashing afterwards does nothing for anyone who already pulled.

faq.q: So why does chaining commands with && actually shrink the image?
faq.a: Because a file that is created and deleted inside one RUN never enters a committed layer at all. apt-get update writes 42 MB of package lists; if the rm -rf of those lists is a separate RUN, the 42 MB is already committed and you have bought a whiteout marker. Put update, install and the cleanup on one line joined with && and the layer is written once, without them. Load the Python example and look at the layer at line 7 to see the difference priced.

faq.q: Why does COPY package.json before COPY . . matter so much?
faq.a: The cache rule is one sentence: a step is reused only if every step before it was reused and its own inputs are unchanged, and for a COPY the inputs include a checksum of the files. Put COPY . . before the dependency install and every source edit changes that checksum, so the install runs again. Copy only the manifest first, install against it, then copy the source. In the two Node examples here that is the difference between a rebuild of about two minutes fifty and one of about forty-five seconds, on the same edit.

faq.q: Do ENV and ARG leak secrets?
faq.a: Yes, and this is the one that surprises people, because neither writes a byte to any layer. Both are stored in the image configuration that travels with the image, and docker history and docker inspect print them for anyone holding it. An ARG default counts too. Pass credentials at run time, or use RUN --mount=type=secret so the value exists during the build and is never part of the filesystem being committed.

faq.q: What does this tool not understand?
faq.a: Heredocs in RUN, which BuildKit supports and this parser does not. Character classes in glob patterns. Quoting, when it splits a shell command on && and ;. It also does not know your packages: an apt or apk package that is not in my size table is modelled at a flat default, and a command it does not recognise at all contributes zero and says so in that layer detail rather than inventing a plausible number. It checks nothing about known vulnerabilities, image signing or the runtime profile the container ends up with — those need a scanner and a running daemon, and this is a reading of one file.

faq.q: Is multi-stage always the answer?
faq.a: Not always, but it is the answer whenever the tools that build the thing are not the tools that run it. Go is the clearest case in the examples here: the build stage carries a compiler and a module cache and comes to about 1.1 GB, and the stage that ships carries a static binary on a distroless base and comes to about 16 MB. For an interpreted language the gap is smaller because the runtime has to ship anyway, and the win comes from leaving the compilers, headers and development dependencies behind instead.

faq.q: Does anything leave my browser?
faq.a: No. There is no server, no upload and no network request of any kind — not to a registry, not to a vulnerability database, not for a base image manifest. That is also why the sizes have to be modelled rather than looked up. Everything is in this tab and gone when you close it, and the page works with the network switched off once it is cached.

faq.q: Is this Windows, or the Windows command prompt?
faq.a: Neither, and it is worth being straight about that. Windows cannot be redistributed and is gigabytes in size, so no website can legitimately offer it. This is FreeDOS - a real, freely licensed operating system that is command-compatible with MS-DOS, which is the system cmd.exe descends from. If you want DIR, CD, COPY and batch files, this is the genuine article. If you need PowerShell or a Windows GUI, nothing in a browser can give you that.
faq.t: A real DOS prompt, running in your browser

faq.q: Is it a real operating system or a simulation?
faq.a: Real. v86 emulates a 32-bit x86 processor in WebAssembly and FreeDOS boots on it from an emulated floppy, exactly as it would on 1990s hardware. The file system, the command interpreter and the batch processor are FreeDOS's own.
faq.t: A real DOS prompt, running in your browser

faq.q: Which commands work?
faq.a: The DOS set: DIR, CD, MD, RD, COPY, DEL, REN, TYPE, MORE, CLS, DATE, TIME, VER, MEM, ATTRIB, FIND, SORT, XCOPY, EDIT and FDISK, plus batch files with ECHO, SET, IF, GOTO and FOR. This particular disk also carries VIM, the NASM assembler, DEBUG, and the games INVADERS, SNAKE and TETRIS. Type HELP for what the system itself reports, or DIR to see everything on the disk.
faq.t: A real DOS prompt, running in your browser

faq.q: Can I run old DOS games or programs?
faq.a: Not from here - there is no way to load a file from your computer into the emulated floppy, and the disk is read-only. For running your own DOS software, a local emulator such as DOSBox is the right tool.
faq.t: A real DOS prompt, running in your browser

faq.q: Does it have internet access?
faq.a: No. No network device is attached, so nothing inside can reach anything outside. That is deliberate.
faq.t: A real DOS prompt, running in your browser

faq.q: Do my files survive a reload?
faq.a: No. The disk image is read-only and memory is discarded when the page unloads, so every boot gives you an identical machine. Files you create with EDIT live only until you leave.
faq.t: A real DOS prompt, running in your browser

faq.q: Does any of this touch a server?
faq.a: Only to download the 720 KB disk image the first time. After that it is cached and the whole machine runs on your own processor. Nothing you type is transmitted anywhere.
faq.t: A real DOS prompt, running in your browser

faq.q: Where do I find the raw headers?
faq.a: Gmail: open the message, click the three-dot menu, choose "Show original". Outlook: File, Properties, then the Internet headers box. Apple Mail: View, Message, All Headers. Thunderbird: View, Headers, All.

faq.q: Are my headers uploaded?
faq.a: No. They are parsed in your browser. This matters more than usual here, because headers carry internal hostnames, IP addresses and recipient addresses - most popular header analysers are web services that receive all of it.

faq.q: Does SPF pass mean the email is safe?
faq.a: No. It means the sending server was authorised for that domain. An attacker who registers a lookalike domain gets SPF, DKIM and DMARC passes on their own domain. Authentication proves origin, not honesty.

faq.q: Can Received headers be faked?
faq.a: The ones added by servers you trust cannot, but a sender can inject fake ones before the message reaches those servers. Only the hops added after the message entered infrastructure you trust are reliable, which is why the timing checks matter.

faq.q: Why is the originating IP private?
faq.a: If the first hop shows a 10.x, 192.168.x or 172.16-31.x address, the message started inside a private network and the public IP appears at the next hop out.

faq.q: Does this send any email or touch their servers?
faq.a: No. It reads public DNS records, which is exactly what every receiving mail server does before accepting a message. Nothing is sent to the domain and no port is touched.

faq.q: Why does it say DKIM not found for a domain I know uses DKIM?
faq.a: Because DKIM selectors cannot be enumerated. The tool guesses sixteen common selectors; a domain using a custom one will show nothing. This is a limitation of DNS, not a bug.

faq.q: What does p=none actually protect against?
faq.a: Nothing. It only asks receivers to send reports. It is the correct first step while you find your legitimate senders, but a domain left at p=none indefinitely is unprotected.

faq.q: Is a passing audit a guarantee nobody can spoof the domain?
faq.a: It means direct spoofing of the exact domain is hard. It does nothing about lookalike domains, display-name spoofing, or compromised legitimate accounts.

faq.q: Can I audit a domain I do not own?
faq.a: Yes, and it is entirely legitimate: every record read here is public DNS that any mail server on the internet consults automatically.

faq.q: Is anything I type here sent anywhere?
faq.a: No. There is no server behind this page and no network call anywhere in the code: no upload, no lookup, no analytics on the numbers you enter. A loan amount, a salary and a tax slab are exactly the details people hand to a random website without thinking about it, and this one has nowhere to send them even if it wanted to. Close the tab and the numbers are gone.
faq.t: Loan EMI, and the four things the brochure stops short of

faq.q: Reduce the EMI or reduce the tenure, which should I pick?
faq.a: Cutting the tenure almost always saves more, often several times more, and the lab computes both on your own numbers so you can see the gap rather than take my word for it. The reason is that interest is charged on the balance, so a rupee taken off the balance early stops accruing interest for every month that was left. Cutting the EMI hands part of that saving back by keeping the debt alive for the full original term. The honest case for cutting the EMI is cash flow, not cost: a smaller instalment is what you want when the monthly payment is the thing straining.
faq.t: Loan EMI, and the four things the brochure stops short of

faq.q: My lender raised the rate and my EMI did not change. Is that good?
faq.a: It means the tenure moved instead, which is the default at almost every lender and needs no signature from you. It is not a favour. The same rise absorbed by a longer tenure costs considerably more in total interest than the same rise absorbed by a higher instalment, and the rate-change tab prices both on your loan. After any repricing, look at your statement for the field that actually changed.
faq.t: Loan EMI, and the four things the brochure stops short of

faq.q: Will my bank’s numbers match these exactly?
faq.a: The EMI will, to the rupee, because everybody uses the same annuity formula. The schedule can drift by a few rupees, because lenders differ on how they round, on whether interest is computed on a daily or a monthly reducing balance, and on what they do with the broken period between disbursal and your first instalment. Those gaps are small and they are not the point. The shape is the point. The sanction letter is the document that binds, not this page.
faq.t: Loan EMI, and the four things the brochure stops short of

faq.q: Why is the effective rate higher than the rate I was quoted?
faq.a: Because a fee is money you borrowed and never received. The effective rate here is the internal rate of return of the actual cashflow: what reached your account on day one, against what leaves it every month until the loan closes. Two loans can carry the same headline rate and different prices, and a loan with a lower rate and a larger fee is regularly the dearer of the two.
faq.t: Loan EMI, and the four things the brochure stops short of

faq.q: The total cost and the effective rate sometimes disagree. Which one is right?
faq.a: The effective rate, and the disagreement is worth understanding. Adding up rupees across twenty years treats money paid today and money paid in year nineteen as the same thing, and they are not. A fee is paid in full on day one; the interest it buys you out of arrives slowly. Discounting them, which is what the effective rate does, is the arithmetic your lender uses on its own side of the deal. The lab shows both figures and says so when they point different ways.
faq.t: Loan EMI, and the four things the brochure stops short of

faq.q: Can I trust the tax panel?
faq.a: Treat it as arithmetic, not advice. I am not a tax professional. The ceilings are written into the code, two lakh under section 24(b) for a self-occupied house and one and a half lakh under 80C, and budgets move those numbers. It also assumes the old regime, which has not been the default since FY 2023-24 and gives you neither deduction on a self-occupied house under the new one. Confirm every figure against the current year. What the panel is genuinely useful for is seeing which years the deduction is worth anything in, which are the early ones, where the interest is largest.
faq.t: Loan EMI, and the four things the brochure stops short of

faq.q: What is in the CSV export?
faq.a: Every instalment of whichever scenario you exported: the month, the opening balance, the payment, how that payment split between interest and principal, any extra you paid, and the closing balance. The numbers are written plain, with no currency symbol and no thousands separators, so a spreadsheet reads the columns as numbers rather than as text it has to be argued with. The file is assembled in your browser and handed over through a blob URL, so it is never uploaded anywhere.
faq.t: Loan EMI, and the four things the brochure stops short of

faq.q: Is base64 a form of encryption?
faq.a: No. It is an encoding with no key, and anyone can reverse it instantly - this page does it in one click. Never use it to protect anything.

faq.q: Is my data sent to a server?
faq.a: No. Every conversion is arithmetic performed in your browser. There is no server behind this page.

faq.q: What is the difference between Base64 and Base64url?
faq.a: The last two characters of the alphabet. Standard base64 uses + and /, base64url uses - and _ so the result is safe in a URL without further escaping. Base64url also usually omits the = padding.

faq.q: Why does my base64 fail to decode?
faq.a: Usually because the length is not a multiple of four, the padding was stripped, or it is actually base64url. The detector line above the result will tell you which.

faq.q: What is Base58 for?
faq.a: It is base64 with the visually confusable characters removed - no 0, O, I or l - which is why Bitcoin addresses and some short links use it.

faq.q: Is my photo uploaded?
faq.a: No. The file is read locally and, if you strip it, re-encoded locally. No network request is made. A tool that asked you to upload a photo in order to remove its GPS data would be a strange bargain.

faq.q: Why does my photo show no EXIF?
faq.a: Either it never had any, or something already removed it. Screenshots have almost none, and most social networks strip metadata when you upload. Photos straight from a camera roll are the ones that carry the most.

faq.q: Does stripping metadata reduce quality?
faq.a: Very slightly. The image is re-encoded as JPEG at high quality, so there is one extra generation of compression. For sharing purposes the difference is invisible.

faq.q: Can I see where the photo was taken on a map?
faq.a: The coordinates are shown so you can paste them into any map. Nothing here contacts a mapping service, because that would tell a third party the location you were checking.

faq.q: Does it handle PNG and HEIC?
faq.a: It reads any image the browser can decode and can strip metadata from all of them. The full EXIF block that phones write lives in JPEG, so that is where the detailed output appears.

faq.q: How does it know the file type?
faq.a: By the magic bytes - a short fixed signature at the start of the file. PDFs start with %PDF, PNGs with a 8-byte sequence ending in PNG, Windows executables with MZ, ZIP-based formats with PK. The tool checks against 33 of these signatures.
faq.t: File type inspector and hex viewer

faq.q: Can it detect a renamed executable?
faq.a: Yes, and it warns explicitly when the extension disagrees with the signature. That is the single most useful thing this tool does.
faq.t: File type inspector and hex viewer

faq.q: Is the file uploaded anywhere?
faq.a: No. It is read locally with the FileReader API and analysed in the page. There is no server and no network request, which is what makes it safe to point at something you do not trust.
faq.t: File type inspector and hex viewer

faq.q: What does high entropy mean?
faq.a: Close to 8 bits per byte means the data is compressed, encrypted or already packed. It is normal for a ZIP or a JPEG. It is more interesting inside a document or an executable, where it can indicate an embedded payload.
faq.t: File type inspector and hex viewer

faq.q: Will it open the file or run it?
faq.a: No. The bytes are read and analysed as data. Nothing is executed, and no embedded content is rendered.
faq.t: File type inspector and hex viewer

faq.q: Is my ruleset uploaded?
faq.a: No. It is parsed and simulated in your browser and nothing is sent anywhere — there is no server here to send it to. That matters more than usual for this one, because a firewall ruleset is a map of a network: internal ranges, which ports are open on which hosts, and which addresses are trusted.

faq.q: Which parts of iptables and nftables does it read?
faq.a: From iptables-save: the filter table, chain declarations and policies, -A and -I, -p, -s, -d, -i, -o, --sport, --dport, multiport, -m state and -m conntrack, --reject-with, and the ACCEPT, DROP, REJECT, RETURN, LOG, jump and goto targets. From nftables: table and chain blocks, type, hook, priority and policy, ip saddr and daddr, ip protocol, tcp and udp sport and dport including sets and ranges, ct state, iif, oif, iifname, oifname, meta l4proto, and accept, drop, reject, return, jump and goto. Anything outside that is named in the output rather than quietly skipped.

faq.q: It says a rule can never match, but that rule clearly works on my host.
faq.a: Two likely reasons, and both are printed. If the rule carries a match this model does not implement — --tcp-flags, a rate limit, an ipset, an ICMP type — the walk treats it as not matching and says so, because pretending it matched would be the worse lie. And if the report claims an earlier rule covers it, read the dimensions it lists: the comparison only knows protocol, addresses, ports, interfaces and conntrack state, so a rule narrowed by anything outside that list may well still be live. If you find a case where it is wrong, tell me.

faq.q: Why is my second packet still NEW?
faq.a: Because ESTABLISHED means the flow has been seen in both directions, not that conntrack holds an entry for it. The kernel sets the seen-reply bit only once traffic comes back, and this model does the same thing. Send the reply and the same packet becomes ESTABLISHED. It is also why the entry is created on ACCEPT and not before: a dropped packet leaves no confirmed entry behind.

faq.q: Should I use DROP or REJECT?
faq.a: REJECT inside a network you run and DROP at the edge is the usual answer, and neither is a security control on its own. DROP makes a scan slow and makes your own troubleshooting slow in precisely the same way, because silence is silence whoever is listening. REJECT fails fast, which is kind to your own services. And DROP hides nothing about a host that answers on any other port, so treating it as concealment is worth being sceptical about.

faq.q: What can this tool not tell me?
faq.a: A great deal. It is a simulator over a model, not netfilter. There is no NAT table, no mangle, no raw, no rate limiting, no ipset, no reverse-path filtering, no packet marks, no TCP flag matching, no IPv6, no routing decision, and no idea what your services are actually listening on. The conntrack table is a dictionary with no timeouts, no TCP state machine and no protocol helpers, so RELATED is a stand-in and INVALID is only ever something you set by hand. It tells you what this model of these rules does with this packet. Test the real thing before you trust it.

faq.q: How do I zoom and pan?
faq.a: Scroll or click to zoom toward the cursor, and drag to pan. The Reset button returns to the full view.

faq.q: What is the Julia set connection?
faq.a: Every point in the complex plane defines a Julia set, and the Mandelbrot set is a map of which ones are connected. Hover over the Mandelbrot to use that point as the Julia constant and watch the Julia set change.

faq.q: Why does it pixelate when I zoom far in?
faq.a: The GPU computes with single-precision floats, which run out of significant digits after a deep zoom. That is a hardware limit, not a bug - the tool says when you have reached it.

faq.q: Does it need a powerful computer?
faq.a: A modern browser with WebGL is enough. It renders on your GPU, so a decent graphics chip makes deep zooms smoother, but it works on integrated graphics too.

faq.q: Is anything uploaded?
faq.a: No. It all runs on your GPU in your browser.

faq.q: Are the hashes real?
faq.a: Yes, and that is the whole point. Every name you see is SHA-1 computed in your browser over the exact bytes git would hash — "blob \0 " for a file, the same for trees, commits and annotated tags. The Object store tab checks four published git constants at start-up, including git’s empty blob e69de29 and its empty tree 4b825dc, and says so out loud if any of them fails. I also built the same three files in a real repository with the same fixed author and date, and real git produced the same commit: fb34cc16e9c9673f876a1c4df9e7794238afc473. You can repeat that.

faq.q: Is this git, or a model of git?
faq.a: The object store is the real thing: real object bytes, real SHA-1, real content addressing, real parent pointers, real refs. The porcelain around it is a model, and it is smaller than git’s. Merge and rebase resolve per file rather than per hunk, so two edits to different parts of one file conflict here and would not in git. The merge base is the first common ancestor found breadth-first. There is no packfile, no zlib and no network. Everything I simplified is named on this page rather than hidden.

faq.q: Why does rebase change the hash when the files are identical?
faq.a: Because the files are not what gets hashed. A commit object contains its tree, its parent, an author line and a committer line, and the hash covers all of it. Rebase replays your change onto a different parent, so the parent line is different and the committer date is new — different bytes, therefore a different name, even when the tree hash is character-for-character the same. Run the "Rebase changes identity" walkthrough and look at the tree column: that is the demonstration.

faq.q: What does detached HEAD actually mean?
faq.a: HEAD is a file. Normally it contains the text "ref: refs/heads/main" — the name of a branch — which is why committing moves the branch and leaves HEAD alone. Detached means HEAD contains a commit hash directly instead. Nothing is broken and nothing is lost; you are standing on a commit that has no label. Check out a commit here and open the Refs & HEAD tab to see the file change.

faq.q: Can I lose work in here?
faq.a: Not permanently, which is also true of a real committed repository. Every command that changes anything gets an Undo button in the Reflog & undo tab, and undo rewinds the refs, the index and the working tree to just before it. Nothing ever deletes an object: a commit you reset away stays in the store, shows in the graph greyed out as unreferenced, and comes back with reset --hard HEAD@{1}. The only thing genuinely at risk, here and in git, is work you never committed.

faq.q: Why did adding the same content twice not write a second blob?
faq.a: Because a blob has no filename in it. A blob is content and a length, nothing else, so two files with byte-identical contents produce byte-identical object bytes and therefore the same hash — the store already has that name taken. The two paths live in the tree object, both pointing at the one blob. The shell says "reused 1 existing object" when this happens, and the object counter in the toolbar does not move.

faq.q: Why is the clock fixed?
faq.a: So the hashes are reproducible. The author is always "Toy User " and the clock starts at 1700000000 and advances a minute per commit, which means the same sequence of commands always gives the same hashes and you can reproduce them with real git. Real git uses your name and your system clock — which is exactly why two commits of identical content made a second apart still get different names.

faq.q: Does anything leave my browser?
faq.a: No. There is no server, no upload and no network request of any kind. The object store lives in this tab and is gone when you close it. That is not a privacy footnote here so much as a design constraint: the hashing had to be implemented locally for the lesson to be checkable.

faq.q: Does this file my GST return?
faq.a: No. It is a working sheet to check your own numbers against before you file. It does not file anything, it is not connected to the GST portal, it has no login and it makes no network call of any kind. It is also not a substitute for your accountant, and GST rules change with every finance act.

faq.q: Is my invoice data uploaded anywhere?
faq.a: No. The JSON files are read with a FileReader and the CSV never leaves the textarea. Everything is arithmetic in this tab. That matters here more than on most pages: this input is your entire customer list, your turnover and your buyers’ GSTINs.

faq.q: It says a GSTIN is valid. Does that mean the buyer is registered?
faq.a: No. A passing checksum means the number is WELL-FORMED: fifteen characters, a state code in 01 to 38 plus 97 and 99, a PAN-shaped middle, an entity code, the Z, and a check digit that matches the first fourteen characters. Whether the registration exists, is active, or belongs to whoever gave it to you can only be answered by the GST portal, and this page never contacts it.

faq.q: It found a gap in my invoice numbers. Is that a problem?
faq.a: A gap is not proof of anything. Cancelled invoices leave gaps, so do numbers reserved and never used, a second series kept in another book, and documents you simply have not exported here. It is worth knowing because it is the first thing a scrutiny notice asks about, and the answer is much easier to give while you still remember it.

faq.q: Why is the B2C large threshold a setting rather than a number in the code?
faq.a: Because it changes. The threshold for reporting an inter-state B2C supply invoice by invoice moved from 2,50,000 to 1,00,000 rupees, and it can move again. The page defaults to 1,00,000, prints the figure it used at the top of every sheet, and lets you type a different one. The threshold applies to inter-state supplies only and is tested against the invoice value including tax; intra-state B2C is small whatever its value.

faq.q: What can I feed it besides the invoice maker’s export?
faq.a: Any CSV with a header row carrying at least date, invoice_no, taxable_value and rate. Tab-separated pastes out of a spreadsheet are detected too. Rows it cannot read are reported by line number with the reason, rather than dropped quietly, because a row that vanishes from a tax working sheet is worse than a row that complains.

faq.q: Is this legal and safe to use?
faq.a: Yes. Every target is a throwaway built in your own browser tab - a fresh in-memory SQLite database, a sandboxed iframe, in-memory fakes. There is no server, nothing is uploaded, and the only system you are attacking is a harmless one running on your own machine. Practising here is exactly what it is for.
faq.t: HackLab — break it to understand it

faq.q: Is the SQL injection real or simulated?
faq.a: Real. It runs against sql.js - the same actual SQLite engine as the SQL lab - and your injection genuinely executes. The difference from attacking a real site is only that the database is a disposable one created in memory when you open the challenge.
faq.t: HackLab — break it to understand it

faq.q: How is the XSS challenge safe if the script really runs?
faq.a: Two ways. The payload runs in a throwaway guestbook page served with a strict connect-src none policy, so it cannot fetch, beacon or websocket a stolen value out - it can only message it back to the challenge, which is how the solve is detected. And what it steals is a hardcoded fake token: this whole site is static, with no accounts, no secrets and no real user data, so even a flawless exploit walks away with a string that was never worth anything. That harmlessness, not any single sandbox trick, is what makes it safe.
faq.t: HackLab — break it to understand it

faq.q: Do I need to know how to code?
faq.a: A little helps, but each challenge shows you the vulnerable query or command as you type, gives progressive hints, and reveals the full solution if you want it. You can learn the pattern by doing it.
faq.t: HackLab — break it to understand it

faq.q: Does breaking the challenge teach me anything defensive?
faq.a: That is the actual point. Every challenge ends with the real-world fix - parameterised queries, output encoding, argument vectors instead of shell strings, authorisation checks. The exploit is the hook; understanding why the fix works is what you keep.
faq.t: HackLab — break it to understand it

faq.q: Is my progress saved?
faq.a: Yes, in your browser's local storage on this device only. Nothing is sent anywhere, and you can reset it any time with the button in the challenge list.
faq.t: HackLab — break it to understand it

faq.q: Is my HAR uploaded anywhere?
faq.a: No. It is read with the browser FileReader API and analysed in the page. There is no server and no network request, which is exactly what makes it safe to point at a file full of your own credentials.

faq.q: What does the redacted copy remove?
faq.a: Every secret it detected - Authorization and other credential headers, cookie values, bearer tokens, API keys, JWTs, private keys and Luhn-valid card numbers - replaced with a marker. The file structure is preserved so it still opens as a HAR. Email addresses are left in by default because they are usually the account the ticket is about; the output notes this.

faq.q: Can it miss a secret?
faq.a: Yes, and it says so. Detection is pattern- and name-based, so an opaque token in a field with an unrecognisable name is indistinguishable from any random string. Always glance over the redacted copy before sending.

faq.q: How do I export a HAR?
faq.a: Open your browser developer tools, go to the Network tab, reproduce the problem, then right-click the request list and choose "Save all as HAR" (or the export icon).

faq.q: What is the largest file it handles?
faq.a: Up to 64 MB. Larger captures start to strain the tab, since all the work happens on your own processor.

faq.q: Is anything uploaded?
faq.a: No. The password you type is hashed and cracked entirely in your browser, in a Web Worker. There is no server and no network request.

faq.q: Why does my strong password never crack?
faq.a: Because brute force scales exponentially with length and character set. That is the point - the tool shows the projected time for a strong password so you can see it is effectively never, at any realistic guess rate.

faq.q: Which hashes can it crack?
faq.a: MD5, SHA-1 and SHA-256 - all fast hashes. Real password storage uses deliberately slow hashes (bcrypt, Argon2) precisely so this kind of guessing is millions of times slower.

faq.q: How fast is it?
faq.a: Millions of guesses per second in a modern browser - fast enough to make the lesson vivid, and slow compared to a GPU cracking rig, which does billions. Either way, a weak password falls instantly and a strong one never does.

faq.q: Does the Stop button really stop it?
faq.a: Yes. It terminates the worker immediately, which is why the cracking runs off the main thread in the first place.

faq.q: Is my file uploaded when I hash it?
faq.a: No. The file is read straight off your disk by the browser and hashed in a Web Worker in this tab. There is no server in this tool, and no request carrying your data is ever made - open the Network tab and you will see nothing leave while you use it. (The page itself loads analytics, like every page on this site; that is a pageview, and it never contains your input.)

faq.q: Which hash should I use?
faq.a: SHA-256 for anything new. It is fast, widely supported and has no known practical attack. Use SHA-512 if you want more margin. Do not use MD5 or SHA-1 for anything that needs to resist a deliberate attack.

faq.q: Can I hash a password with this?
faq.a: You can, but you should not store the result. Passwords need a slow, salted algorithm such as bcrypt, scrypt or Argon2id. A fast hash like SHA-256 is exactly the wrong tool because it lets an attacker try billions of guesses per second.

faq.q: What is the largest file I can hash?
faq.a: There is no limit. Up to 256 MB the file is read in one piece and handed to the browser's own hash implementations, which are around sixteen times faster; past that it is streamed on a background thread in fixed-size pieces, so the memory used stays flat however big it gets. Nothing is uploaded either way, so a large file costs you time on your own processor rather than bandwidth.

faq.q: Does this work offline?
faq.a: Text mode does, as soon as the page has loaded. Hashing a file fetches one small background script the first time you do it, so do that once while you are connected; after that it is served from your browser cache and works disconnected.

faq.q: Is this a real network connection?
faq.a: No. It is a simulation running as arithmetic in your browser. No socket is opened, no packet is sent, and the only real HTTP involved is the request that delivered this page. Move a slider and the three runs are recomputed from scratch; that is all it is doing.
faq.t: HTTP/1.1, HTTP/2 and HTTP/3, raced on the same link

faq.q: Why does HTTP/2 fall apart when I raise the loss slider?
faq.a: Because HTTP/2 multiplexed its streams on top of a single TCP connection, and TCP delivers one ordered byte stream. When a segment goes missing, TCP will not hand the application anything that comes after the hole - not for the stream that lost the packet, and not for the fifteen that did not. So one lost packet freezes every stream until the retransmit arrives. That is TCP head-of-line blocking, it cannot be fixed above the transport, and it is the entire reason HTTP/3 exists.
faq.t: HTTP/1.1, HTTP/2 and HTTP/3, raced on the same link

faq.q: Is HTTP/3 always faster?
faq.a: No, and this lab will show you that if you look. On a clean link HTTP/3 is ahead by about one round trip of handshake and very little else. Under loss it is clearly better than HTTP/2, but it is not immune: QUIC runs congestion control too, so a lost packet still cuts its sending window. UDP is also deprioritised or blocked outright on some networks, and QUIC does more work in userspace, which costs CPU. It is a real improvement, not magic.
faq.t: HTTP/1.1, HTTP/2 and HTTP/3, raced on the same link

faq.q: Why does HTTP/1.1 sometimes beat HTTP/2 here?
faq.a: Because six connections have six congestion windows and six independent recoveries, and one connection has one. Under loss that is a large advantage, and it is a real one that was argued about at length when HTTP/2 was young. HTTP/2 trades it for multiplexing, header compression and a single handshake, which is the right trade on most links and the wrong one on a bad mobile connection.
faq.t: HTTP/1.1, HTTP/2 and HTTP/3, raced on the same link

faq.q: Are the HPACK byte counts real?
faq.a: Yes, with one stated exception. The encoder uses the real RFC 7541 static table indices, real integer prefix encoding, and a dynamic table with real entry sizing of name plus value plus 32 bytes and real eviction at the table limit. What it does not do is Huffman-code the literal values, which HPACK permits - the H bit is simply zero. Huffman would take roughly a fifth more off the literals and nothing at all off the indexed fields, and the indexed fields are the point.
faq.t: HTTP/1.1, HTTP/2 and HTTP/3, raced on the same link

faq.q: How accurate is the simulation?
faq.a: It is calibrated to show the mechanism, not to predict your numbers.
