A lost packet stops the affected scope dead for one round trip, which overstates the cost on a fast link because real TCP keeps sending until the receive window fills, and understates it whenever loss arrives in bursts or a retransmission timeout fires. Queueing, buffer bloat, server push, TLS session tickets and CDN behaviour are not modelled at all. Treat the shapes as true and the milliseconds as illustrative.
faq.t: HTTP/1.1, HTTP/2 and HTTP/3, raced on the same link

faq.q: Is anything uploaded?
faq.a: No. Every round trip and every byte counted here is computed locally, and the page makes no network request of its own.
faq.t: HTTP/1.1, HTTP/2 and HTTP/3, raced on the same link

faq.q: Is 0.1 + 0.2 a bug in JavaScript?
faq.a: No. Every language using IEEE-754 binary doubles gives the same answer — C, Java, Python, Rust, Go, Swift, and the cell in your spreadsheet. Some of them hide it by printing fewer digits by default. The bits are identical; only the printing differs.
faq.t: IEEE-754, one bit at a time

faq.q: Why does the exact value so often end in a 5?
faq.a: It always does, for any double that is not a whole number. Strip the factors of two out of the significand and what is left is odd, and the value becomes that odd number times a power of five over a power of ten. An odd number times a power of five ends in 5, so every non-integer double does too.
faq.t: IEEE-754, one bit at a time

faq.q: Should I use a decimal type instead?
faq.a: For money, yes — cents are decimal, and decimal arithmetic keeps them exact. For measurement, science and graphics, no: binary floating point is faster, has a far wider range, and decimal has exactly the same problem with one third that binary has with one tenth. Neither is more accurate in general; they are exact about different things.
faq.t: IEEE-754, one bit at a time

faq.q: Can a NaN payload be used to carry information?
faq.a: Only into and out of a typed-array view, which moves raw bytes and will faithfully carry any payload you write. Through arithmetic, no: the standard says the NaN an operation returns is implementation-defined, so an engine may hand back a different one and some operations do. The NaN panel runs both experiments in your browser and reports what actually happened rather than telling you in advance — the answer is not the same everywhere.
faq.t: IEEE-754, one bit at a time

faq.q: Is Kahan summation always worth it?
faq.a: It does about four times the arithmetic of a naive loop, so not always. Sorting by magnitude first, or pairwise summation — which is what NumPy does — recovers much of the benefit for less. And any of them can be silently removed by a compiler permitted to re-associate floating point, which is one of the things -ffast-math permits: the compensation terms are exactly what it will prove to be zero.
faq.t: IEEE-754, one bit at a time

faq.q: Why do large IDs from an API arrive as strings?
faq.a: Because a double stops being able to hold consecutive integers above 2^53, which is 9007199254740992. A 64-bit database id larger than that cannot survive being parsed into a Number, and the failure is silent — the value is not rejected, it is quietly changed to a nearby one. The spacing panel shows exactly where that starts.
faq.t: IEEE-754, one bit at a time

faq.q: Is my image uploaded?
faq.a: No. The file is read, decoded, resized and re-encoded by your own browser, and the ZIP is assembled in the same tab. There is no upload step and no server to upload to. Open your Network tab while you use it - that is the only proof worth anything, and it is the reason this page exists at all.
faq.t: Compress, convert and resize images without uploading them

faq.q: Which formats can this browser actually write?
faq.a: It depends on the browser, so the page probes at load rather than promising. JPEG and PNG are everywhere. WebP encoding is in every current browser. AVIF encoding is not - it is in Chromium-based browsers and, at the time of writing, not in Safari or Firefox. Any format this browser cannot write is disabled in the menu with the reason attached, rather than quietly coming back as a PNG wearing the wrong extension.
faq.t: Compress, convert and resize images without uploading them

faq.q: Why did my file get bigger?
faq.a: Almost always because the original was already compressed harder than the setting you asked for. Re-encoding a JPEG that was saved at quality 60 at quality 90 produces a larger file that looks slightly worse, because nothing can recover what the first encoder threw away. Asking for PNG output from a photograph does the same thing more dramatically. The row tells you it grew instead of hiding it.
faq.t: Compress, convert and resize images without uploading them

faq.q: Does resizing here lose quality?
faq.a: Yes, and unavoidably. Making an image smaller throws pixels away, and every lossy re-encode is another generation of loss on top of the first. So do it once, from the largest original you have, rather than repeatedly from copies of copies. If you only need the file smaller and not the dimensions, lower the quality and leave the dimensions alone.
faq.t: Compress, convert and resize images without uploading them

faq.q: How is the ZIP made without a library?
faq.a: Field by field: a local file header per member, a central directory listing them all, and an end-of-central-directory record. Every member is stored rather than deflated, because JPEG, WebP, PNG and AVIF payloads are already entropy-coded and compressing them a second time saves a fraction of a percent in exchange for a megabyte of library. It is an ordinary ZIP and every unarchiver opens it.
faq.t: Compress, convert and resize images without uploading them

faq.q: Which timestamp formats does it read?
faq.a: Apache and nginx combined, syslog RFC 3164 and RFC 5424, ISO 8601 with and without an offset, Windows Event Log style, JSON lines with a timestamp field, and epoch in both seconds and milliseconds. Detection is per line, so a file that changes format part way through still merges.

faq.q: Why does it ask me for a year?
faq.a: Because RFC 3164 syslog does not record one. It defaults to the current year, and you should change it when working an older incident. The case to watch is a December log read with January's year, which lands every line twelve months out without looking wrong.

faq.q: Can it tell me which machine has the correct clock?
faq.a: No, and it will not pretend to. It can tell you that two sources disagree, by how much, and whether the gap looks like a timezone mistake rather than drift. Deciding which one is right needs something outside the logs, usually NTP.

faq.q: Is anything uploaded?
faq.a: No. There is no network call in this page at all. Incident logs carry hostnames, internal addresses and usernames, which is exactly the material you should not paste into a website you do not control — so this one does the work in your tab and keeps nothing.

faq.q: What do the exports contain?
faq.a: Markdown gives you a table plus a narrative list, ready to paste into an incident report. CSV is RFC 4180 quoted so it opens cleanly in a spreadsheet. Both carry the UTC time, the original line, its source and the offset that was applied.

faq.q: Does it detect the incident for me?
faq.a: No. It normalises, merges and orders, and flags the timing problems it can prove. Reading the result is still your job — it is a timeline builder, not a detection engine, and a tool that claimed otherwise would be selling you something.

faq.q: Is this really free?
faq.a: Yes, permanently. There is no server doing the work, so there is no cost to pass on. No account, no trial, no execution limits.
faq.t: Online compilers that run on your machine, not ours

faq.q: Does my code get uploaded?
faq.a: No. Every language here runs inside your own browser using your CPU and RAM. Your code is never transmitted, and there is no server that could receive it. You can open your browser's Network tab and watch: the only requests the playground makes for its work are for the runtime files themselves. The page around it does load Google Analytics — like every page on this site — and that carries a page view, not your code.
faq.t: Online compilers that run on your machine, not ours

faq.q: Can I install libraries or packages?
faq.a: No. pip, npm, LuaRocks and every other package manager need a registry to resolve against, and the page's script-src policy refuses code fetched from one. Standard libraries only.
faq.t: Online compilers that run on your machine, not ours

faq.q: Why is the first run slower than the rest?
faq.a: Most languages need a runtime downloaded once — between 420 KB and 19 MB depending on the language. Your browser caches it, so every run after that starts immediately, and the playground then works with no internet connection at all.
faq.t: Online compilers that run on your machine, not ours

faq.q: What happens if I write an infinite loop?
faq.a: Your program runs in a Web Worker, isolated from the page, so the tab stays responsive. A warning with a Cancel button appears after a few seconds, and anything still running at sixty seconds is stopped automatically.
faq.t: Online compilers that run on your machine, not ours

faq.q: Does this work on a phone?
faq.a: Yes, though the editor is more comfortable on a larger screen. The lighter languages - JavaScript, Lua and SQL - are the best fit for a phone.
faq.t: Online compilers that run on your machine, not ours

faq.q: Can I use it offline?
faq.a: Yes. Once a language's runtime is cached, that playground keeps working without a connection.
faq.t: Online compilers that run on your machine, not ours

faq.q: Does this tell me whether the ID is real?
faq.a: No, and it is worth being blunt about it. This checks format and checksum only. It performs no lookup against any database or registry. It cannot tell you that an ID is real, that it belongs to the person who gave it to you, or that it has not been cancelled. A number that passes every check here can be entirely fictional — a valid checksum only means the number was constructed the way a real one would be. Real verification means the official route: the issuing authority, its own portal, its own consent flow.
faq.t: Indian ID checker — format and checksum only

faq.q: Is anything I paste uploaded?
faq.a: No. There is no server to upload to and the code makes no network request of any kind, which you can watch in your own Network tab while it runs. Nothing is written to storage either. Aadhaar goes further and is echoed masked to the last four digits, in the output and in the CSV, because a full number sitting in a screenshot or a downloaded file is exactly the accident this tool should not help you have.
faq.t: Indian ID checker — format and checksum only

faq.q: Why does an obviously made-up number pass?
faq.a: Because a checksum is arithmetic over the digits, not a membership test. Any eleven digits plus the correct twelfth will satisfy Verhoeff, and the Fake test Aadhaar button does exactly that so you can exercise your own validator without touching a real number. That is the point the whole page is built around: passing here means well-formed, and nothing more.
faq.t: Indian ID checker — format and checksum only

faq.q: Why is my bank, or my UPI handle, not in the list?
faq.a: Because both lists were typed out offline and both go stale. Bank amalgamations retire IFSC prefixes, and a new UPI handle appears whenever an app signs a new sponsor bank — and a page that makes no network request cannot notice either. A code missing from those lists is not evidence of anything. The same goes for RTO codes on number plates: those lists are long and they change, so this page names the state and deliberately does not claim to know the office.
faq.t: Indian ID checker — format and checksum only

faq.q: Can I use this for KYC or to check a customer document?
faq.a: It is not built for that and it cannot do it. A format check tells you a field was typed correctly; it says nothing about identity, and nothing here is advice about meeting an obligation. Where a rule changes with a finance act, varies by state, or depends on something you have not told the page, the output says so rather than printing a confident number. Use this to catch typos before a form rejects them, and use the official channel for anything that matters.
faq.t: Indian ID checker — format and checksum only

faq.q: What happens when a line could be two different things?
faq.a: It says so and checks it as each candidate instead of silently picking one. In practice these six formats collide rarely, because they differ in length and in where the letters and digits sit — but a bare twelve-digit number is also an account number and a hundred other things, and the output points that out rather than announcing “Aadhaar” with confidence it has not earned. Anything matching nothing is reported as unrecognised, with a count of its digits and letters so you can see what you actually pasted.
faq.t: Indian ID checker — format and checksum only

faq.q: Does anything I type leave my browser?
faq.a: No. There is no server behind this page, so there is nowhere for it to go. Your client list, your rates, your GSTIN and whatever you type into the payment details box are held in the page while the tab is open, and the only copies that ever exist are the ones you make on purpose: a printed PDF, a downloaded .json file, or a draft you save into this browser. There is also no share link anywhere in this tool, deliberately - a link that carried the form would carry the payment details with it, into browser history and into whatever app you sent it through.

faq.q: Is this accounting software, or tax advice?
faq.a: Neither. It is a document generator: it lays out one invoice or one quotation and prints it. It keeps no ledger, tracks nothing across documents, files no return, and cannot tell you what rate your work attracts or whether you should be registered at all. Those are questions for a chartered accountant, and the arithmetic here does not replace one. What it does do is the part software should never get wrong - the tax split, the rate-wise summary and the totals.

faq.q: How does it decide between CGST plus SGST and IGST?
faq.a: By comparing two state codes: yours, and the place of supply. Same state means the supply is intra-state, so the tax splits into CGST and SGST at half the rate each. Different states means inter-state, so it is IGST at the whole rate. If your state is a union territory without its own legislature - Chandigarh, Lakshadweep, Ladakh, the Andaman and Nicobar Islands, Dadra and Nagar Haveli and Daman and Diu, or Other Territory - the state half is UTGST rather than SGST. Delhi, Puducherry and Jammu and Kashmir have legislatures, so they take SGST. Until both states are set the tool refuses to pick, because guessing is exactly how the wrong tax gets charged.

faq.q: What if I am not registered for GST?
faq.a: Switch the tax treatment to "not registered" and the tax columns disappear, no GST is charged, and the document prints as a plain invoice with a line saying no tax has been charged. If you are under the composition scheme, choose that instead: it prints as a Bill of Supply and carries the declaration a composition taxable person is required to print, because a composition dealer may not collect tax on supplies. The heading changes with the mode for the same reason - only a registered person issues a tax invoice.

faq.q: How do I get a PDF?
faq.a: Press "Print / Save as PDF" and choose "Save as PDF" as the destination in your browser's print dialog. The page is set up so that only the document prints - no site header, no toolbar, no form, no site byline - on A4 with the sheet carrying its own margins. There is no PDF library on this page on purpose: your browser already has an excellent one, and nobody can put a paywall in front of your own print dialog.

faq.q: Where do my bank details go?
faq.a: Into a plain text box, onto the printed document, and nowhere else. The tool never asks for an account number as a structured field, never validates one, never puts one in a link, and never sends one anywhere. If you save a draft, that text is part of what is written into this browser's storage on this device - which is why the draft is saved only when you press Save, and why there is a button to delete it. On a shared machine, print the PDF and skip the draft.

faq.q: Will my draft still be here tomorrow?
faq.a: Only if you pressed "Save draft", and only in this browser on this device. A saved draft survives closing the tab, and the page tells you it is there rather than loading it for you - a form full of client details and payment terms should not reappear on its own for whoever opens this page next on the same computer. "Load draft" brings it back, "Delete saved draft" removes it. If you want a copy you can move or keep, press "Download data" and you get an invoice-data.json file you own.

faq.q: Why does it say my GSTIN is wrong?
faq.a: A GSTIN is fifteen characters - a two-digit state code, the ten-character PAN of the holder, an entity number, a fixed Z, and a check character computed from the other fourteen. The check character catches the ordinary typo that a length check cannot, because a transposed pair is still fifteen characters long. The tool also says so when the state code at the front does not match the state you picked. None of it blocks printing: it is your number, and the warning is there to be read, not obeyed.

faq.q: Can I bill in dollars for an export?
faq.a: Not in this version - every amount is in rupees, and I would rather say so than print a dollar sign in front of arithmetic built for INR. The export mode does the other half of the job: it charges no tax, prints the zero-rated declaration for a supply made under a Letter of Undertaking, and leaves the rate column showing what would otherwise have applied. For a foreign-currency invoice you need the conversion rate and the date it was taken, which is bookkeeping, not layout.

faq.q: Why is there a round-off line?
faq.a: Because tax at 18 percent on an odd number almost never lands on a whole rupee, and the total on an Indian invoice is normally rounded to one. The tool computes every amount in paise, rounds the grand total to the nearest rupee, and prints the difference as its own line so that the column can still be added up by hand and reconciled. A total that quietly differs from the sum of the lines above it is the kind of thing an accounts department sends back.

faq.q: Is this JavaScript compiler really free?
faq.a: Yes, and it always will be. There is no server cost to cover because your browser does the work, so there is nothing to meter or bill for.

faq.q: Does my code get sent to a server?
faq.a: No. Your program is turned into a Blob and handed to a Web Worker inside the same tab. No request carrying your code is ever made — you can confirm it in the Network tab.

faq.q: Can I use fetch or the DOM?
faq.a: The DOM, no — a Web Worker has no document or window, which is also why your code cannot reach this page. fetch and XMLHttpRequest do work: the Worker still runs inside your browser, so a program can reach the network just as one typed into the console could. This page never sends your code anywhere, but treat something you pasted from elsewhere the way you would treat running it in your own console.

faq.q: Can I use npm packages?
faq.a: No. There is no registry wired up, and the page's script-src policy refuses code fetched from a CDN, so there is nothing for an import to resolve against. Everything must be self-contained in the single file you write.

faq.q: What happens if I write an infinite loop?
faq.a: Nothing bad. The worker is separate from the page, so the tab stays responsive. After a few seconds a warning appears with a Cancel button, and the run is stopped automatically at sixty seconds.

faq.q: Does it work offline?
faq.a: Yes. JavaScript needs no runtime download at all, so once the page itself is cached the playground works with no connection.

faq.q: Is my token sent anywhere?
faq.a: No. The token is decoded and verified in your browser using the built-in WebCrypto API. There is no server in this tool and no network request carries the token. Open the Network tab in developer tools and you will see the page's ordinary traffic - this page, like every page on the site, loads Google Analytics - but nothing you paste into the tool ever leaves your tab.

faq.q: Can it verify RS256 or ES256 tokens?
faq.a: Signature verification here covers HS256, HS384 and HS512, which use a shared secret. RS and ES algorithms are verified with a public key rather than a secret; the token is still fully decoded and all claims are checked, but the signature is not.

faq.q: Why does it say my token is expired when the app still works?
faq.a: Expiry is compared against your device clock. If your clock is wrong, so is the answer. Servers also commonly allow a small amount of clock skew.

faq.q: Is a JWT encrypted?
faq.a: No. A standard JWT is signed, not encrypted, and its payload is readable by anyone holding it. If you need the contents hidden, that is JWE, which is a different thing.

faq.q: What should I do if I pasted a real token into another site?
faq.a: Treat it as compromised and invalidate the session. Anything with a long expiry and no revocation path is worth rotating.

faq.q: Does any of this reach your server?
faq.a: No. Every value in the table is computed in your tab and thrown away when you close it, and this page stores nothing of its own. Its one request is the WebRTC probe, which asks the Google and Cloudflare STUN servers what address you appear to come from — there is no way to learn a public address without showing it to somebody. Analytics loads here as on every page of this site, so Google does receive the ordinary pageview signals: browser, screen size, language, and a location derived from your address. Several of those are rows in the table above, which on this page of all pages is worth saying plainly.
faq.t: What your browser tells every website

faq.q: Why is my public address missing?
faq.a: Gathering finished without one, usually because a firewall is dropping UDP; the five-second timer is only the outer bound. If WebRTC is switched off in your browser altogether, the row reads unavailable rather than going blank. Extensions that merely restrict which addresses WebRTC may use often still let the public one through, so a blank here is the stronger signal.
faq.t: What your browser tells every website

faq.q: I use a VPN. Should the public address be the VPN one?
faq.a: Yes. Compare the address above against whatever address your VPN provider says it is giving you. If they differ, the WebRTC request escaped the tunnel and every site you visit can read your real address the same way this page just did. That is what a VPN leak is.
faq.t: What your browser tells every website

faq.q: Why is my local address a random name ending in .local?
faq.a: Your browser replaced the real one. Chrome and Firefox hide the local address behind a random mDNS name unless the site already holds camera or microphone permission, so seeing that name means the defence is working. The public address gets no such protection, because it is how packets find their way back to you.
faq.t: What your browser tells every website

faq.q: Does clearing cookies change the canvas fingerprint?
faq.a: No. This page stores nothing of its own, so the number is recomputed from the same drawing on each visit, and it comes out identical because your GPU, driver and fonts have not changed. Private browsing often does not change it either. The value shown belongs to this page and its particular drawing; another site drawing something else gets a different number with the same staying power.
faq.t: What your browser tells every website

faq.q: Is this a real Linux or a simulation of one?
faq.a: A real one. v86 emulates a 32-bit x86 processor in WebAssembly, and a genuine Linux kernel boots on it with a BusyBox userland. Pipes, redirection, signals, /proc and the process table are the kernel's own implementations, not imitations.
faq.t: A real Linux terminal, running in your browser

faq.q: Can I run Python or compile C in here?
faq.a: No, and this is the most common misunderstanding. The image is BusyBox only - there is no Python, Perl, Ruby or gcc inside it. Adding them would mean a multi-hundred-megabyte disk image. The emulated machine also cannot reach the language runtimes used by /labs: those live in JavaScript, and this is a separate CPU with its own memory. For running code, use the language playgrounds in Labs instead.
faq.t: A real Linux terminal, running in your browser

faq.q: Is it safe to run a fork bomb?
faq.a: Yes - that is precisely the point. The emulated machine is given a fixed 64 MB of RAM that it physically cannot exceed. A fork bomb exhausts the emulated process table and the emulated kernel responds exactly as a real one would, which is genuinely interesting to watch. Your browser and your computer are unaffected. Press Reboot when you have seen enough.
faq.t: A real Linux terminal, running in your browser

faq.q: Which commands are available? There is no man, apt or info.
faq.a: There are 227 of them, all provided by BusyBox as a single binary. That covers ls, cat, grep, sed, awk, find, vi, tar, du, df, ps, kill, mount, wget, diff, cpio, crond and most of what you would reach for day to day. What is missing is documentation and packaging: BusyBox ships no man pages (they would multiply the image size), so use command --help instead, and there is no apt or apk because Buildroot has no package manager and the machine has no network to fetch from. Run busybox --list to see the full set.
faq.t: A real Linux terminal, running in your browser

faq.q: Does it have internet access?
faq.a: No. There is no network device attached, so ping, wget and apt will all fail. That is deliberate: it keeps the machine completely sealed, and it means nothing you do inside can reach anything outside.
faq.t: A real Linux terminal, running in your browser

faq.q: Do my files survive a reload?
faq.a: No. The disk is read-only and the RAM disappears when the page unloads. Every boot gives you an identical fresh machine, which also means you can break it as thoroughly as you like.
faq.t: A real Linux terminal, running in your browser

faq.q: Does any of this touch a server?
faq.a: Only to download the 8 MB machine image the first time. After that your browser has it cached and the whole thing runs on your own processor. Nothing you type is transmitted anywhere.
faq.t: A real Linux terminal, running in your browser

faq.q: Why is it slower than my real machine?
faq.a: Every x86 instruction is being interpreted by WebAssembly rather than run natively. For a shell and BusyBox tools that is perfectly comfortable; it is not the place to benchmark anything.
faq.t: A real Linux terminal, running in your browser

faq.q: Is my log uploaded anywhere?
faq.a: No. The file is read with the browser FileReader API, or taken straight from the textarea, and every count is computed in the page. There is no server and no network request, which is what makes it reasonable to point at a production log - a file that lists your usernames, your source addresses and your working hours.

faq.q: Why does it call one source brute force and another a spray?
faq.a: Because they are different attacks and they need different responses. Many attempts against one or two accounts is brute force: someone wants that account, and lockout policy applies. Attempts spread thinly across many accounts is a password spray: one or two guesses each, deliberately under the lockout threshold, so lockout will not fire and per-account alerting will not see it. The thresholds used are printed in the report.

faq.q: It flagged an account signing in from two places. Is that account compromised?
faq.a: Not on this evidence. All the tool can say is that one account authenticated successfully from two different addresses a few minutes apart. It has no idea where either address is - there is no GeoIP database here and no lookup is made, because sending your log's addresses to a geolocation service would undo the point of analysing the file locally. A VPN connecting, a phone moving between mobile data and wifi, or a scheduled job on a second host all produce the same pattern.

faq.q: Which formats does it read, and what if mine is not one of them?
faq.a: Linux auth.log and secure, nginx and Apache access logs, IIS W3C extended, Windows Security event exports as CSV, and generic syslog as a fallback. If the detection picks the wrong one, choose the right one in the format selector and press Analyse. If your format is genuinely none of these, the generic syslog path will still give you a timeline, the programs writing the most lines, and the most repeated messages - and I would like to hear which format it was.

faq.q: How big a log can it handle?
faq.a: Up to 16 MB or 200,000 lines, whichever comes first. Past that it stops and says so in the report rather than quietly analysing part of the file and presenting the counts as complete. For anything larger, split it first - all the work happens on your own processor, in one tab.

faq.q: Which version of Lua is this?
faq.a: Lua 5.4, compiled to WebAssembly. It is the genuine reference implementation, so language behaviour matches the official manual.

faq.q: Can I use LuaRocks modules?
faq.a: No. There is no package manager and no network access, so only the standard libraries that ship with Lua are available.

faq.q: Does state carry over between runs?
faq.a: No. A fresh Lua state is created for each run and closed afterwards, so globals from a previous run never leak into the next one.

faq.q: How do I read input?
faq.a: Use io.read() and put your input in the Input panel, one line per read, before running.

faq.q: Why is Lua so much faster to start than Python?
faq.a: Lua is a famously small language — the whole interpreter is about a 150 KB download here (420 KB unpacked), against roughly 5.5 MB compressed for CPython and its standard library.

faq.q: Does this run the file?
faq.a: No. It reads the bytes as data and prints what the structures say. Nothing is executed, emulated or unpacked, and no embedded content is rendered.
faq.t: Static malware triage, and an EICAR test file

faq.q: Is this a sandbox?
faq.a: No, and it is not a substitute for one. Static triage tells you what a binary declares it can do. A packed sample declares almost nothing, and the only way to find out what it actually does is to detonate it in an isolated environment and watch. This is the cheap pass you do first, to decide whether the expensive one is worth it.
faq.t: Static malware triage, and an EICAR test file

faq.q: How is this different from the file inspector?
faq.a: The file inspector answers what a file is - magic bytes, hex dump, strings, entropy, extension mismatch. This page starts one question later, once the answer is an executable, and asks what that executable can do. None of the file inspector's work is repeated here.
faq.t: Static malware triage, and an EICAR test file

faq.q: Is my sample uploaded anywhere?
faq.a: No. It is read locally and parsed in the page. There is no server, no network request and no lookup against any threat-intelligence service. The hashes are shown so you can take them to a source you already trust, yourself.
faq.t: Static malware triage, and an EICAR test file

faq.q: Does it verify the code signature?
faq.a: No. It reads the certificate table and prints the subject, issuer and validity dates, and it says so in the report. It does not recompute the Authenticode hash, walk the chain to a trusted root, or check revocation. A stolen certificate and a valid one look identical here.
faq.t: Static malware triage, and an EICAR test file

faq.q: Which formats does it parse?
faq.a: Windows PE in the most depth: headers, sections, imports, exports, resources and the certificate table. ELF and Mach-O are parsed far enough to identify and orient - class, machine, type, entry point, sections or segments with entropy, and linked libraries.
faq.t: Static malware triage, and an EICAR test file

faq.q: What is the EICAR test file?
faq.a: Sixty-eight harmless ASCII characters defined by the European Institute for Computer Antivirus Research. Every antivirus product agrees to report it as if it were a virus, so you can test that a scanner is switched on without owning malware. It contains no code and does nothing when run.
faq.t: Static malware triage, and an EICAR test file

faq.q: Will the EICAR file harm my machine?
faq.a: No. It has no payload at all. It will, however, set off your own antivirus the moment it is written to disk, and on a managed machine that usually raises an alert in a security team's console. Tell your IT or security team before you download one, not after.
faq.t: Static malware triage, and an EICAR test file

faq.q: Can I edit the rules?
faq.a: Yes. The rule pane is editable and the built-in rules are there to be read and changed. The engine takes a small subset of YARA syntax: quoted and hex patterns with nocase, wide and ascii, and conditions built from all, any, N of them, filesize, uint8, uint16, uint32, at, counts, and and, or, not. Regular expressions, jumps, string sets and modules are not supported, and a rule using them says so rather than failing quietly.
faq.t: Static malware triage, and an EICAR test file

faq.q: Can this tell me whether a photo is a deepfake?
faq.a: No, and neither can anything else that runs in a browser. It surfaces the signals a forensic examiner would look at and explains what each one does and does not imply. Every signal here has innocent causes, and a competent fake - or one extra re-save - erases all of them. If a tool hands you a percentage, that number was invented.

faq.q: Why is there no score or confidence percentage?
faq.a: Because there is nothing honest to compute one from. A score implies the signals combine into a measurement of authenticity, and they do not: they measure processing history. Putting a number on the page would make it look more reliable than it is, which is the exact failure this page exists to avoid.

faq.q: Why does my untouched photo show signals?
faq.a: Because ordinary handling produces them. Cropping, resizing, a messaging app, a CMS thumbnailer, a phone camera's own processing, and simply opening and re-saving a file all leave recompression and noise differences behind. That is why nothing in the output is phrased as a finding.

faq.q: Why is there no face swapper in the playground?
faq.a: Because that tool's dominant real-world use is non-consensual imagery, with fraud second, and building it on the same page as a detector meant to fight it would be indefensible. The playground applies individual artefacts to your own image instead, so you can watch one signal move at a time. That is what actually teaches someone to read these.

faq.q: Does it verify Content Credentials or C2PA?
faq.a: It reports whether a manifest is present, and it does not check the signature. Verifying one needs a certificate chain and a trust list, which means a network request, and this page makes none. Presence is not validity - take the file to a C2PA verifier if the claim matters.

faq.q: What does it do with video?
faq.a: It samples nine frames through a video element and a canvas, compares their fine-detail energy, and lets you run every still analysis on any one of them. It does no codec or container work at all, so it sees nothing of the encoder, the GOP structure or the container metadata.

faq.q: Why does the ELA map look bright all over my image?
faq.a: Sharp edges, saturated colour and fine texture are bright in the ELA of every untouched photograph ever taken, and a screenshot or a re-saved file carries one uniform compression history that makes the whole map meaningless. ELA shows recompression, not manipulation.

faq.q: Is my file uploaded?
faq.a: No. Every pixel is read in this tab, and the only file that leaves is one you ask to download. A tool that made you upload a photograph in order to check whether it could be trusted would be a strange bargain.

faq.q: Is my dump uploaded?
faq.a: No. It is read and scanned in your browser with no network request. Memory dumps are among the most sensitive files there are, so local-only is essential.

faq.q: Why UTF-16 and not just ASCII?
faq.a: Because Windows stores most of its strings as UTF-16LE. A tool that only extracts ASCII misses the majority of the interesting text in a Windows memory dump - URLs, commands, filenames.

faq.q: What can it carve out?
faq.a: It reports embedded file signatures (PNG, JPEG, PDF, ZIP, PE executables and more) with their offsets, so you can see what is buried inside and where. It flags them; a full carve to separate files is a next step.

faq.q: How big a file can it take?
faq.a: Up to 512 MB. It processes in chunks and reports progress, and caps results per category, saying so when it truncates.

faq.q: What is the entropy map for?
faq.a: To show where the random-looking (compressed or encrypted) regions are. Encryption and compression both push entropy near 8 bits per byte, so a high-entropy block stands out.

faq.q: Is the text I paste uploaded anywhere?
faq.a: No. The character tables, the decoder and the scoring are all in one JavaScript file that runs in your tab. There is no network call of any kind. Broken text is usually real customer data — names, addresses, subject lines — which is exactly the sort of thing that should not be pasted into an unknown server to be tidied up.

faq.q: What is the difference between REVERSIBLE and LOSSY here?
faq.a: Reversible means every original byte is still present in what you pasted, just read through the wrong table, so the repair is exact rather than a reconstruction. A mis-decode, a doubled entity and a stray BOM are all reversible. LOSSY means bytes were discarded before you ever saw the text — that is what U+FFFD marks — and no amount of processing brings them back. The report labels every finding one way or the other and never blurs the two.

faq.q: What does the confidence number actually mean?
faq.a: It is a score over four measured signals, and all four are printed alongside it: whether every character maps to a byte in that charset, whether those bytes pass a strict UTF-8 decode, how far the count of damage markers fell, and whether any marker is left. It caps at 99 on purpose. Nothing here can prove the result is what the author typed, only that one wrong-decode story explains every byte.

faq.q: Why does it bother with CP437 and KOI8-R?
faq.a: Because they still turn up. CP437 is the IBM PC character set and remains the default code page of a great many Windows consoles, so exports from old tooling arrive looking like line-drawing art. KOI8-R is what a large amount of archived Russian mail is stored in. They are rarer than Windows-1252 and are tried after it, but they are tried properly, with their own tables, not guessed at.

faq.q: It did not repair my text. What now?
faq.a: Read the rejection reasons in the hypothesis table — each one names the character or the byte that ruled that charset out, which is often more useful than a repair would have been. If the answer is a replacement character, the text cannot be recovered from here and you need the file from before the bad decode. If it is a charset this tool does not carry, it says so rather than forcing a wrong answer onto your text.

faq.q: Can it break text that was fine to begin with?
faq.a: A whole-text repair is only accepted if every character maps to a byte and those bytes pass a strict UTF-8 decode, which ordinary prose fails almost immediately — a lone é is byte E9, and E9 is not a valid UTF-8 sequence. The run-targeted mode is weaker, because it picks its own boundaries, so it scores lower, and it names the runs it repaired and the runs it refused — the first five of each, with a count of anything past that. Nothing is applied to your input until you press a button.

faq.q: Which algorithms does it cover?
faq.a: CPU scheduling: FCFS, SJF, shortest remaining time, round robin, and priority in both preemptive and non-preemptive forms. Page replacement: FIFO, LRU, optimal, clock and LFU. Disk scheduling: FCFS, SSTF, SCAN, C-SCAN, LOOK and C-LOOK. Memory allocation: first, best, worst and next fit. Plus the Banker algorithm for deadlock avoidance.

faq.q: My textbook gets a different answer - who is wrong?
faq.a: Probably neither. The usual culprits are the round robin ordering when a process arrives at the same instant a quantum expires, whether SCAN travels to the edge of the disk, and whether a low priority number means high priority. This page states each convention it uses, so you can see exactly where the two workings diverge.

faq.q: Why does the safe sequence differ from mine?
faq.a: A safe state usually has several safe sequences, and any one of them proves the state is safe. This runs the lowest-numbered process whose need fits at each round, so the result is reproducible; your book may pick a different one. If both sequences let every process finish, both are correct.

faq.q: Does it show the Belady anomaly?
faq.a: Yes - there is a preset for it. Load the Belady string under page replacement, run FIFO with three frames, then change it to four and watch the fault count go up rather than down. LRU and optimal cannot do that, and you can check both in the same two clicks.

faq.q: Is anything uploaded?
faq.a: No. Every simulation is arithmetic running in your tab. There is no server, no network request, and nothing is stored beyond the consent you gave once for the Labs section.

faq.q: Does this look anyone up?
faq.a: No. There is no fetch, no XHR, no remote image and no username probed against a site. Everything on this page is string matching and arithmetic in your own tab, over text and files you supplied yourself. Open your browser's Network tab and use the tool: nothing appears.
faq.t: What a stranger can learn about you

faq.q: Can I check somebody else with this?
faq.a: Please do not. The tool cannot tell whose text you pasted, so nothing stops you technically, and that is exactly why the rule is written down rather than enforced. It exists so you can look at your own exposure. Pointing it at another person turns a self-check into surveillance, and if that is what you want, this is the wrong page.
faq.t: What a stranger can learn about you

faq.q: Why does it not tell me which accounts my username has?
faq.a: Because a tool that takes a handle and returns a list of that person's accounts is a stalking tool, whatever the intention of whoever wrote it. So this shows you how enumeration works, prints the variants a tool would derive, and hands you the checklist of account types to work through in your own browser. The searching stays a deliberate act by you, on you.
faq.t: What a stranger can learn about you

faq.q: Does a clean result mean I am safe?
faq.a: No, and the output says so. This only knows the patterns in its own rule table. Plenty of real disclosure is an ordinary sentence with no pattern in it: the cafe you are always in, the ceiling of a hospital ward, the fact that you replied at three in the morning. A clean result means no rule matched, not that nothing was given away.
faq.t: What a stranger can learn about you

faq.q: Why does it not read the EXIF in my photo itself?
faq.a: Because that tool already exists here and does it properly. This one walks the file's segments to tell you whether a metadata block is present, then sends you to the EXIF viewer at /labs/exif to decode the tags and download a stripped copy. What it adds instead is the half that stripping does not fix: reflections, documents, house numbers, uniforms and barcodes, which live in the pixels.
faq.t: What a stranger can learn about you

faq.q: Is anything I paste or drop uploaded?
faq.a: No. There is no server to upload to and no request is made. Your photo is decoded from a blob URL, which is a local address for bytes already in the tab, and your text never leaves the textarea. Nothing is stored either: reload the page and it is gone.
faq.t: What a stranger can learn about you

faq.q: Why is there no risk score?
faq.a: Because nothing here is calibrated against a measured population, so a number would be invented. It would also be the part people remembered instead of the reasons, and the reasons are the useful bit. Findings are grouped as high, medium and low, and each one names the door it opens.
faq.t: What a stranger can learn about you

faq.q: Is anything about my passkey sent to a server?
faq.a: No, and there is no server here to send it to. The challenge is generated in this page, the public key is kept in this browser's localStorage, and the signature is verified in this tab with Web Crypto. Open your Network tab and press every button on this page; nothing carrying anything you did will appear. The private key was never available to send in the first place, because no WebAuthn call returns one.

faq.q: Is this a real passkey or a simulation?
faq.a: Real. The page calls navigator.credentials.create and navigator.credentials.get, your own authenticator answers, and every structure on screen is decoded from what it returned. The one simulated thing is the lookalike origin, because a browser will not let a page produce a genuine assertion for a domain it is not served from, and that refusal is exactly the lesson.

faq.q: Can I use this passkey to sign in to something else?
faq.a: No. It is scoped to this site's RP ID, so no other site will ever be offered it. It also protects nothing here, because there is no account behind it and no server checking anything. It exists so you can watch the machinery, and then delete it in whichever password manager or security key stored it.

faq.q: Why did the AAGUID come back as all zeroes?
faq.a: Because the authenticator declined to identify its model, which is the normal and privacy preserving answer. An identifier for the make and model attached to every registration would be a tracking signal, so platform authenticators and synced passkey providers usually return zeroes unless a site asks for attestation and the platform agrees to supply it.

faq.q: What do the BE and BS flags actually change for me?
faq.a: They tell you where the private key lives. BE set means the credential is the kind that can be synced to an account; BS set means it currently is. A synced passkey survives a lost phone and inherits the security of the account it syncs through. A device bound one does not survive the phone, which is why anyone relying on a hardware key is told to enrol a second one.

faq.q: Is my password sent anywhere?
faq.a: No. It is analysed by JavaScript in your browser as you type. There is no server, no logging and no network request. A password strength checker with a server behind it is a password collection service with a helpful interface.

faq.q: Does it check whether my password was in a data breach?
faq.a: No, deliberately. Every breach-check service needs to receive something derived from your password. Doing that well requires k-anonymity and a network call, and this page makes no network calls at all. Use Have I Been Pwned separately if you want that check.

faq.q: Why does my password score lower than on other sites?
faq.a: Because most meters score composition - did you include a capital and a symbol - rather than entropy. This one subtracts for dictionary words, keyboard runs, dates and the common Capital-word-digits-symbol shape, because attackers try all of those first.

faq.q: Is the generator actually random?
faq.a: It uses crypto.getRandomValues, the browser cryptographic random source. It does not use Math.random, which is predictable and must never pick a password.

faq.q: How long should a password be?
faq.a: For something protecting real value, 16 characters random or five random words. For your password manager master password, longer, and never reused anywhere.

faq.q: Is my capture uploaded?
faq.a: No. It is parsed in your browser with the FileReader API and no network request. Captures contain credentials and internal detail, so local-only is the only responsible design.

faq.q: What formats does it read?
faq.a: Classic PCAP (both byte orders and the nanosecond variants) and PCAPNG. It dissects Ethernet, IPv4/IPv6, TCP, UDP, ICMP and ARP.

faq.q: Can it really recover passwords?
faq.a: For unencrypted protocols, yes - HTTP Basic auth, FTP, Telnet, SMTP/POP3/IMAP login. That is the point: it shows exactly what an attacker on the wire would see, which is the argument for never using those protocols in the clear.

faq.q: Can it read HTTPS traffic?
faq.a: No. TLS-encrypted payloads stay encrypted - it will show that the connection happened and to where, but not the contents. That is the whole reason HTTPS exists.

faq.q: How big a capture can it handle?
faq.a: Up to 128 MB, and it dissects the first 50,000 packets, saying so if it stops there.

faq.q: Is my document uploaded?
faq.a: No. There is no server here to upload it to. The file is read with FileReader, parsed in this tab, and handed back as a blob URL. That matters more for PDFs than for almost anything else, because the documents people put into a free PDF site are contracts, bank statements, medical letters and passport scans.
faq.t: PDF tools that never see your document

faq.q: Can it open a password-protected PDF?
faq.a: No. If the trailer carries an /Encrypt dictionary then the strings and streams are ciphertext, and copying them into a new file unchanged would produce something that opens and then shows nothing. So it reports what the encryption is and refuses. Remove the protection in the application that made the file, then come back.
faq.t: PDF tools that never see your document

faq.q: Will merging change my images or fonts?
faq.a: No. Content streams, embedded font files and image data are copied byte for byte with their original filters intact. Nothing is decoded and re-encoded, which is why there is no quality setting anywhere on this page and why the pixels that come out are the pixels that went in.
faq.t: PDF tools that never see your document

faq.q: What does the output leave behind?
faq.a: Bookmarks, the AcroForm dictionary and any filled form data, document-level JavaScript, and the tagged-PDF structure tree that screen readers use. All four index the whole original document, and half a copy of an index is worse than none. If you need any of them preserved, this is the wrong tool, and I would rather say so here than have you find out afterwards.
faq.t: PDF tools that never see your document

faq.q: Why did it say the cross-reference index was rebuilt?
faq.a: Because the index inside the file did not lead anywhere usable, so the whole file was scanned for objects instead. That happens with a truncated download, a file something was still writing, or one edited by a program that got its offsets wrong. Rebuilding is what real readers do and the pages usually come back intact - but it is worth knowing the file is damaged.
faq.t: PDF tools that never see your document

faq.q: Does it make the file smaller?
faq.a: No, and a merged file is often a little larger than the parts it came from. Nothing is recompressed, and the output uses a plain cross-reference table rather than the compressed one modern producers write, which costs about twenty bytes per object. A tool that shrank your document would have to re-encode its images, and that is precisely what this one refuses to do.
faq.t: PDF tools that never see your document

faq.q: Are the swatches photographs of the real elements?
faq.a: No, and they are not trying to be. This site ships no licensed photographs and fetches nothing from anywhere else, so every swatch is drawn in your browser from an explicit descriptor - one base colour, a phase, and a surface kind such as lustrous metal, brittle crystal, glowing gas or liquid metal - using CSS gradients and inline SVG. The aim is that a metal reads as metal and a gas reads as a gas, not that it passes for a photograph.
faq.t: The periodic table, drawn as the elements actually look

faq.q: How accurate are the numbers?
faq.a: The atomic weights are the IUPAC abridged values; melting and boiling points are in kelvin at one atmosphere; radii are the empirical (Slater) values, which is why the noble gases have none - those values come from bond lengths and the noble gases do not form the bonds. Everything is stated to the precision the source gives it. Where a value is genuinely disputed or has never been measured, the page says unknown rather than filling the gap with something plausible.
faq.t: The periodic table, drawn as the elements actually look

faq.q: Why do so many of the heavy elements say unknown?
faq.a: Because nobody has measured them. Above fermium the elements have never existed in weighable amounts - most have been made a few atoms at a time and lasted milliseconds - so their melting points, densities and radii are relativistic-chemistry predictions rather than measurements, and several have no accepted prediction at all. Those elements carry a warning in the panel and their unmeasured values read unknown. A number invented to fill the cell would look more complete and be worse than useless.
faq.t: The periodic table, drawn as the elements actually look

faq.q: Why are the lanthanides and actinides in separate rows at the bottom?
faq.a: Purely to make the table fit. Elements 57 to 71 and 89 to 103 belong between groups 2 and 3 of periods 6 and 7; leaving them there makes the table 32 columns wide. Pulling them out is the conventional compromise, and the 57-71 and 89-103 markers stand where the block really belongs - pressing Enter on one jumps down to the row. IUPAC assigns no group numbers across the f-block, and which two of these elements belong in group 3 is still argued over, so this table shows no group number for them rather than picking a side.
faq.t: The periodic table, drawn as the elements actually look

faq.q: What does the temperature slider do?
faq.a: Set the colouring to state at temperature and the slider recolours every element solid, liquid or gas for that temperature at one atmosphere, worked out from its melting and boiling points. At 298 K only mercury and bromine are liquid; wind it up and you can watch the table melt in order. Three elements are handled as special cases: carbon and arsenic sublime rather than melt at atmospheric pressure, and helium does not freeze at atmospheric pressure at any temperature.
faq.t: The periodic table, drawn as the elements actually look

faq.q: Is the shell diagram how electrons really behave?
faq.a: No. Electrons do not orbit the nucleus in rings; they occupy probability clouds with shapes the diagram cannot show. A Bohr picture is wrong about where the electrons are and right about how many are in each shell, which is the fact it is here to make visible. The ring counts are summed straight out of the electron configuration printed beside them, so the picture and the text cannot drift apart.
faq.t: The periodic table, drawn as the elements actually look

faq.q: Can I use it with a keyboard?
faq.a: Yes. Tab into the table and the arrow keys move between elements by their real position, skipping the gaps; Home and End jump to the ends of a row, Ctrl+Home and Ctrl+End to hydrogen and oganesson. Moving the selection updates the detail panel, which is announced as a live region, and every tile carries a spoken label with the name, symbol, number, category, group and period.
faq.t: The periodic table, drawn as the elements actually look

faq.q: Does it run on my machine?
faq.a: Entirely. The element data is embedded in the page's own JavaScript, the swatches and diagrams are drawn in your browser, and there is no network call of any kind. Once the page is cached it works offline.
faq.t: The periodic table, drawn as the elements actually look

faq.q: Is this real Perl?
faq.a: Yes — Perl 5 compiled to WebAssembly through the WebPerl project. The regex engine in particular is the genuine one, which is the part most worth having.

faq.q: Can I install CPAN modules?
faq.a: No. CPAN needs a network and a toolchain, neither of which exists here. The core modules that ship with Perl are available.

faq.q: Why is the first run slow?
faq.a: Perl and its library come to about 3.8 MB compressed, downloaded once and then cached by your browser; they unpack to roughly 16 MB in the cache.

faq.q: Can I read from STDIN?
faq.a: Not currently — the program runs with no interactive input, so put your data in the script itself. The examples above all do.

faq.q: Is my Perl code private?
faq.a: Entirely. It runs in your browser and is never transmitted anywhere.

faq.q: Is anything I paste uploaded?
faq.a: No. The message is parsed in your browser and nothing is sent anywhere. That matters more here than almost anywhere else in Labs, because a phishing report carries the recipient's address, internal hostnames and often the contents of a real business conversation.

faq.q: Why is there no percentage or risk score?
faq.a: Because there is no calibration behind one. A number would imply that the checks were weighed against a measured population of real mail, and they were not. It is also the part people would remember instead of the reasons, and the reasons are the useful bit. Findings are grouped by severity and quoted with the bytes that produced them.

faq.q: Does a clean result mean the email is safe?
faq.a: No, and the tool says so in the output. A plain message from a real colleague's compromised mailbox, with a genuine signature and a genuine reply address, passes every check here and is still fraud. These checks catch impersonation and misdirection. They cannot catch a legitimate mailbox in the wrong hands.

faq.q: Where do I get the raw message?
faq.a: Gmail: open the message, three-dot menu, Show original. Outlook: File, Properties, Internet headers, and copy the body separately. Apple Mail: View, Message, Raw Source. A body pasted on its own works too, and so does a single URL - you just get fewer checks, and the tool says which ones it skipped.

faq.q: Why does it not analyse the Received headers?
faq.a: Because that is a whole tool on its own and it already exists. The hop chain, the timing between hops and the originating IP are handled by the email header analyser at /labs/email-headers. This one reads the parts of a message a human is asked to trust: the name in the From line, the text of a link against where it goes, the name of an attachment, and the wording.

faq.q: Why does a legitimate email trip several checks?
faq.a: Because ordinary bulk mail is built out of the same parts as a phishing email. A click-tracker is a redirect chain, a mailing provider puts a different domain in the envelope, and an unsubscribe link is a per-recipient token. The legitimate worked example exists to show exactly that, and every one of those findings is reported as low with the reason it is probably fine.

faq.q: Is this really PHP 8?
faq.a: Yes — PHP 8.4, compiled to WebAssembly. Enums, match expressions and readonly properties all work, which is the quickest way to confirm it for yourself.

faq.q: Can I use Composer packages or Laravel?
faq.a: No. Composer needs a network and a package repository, and frameworks additionally need a web server and usually a database. This runs single PHP scripts.

faq.q: Do $_GET and $_POST work?
faq.a: No. Those are populated by a web server handling a request; there is no request and no server here. Put your data in the script.

faq.q: Can I connect to MySQL?
faq.a: No. There is no network access at all. For databases, the SQL and PostgreSQL playgrounds run real engines locally instead.

faq.q: Do I need the <?php tag?
faq.a: No — it is added automatically if your script does not start with one. Including it yourself is fine too.

faq.q: Is this really PostgreSQL, or something compatible?
faq.a: It is genuinely PostgreSQL — the server source, compiled to WebAssembly by the PGlite project. That is why JSONB, window functions and Postgres' own error messages all behave exactly as they do on a real install.

faq.q: How is this different from the SQL playground?
faq.a: The other one runs SQLite, which is a different database with a different dialect. SQLite is a 350 KB download and starts instantly; Postgres is a 5.5 MB download and gives you the full feature set. Use SQLite to practise general SQL, and this when you specifically need Postgres behaviour.

faq.q: Does my data persist?
faq.a: No. A fresh in-memory database is created per run, which is why the starter script carries its own schema. Keep the CREATE and INSERT statements at the top.

faq.q: Can I install extensions like PostGIS?
faq.a: No. Only what is bundled is available, and there is no network to fetch anything from.

faq.q: Is my SQL private?
faq.a: Completely. The server runs in your browser's memory and is destroyed when the run ends. Nothing is transmitted.

faq.q: Is this a real chip layout?
faq.a: It is an accurate illustration of the hierarchy rather than a photograph of one specific processor. The containment and the data paths are real - package holds the die, the die holds cores and cache, a core holds a pipeline, and so on down to transistors - but the geometry is stylised so each level stays readable.

faq.q: How do I move around?
faq.a: Scroll to zoom in and out, use the + and - buttons or the depth slider, or click a level on the depth rail to jump straight there. Play/pause controls the data animation and reset returns you to the package view.

faq.q: How is this different from the CPU simulator?
faq.a: The CPU simulator runs code - you write assembly and step through it watching registers change. This one is the physical journey: what a processor is made of, from the outside in. One is about execution, the other about structure.

faq.q: Does it need a powerful machine?
faq.a: No. It is canvas 2D drawing, not 3D rendering, so it runs comfortably on any modern browser and respects your reduced-motion setting if you have one.

faq.q: Is anything uploaded?
faq.a: No. Every frame is drawn in your browser and there is no network request.

faq.q: Is this real Python or a simulation?
faq.a: It is real CPython, compiled to WebAssembly through the Pyodide project. The interpreter is the genuine article, which is why tracebacks and edge-case behaviour match what you get locally.

faq.q: Can I use pip install, NumPy or pandas?
faq.a: No. This playground is deliberately limited to the standard library. Installing packages requires a package index and network access, and neither is available by design.

faq.q: How do I give input to input()?
faq.a: Type it into the Input panel below the output, one value per line, before pressing Run. Each call to input() consumes the next line.

faq.q: Why is the first run slower?
faq.a: CPython plus the standard library is about 5.5 MB compressed, downloaded once. It unpacks to roughly 12 MB in the browser cache, so subsequent runs start almost instantly — and it then works offline.

faq.q: Is my Python code private?
faq.a: Completely. The interpreter runs in your browser using your own memory and CPU. Your code is never transmitted, stored or seen by anyone.

faq.q: What if my program never finishes?
faq.a: It runs in a Worker separate from the page, so your tab stays usable. A warning with a Cancel button appears after a few seconds, and the run is killed at sixty seconds.

faq.q: Can I scan a QR code to receive money?
faq.a: No. There is no such thing on UPI. Every UPI QR code is a request for the person scanning it to pay. A pay QR and a supposed receive QR look identical because there is only one kind. Anyone telling you to scan a code, or to enter your UPI PIN, in order to receive a refund or a prize is taking money out of your account. Receiving money on UPI never needs your PIN.
faq.t: vCard, Wi-Fi and UPI QR payload builder

faq.q: Can this tell me whether a UPI address is genuine?
faq.a: No, and it says so on screen every time. Checking that a VPA exists or belongs to anyone means asking NPCI, which is a network request, and this page makes none. What it can do is read the string: the shape of the handle, whether the amount is fixed or left for you, whether the payee name borrows authority or contains letters from another alphabet drawn like Latin ones. All of that is judged on the text, not on reality.
faq.t: vCard, Wi-Fi and UPI QR payload builder

faq.q: Why does it not draw the QR code?
faq.a: Because the QR encoder already exists at /labs/qr and there should be exactly one of it on this site. Two encoders means two things to check and two places for a bug to hide. This page produces the exact string; paste it into /labs/qr and that page draws the square, picks the mask and tells you which version it needed.
faq.t: vCard, Wi-Fi and UPI QR payload builder

faq.q: What is line folding and why does it matter?
faq.a: iCalendar and vCard say a line should not exceed 75 octets, and a longer one is split by a line break plus a single space. Almost nothing implements it, and the rule that gets missed most is that the split must not fall inside a multi-octet character. Skip that and a description in Devanagari or with an emoji arrives corrupted, silently. The folder here counts octets, never splits a character, and prints the length of every line so you can see it.
faq.t: vCard, Wi-Fi and UPI QR payload builder

faq.q: Is it safe to put my Wi-Fi password in a QR code?
faq.a: The password is inside the code in clear text and there is no way around that; the format has no room for anything else. Anyone who photographs the printed square has it permanently. On a guest network that reaches the internet and not the printer, the NAS or the cameras, that is a reasonable trade. On your main network it hands out the keys to everything on it.
faq.t: vCard, Wi-Fi and UPI QR payload builder

faq.q: Does anything I type here leave my browser?
faq.a: No. There is no fetch and no XHR in the code, no URL found in a payload is opened, resolved or previewed, and no address is looked up anywhere. That matters more here than on most pages, because the things people paste into a payload tool are Wi-Fi passwords, home coordinates and payment addresses.
faq.t: vCard, Wi-Fi and UPI QR payload builder

faq.q: Does anything here open the link inside a QR code?
faq.a: No. The payload is printed as text and handed to you with a Copy button. There is no automatic navigation, no preview fetch and no redirect following, because requesting a URL tells whoever made the code that someone is looking at it.

faq.q: Can a QR code be used to send me money?
faq.a: No. A UPI QR code names an account to pay, and your PIN authorises money leaving your account. Scanning one can only send. If somebody asks you to scan a code so that you can receive a refund, a prize or a deposit, the money moves the other way and it is a scam.

faq.q: What is quishing?
faq.a: Phishing delivered as a QR code. It works because a picture carries no link for a mail gateway or a chat filter to check, and because you cannot hover a square to see where it goes. The physical version is a printed sticker placed over a real code on a parking meter, a restaurant table or a donation box.

faq.q: Why will it not read my photo?
faq.a: Usually the code is too small in the frame, cut off at an edge, badly blurred, or shot at a steep angle. Fill more of the frame, leave a margin of blank space around the code, and shoot square-on. This reads model 2 QR codes only - Micro QR, Data Matrix, Aztec and PDF417 look similar and are different formats.

faq.q: Is what I type or scan uploaded anywhere?
faq.a: No. The encoder and the decoder both run in this tab and there is no network call in either. A Wi-Fi password you type into the generator, and a payment code you drop into the inspector, stay on your machine.

faq.q: Is a rainbow table just a big lookup table?
faq.a: No, and conflating the two is the most common mistake here. A lookup table maps every digest straight to its plaintext. A rainbow table stores only the start and end of long chains built by alternating a hash and a reduction function, then walks a target hash to find a matching endpoint. It trades computation at crack time for a much smaller stored table. Step 4 builds a real one so you can watch the walk.
faq.t: Salt and rainbow tables, built live in your browser

faq.q: Does salting make a password uncrackable?
faq.a: No. The salt is stored in the clear next to the hash, so an attacker targeting one account simply re-hashes the wordlist with that account’s salt, and a weak password still falls. What salting removes is the ability to attack everyone at once with a single precomputed table. Combine a salt with a deliberately slow hash and each of those per-user attacks also becomes expensive. Step 3 demonstrates both halves.
faq.t: Salt and rainbow tables, built live in your browser

faq.q: Why does the rainbow demo use MD5 and not SHA-256?
faq.a: The chain walk needs tens of thousands of fast, sequential hashes, and crypto.subtle is asynchronous, which makes that slow and awkward. MD5 is implemented directly in the page, runs synchronously, and is exactly the fast, unsalted, legacy hash that rainbow tables were ever effective against. The lookup-table steps still let you pick SHA-1 and SHA-256.
faq.t: Salt and rainbow tables, built live in your browser

faq.q: Are the speed numbers a real benchmark?
faq.a: No. They are one browser, on one machine, on one day, and they move with JIT warm-up and thermal state. The SHA-256 rate is also throttled by per-call overhead in JavaScript, so it sits far below what native code or a GPU manages. Use the ratio between the fast and slow hash, which is the honest signal; do not read either absolute rate as a hardware figure.
faq.t: Salt and rainbow tables, built live in your browser

faq.q: Is my pasted hash uploaded anywhere?
faq.a: No. Everything runs in this browser tab. SHA-1 and SHA-256 go through the browser’s built-in crypto.subtle, which is local, and MD5 is implemented in the page itself. There is no fetch, no upload and no server. A hash you paste never appears in your Network tab.
faq.t: Salt and rainbow tables, built live in your browser

faq.q: Can this crack my real password hash?
faq.a: Only if the plaintext happens to be one of the few thousand common passwords in the built-in wordlist and the hash is unsalted. That is the point: weak, unsalted hashes fall instantly, and anything else does not. This is a teaching demonstration, not a cracking rig, and it says its limits out loud in the output.
faq.t: Salt and rainbow tables, built live in your browser

faq.q: Does this page encrypt anything on my machine?
faq.a: No. There is no cipher anywhere in this page, no call to any cryptography API, and no file of yours is read at any point. The file tree is invented and lives in this tab's memory. The key strings on screen are labels produced by a counter so that stepping backwards shows the same value it showed going forwards. It is a diagram that moves, not a program that does anything.
faq.t: How a ransomware incident actually unfolds

faq.q: Is this a guide to building ransomware?
faq.a: No, and it is written to be useless as one. There is no sample, no code, no tool named, no command shown and no evasion technique described in a way anybody could act on. Every stage is named at the level a board paper names it, because helping somebody write that board paper is the entire purpose. The audience for this page is people who have to fund backups.
faq.t: How a ransomware incident actually unfolds

faq.q: Why is paying the only way back without a backup?
faq.a: Because of how the keys are arranged. Each file gets its own fresh symmetric key, and that key is immediately wrapped with a public key shipped inside the binary, then discarded from memory. The wrapped key sits on your own disk next to the file. Only the matching private key opens it, and that private key never came near your network. So the thing you need is right there in front of you and cannot be opened, and the only party who can open it is the one asking for money.
faq.t: How a ransomware incident actually unfolds

faq.q: Does an offline backup really break the model?
faq.a: It breaks the leverage, which is the part that matters. Finding and deleting your backups is a deliberate, targeted step taken before anything is encrypted, precisely because a restore is the only thing that makes the ransom optional. A copy that is genuinely offline, or immutable because the storage enforces retention rather than an account that can be taken over, survives that step. It does not stop the intrusion, it does not un-copy the data they stole, and it is worthless if nobody has ever tested a restore from it.
faq.t: How a ransomware incident actually unfolds

faq.q: Does paying actually get the data back?
faq.a: Paying buys a decryption tool written by the people who broke your estate, not a restore. Those tools are routinely slow, sometimes buggy, and partial or corrupted returns are normal rather than exceptional. You still have to rebuild the identity plane, because you are not handing an environment back to production while somebody else has held domain admin in it for three weeks. And the copy of your data they took before any encryption started is still theirs. Whether paying is even lawful depends on who is on the other end, and that is a question for a lawyer rather than for this page.
faq.t: How a ransomware incident actually unfolds

faq.q: Which one control should we buy first?
faq.a: The page deliberately refuses to answer that, because the answer changes with the door. Switch multi-factor authentication on and the exposed remote desktop route dies at stage one, while the phishing route is entirely unaffected and the unpatched appliance route does not even see a login prompt. That is the argument for depth: a single control halts one path, and the operator is running the same playbook against a list you are one line of. If you want a starting point rather than an answer, the two that change the ending rather than the story are backups you have restore-tested and somebody rostered to read the alerts you already generate.
faq.t: How a ransomware incident actually unfolds

faq.q: Where do the numbers in the cost panel come from?
faq.a: From you. The panel does arithmetic on figures you type, and the defaults are illustrative placeholders rather than a benchmark. Published figures for downtime cost, ransom size, restore rate and decryptor failure disagree with each other by an order of magnitude depending on who was surveyed and who paid for the survey, so quoting one would look authoritative and tell you nothing. The shape of the arithmetic is the finding: the first steps are identical whichever way you go, and the paths only separate later than people expect.
faq.t: How a ransomware incident actually unfolds

faq.q: What is RDAP and why not just use WHOIS?
faq.a: RDAP is the ICANN-mandated replacement: same registry data, structured JSON, over HTTPS, with proper internationalisation and access control. WHOIS is an unstructured text protocol from 1982 over raw TCP port 43, which no browser can open.

faq.q: Does this go through a proxy?
faq.a: No. Your browser requests rdap.org, which redirects to the registry authoritative for that TLD, and your browser follows the redirect directly. I never see the query.

faq.q: Why does it fail for some domains?
faq.a: Either the TLD has no RDAP service, or its registry omits the CORS headers a browser needs. Both are common with country-code TLDs, and the browser will not say which it was.

faq.q: Why is the registrant hidden?
faq.a: GDPR. Registries redact personal contact data for registrants in scope, so you usually see the registrar and little else.

faq.q: Can I check whether a domain is available?
faq.a: Indirectly - a 404 usually means unregistered. A registrar’s search is the reliable way, and note that some registrars have historically front-run availability searches.

faq.q: How is this different from the regex engine lab?
faq.a: The engine lab steps a backtracking matcher, which is what almost every language ships. This one compiles the pattern into a machine first: parse tree, NFA, DFA, minimal DFA, then run. Both are on the site because the comparison is the interesting part, and the last tab here runs them side by side with step counters.
faq.t: Regex to NFA to DFA, and back to why one of them cannot be slow

faq.q: Why does it refuse backreferences?
faq.a: Because it cannot do them, and neither can anything else in this family. A backreference needs the machine to remember an arbitrarily long earlier match and compare it again. A finite automaton has finitely many states and no other memory, so no automaton recognises that language. RE2 and Go's regexp refuse them for exactly the same reason.
faq.t: Regex to NFA to DFA, and back to why one of them cannot be slow

faq.q: Are the step counts real or modelled?
faq.a: Counted. There is a real recursive backtracking matcher and a real DFA loop on this page, each incrementing its own counter, and the plot is drawn from those counters. The backtracker is capped so it cannot hang the tab, and any capped point is marked on the plot and labelled in the table.
faq.t: Regex to NFA to DFA, and back to why one of them cannot be slow

faq.q: Why Moore's algorithm and not Hopcroft's?
faq.a: Hopcroft is faster, and for a production tool it is the right choice. Moore refines the partition in visible rounds, and the round in which two states come apart names the character that separated them. That narration is the entire point of the minimisation tab; Hopcroft's worklist order is efficient and unexplainable.
faq.t: Regex to NFA to DFA, and back to why one of them cannot be slow

faq.q: Does it handle Unicode?
faq.a: Not really, and it says so. The alphabet is the 128 ASCII codes plus one catch-all symbol for everything above U+007F, so the machine cannot tell two non-ASCII characters apart. Real engines fold the alphabet into equivalence classes the same way; they just have the Unicode tables to do it properly.
faq.t: Regex to NFA to DFA, and back to why one of them cannot be slow

faq.q: Does anything I type get uploaded?
faq.a: No. There is no server to upload to. The parser, both simulators and the drawing all run in your tab, which is why a pattern you are debugging at work can go in the box safely.
faq.t: Regex to NFA to DFA, and back to why one of them cannot be slow

faq.q: Does this use the built-in RegExp?
faq.a: No. The pattern is parsed by a recursive descent parser written for this page, compiled to a state machine, and run by three separate engines. JavaScript RegExp appears only in the test suite, as the reference the three are checked against.

faq.q: Why does it match the whole string instead of searching?
faq.a: Because partial matching brings in leftmost-longest rules, capture semantics and anchoring behaviour that differ between engines, and all of that would bury the lesson. Whole-string matching is unambiguous and makes the comparison against RegExp exact.

faq.q: Is my language vulnerable to ReDoS?
faq.a: If it uses a backtracking engine - Perl, Python, Java, .NET, Ruby, JavaScript - then yes, given the wrong pattern and attacker-controlled input. Go and Rust use RE2-style linear engines and are not. The defence is to avoid nested quantifiers over overlapping text, and to bound how long a match may run.
