faq.q: What does the static warning check?
faq.a: It looks for a quantifier directly inside another quantifier, and for an alternation inside a quantifier whose branches can match the same text. Those are the shapes that produce exponential backtracking. It is a heuristic, deliberately - deciding this exactly is not something a page should pretend to do, so the measured profile is the real answer.

faq.q: Which syntax is supported?
faq.a: Literals, dot, star, plus, question mark, alternation, groups, character classes with ranges and negation, and the shorthands for digit, word and space. Backreferences and lookaround are deliberately absent: they are exactly the features a state machine cannot express, which is why backtracking engines exist in the first place.

faq.q: What is ReDoS?
faq.a: Regular expression denial of service: a pattern whose matching time grows exponentially with input length, so a short crafted string can hang the process that evaluates it.

faq.q: How does the ReDoS check work?
faq.a: It runs your pattern against deliberately pathological strings of increasing length and measures the time. If it crosses a threshold, the growth is exponential and the pattern is flagged. It is an empirical test, not a formal proof, so a clean result means "no blow-up observed" rather than "provably safe".

faq.q: Which regex flavour is this?
faq.a: JavaScript, since it runs in your browser. Most of what you write will behave the same in PCRE, but lookbehind support, named group syntax and some Unicode property escapes differ.

faq.q: Is my pattern or test data sent anywhere?
faq.a: No. Both stay in your browser.

faq.q: Why does my pattern with a huge match count feel slow?
faq.a: The tool caps display at 60 matches and stops iterating at 5000 to keep the page responsive. A pattern that matches an empty string can also loop, which is guarded against.

faq.q: Is my hive file uploaded?
faq.a: No. It is parsed in your browser from the raw bytes, with no server and no network request.

faq.q: Which hives can it read?
faq.a: Any raw regf hive: SYSTEM, SOFTWARE, SAM, SECURITY, NTUSER.DAT, UsrClass.dat and Amcache. It recognises the common ones and surfaces their notable artefacts, and lets you browse any key tree directly.

faq.q: What forensic artefacts does it surface?
faq.a: Autostart (Run/RunOnce) keys, USB device history, RecentDocs, TypedURLs, RunMRU, the ROT13-decoded UserAssist run counts, installed programs, and user accounts - depending on which hive you load.

faq.q: Where do I get a hive file?
faq.a: On a live system they are locked, so they are usually taken from a forensic image or a volume shadow copy. NTUSER.DAT sits in each user profile; SYSTEM, SOFTWARE and SAM live in Windows\System32\config.

faq.q: Does it decode the timestamps?
faq.a: Yes. Key write times are Windows FILETIMEs and are shown as readable UTC.

faq.q: Why compare net worth instead of the EMI and the rent?
faq.a: Because the EMI and the rent are not the same kind of thing. Part of every EMI repays principal, which is savings you still own; rent buys you a month of shelter and nothing else. Meanwhile the renter is holding the down payment and the stamp duty. Net worth at the end of a stated horizon is the only comparison where both of those are counted, which is why this page computes that and refuses to headline the monthly figures.
faq.t: Rent versus buy, compared on net worth rather than on the monthly outgo

faq.q: What stamp duty rate should I put in?
faq.a: Whatever your state charges, which is why it is a field and not a constant. Stamp duty and registration are levied by the state, the rates differ by several percentage points across India, several states charge less when the buyer is a woman, and the duty may be assessed on the government ready-reckoner value rather than on the price in your agreement. This page has no way of knowing which state you are in, so it asks.
faq.t: Rent versus buy, compared on net worth rather than on the monthly outgo

faq.q: Does it handle 80C, section 24(b) and HRA?
faq.a: Yes, as an option that is off by default, and only for the old regime. Section 24(b) interest on a self-occupied property, 80C principal — sharing one ceiling with your PF, insurance and ELSS, and competing with the stamp duty in the year you buy — and the renter’s HRA exemption under 10(13A) as the least of its three tests, with the metro split. Every ceiling is a field, because they move with each Finance Act. The new regime removes all of it, so if you are in the new regime leave the toggle off. None of this is tax advice.
faq.t: Rent versus buy, compared on net worth rather than on the monthly outgo

faq.q: Why does it not just tell me which one is better?
faq.a: Because it does not know, and neither does anything else that claims to. The result is dominated by property appreciation and investment return, and those are forecasts. The sensitivity grid moves each of them by up to four points and recomputes the crossover year twenty-five times; the answer routinely flips inside that range. Printing one confident number on top of that would be dishonest, so the page prints the spread instead.
faq.t: Rent versus buy, compared on net worth rather than on the monthly outgo

faq.q: Does it model prepayment, a rate reset or an under-construction flat?
faq.a: No. There is no prepayment, no floating-rate reset, no loan top-up, no GST on an under-construction purchase, no possession delay and no one-time society corpus. Rent is assumed to be paid every month with no gap and no move. If you want to see what prepaying or a rate change does to a loan on its own, the loan and EMI lab handles all of that in detail.
faq.t: Rent versus buy, compared on net worth rather than on the monthly outgo

faq.q: Is anything I type uploaded?
faq.a: No. There is no server behind this page and no network request is made. The whole model — the amortisation, both portfolios, the tax arithmetic and the twenty-five sensitivity runs — is computed in your browser tab. A property price, a rent and a salary are not details worth handing to a website, which is exactly why the work happens here.
faq.t: Rent versus buy, compared on net worth rather than on the monthly outgo

faq.q: Is it really free, with no watermark?
faq.a: Yes. No account, no watermark, no paywall at the download step. The usual trick is to let you build the whole resume and then charge at the export button; this one cannot charge you there because the export button is your browser's print dialog.

faq.q: Is my data uploaded anywhere?
faq.a: No. There is no server behind this page, so there is nowhere to upload to. That matters for this particular form: name, phone, email, photo, and your entire work history are exactly the data resume sites collect and monetise. Here the form, the templates and the preview are all rendered in your own browser and nothing leaves it.

faq.q: How do I get a PDF?
faq.a: Press "Print / Save as PDF", and in the print dialog choose "Save as PDF" as the destination. The page is set up so only the resume prints — no site header, no buttons — on A4 with proper margins. Every browser has shipped this for years; it is the same engine paid sites use behind their download button.

faq.q: Will my data still be here tomorrow?
faq.a: No — and that is deliberate. Nothing you type is written to this device: the draft lives in the page's memory for that one session, so closing or reloading the tab clears it, and the next person to open this page on the same computer finds an empty form. Nothing to leave behind on a library PC, nothing for anyone to read later. The trade is that you have to keep a copy on purpose — press "Download data" before you leave and you get a resume-data.json file you own, and "Load data" brings it straight back. "Clear everything" empties the form on the spot.

faq.q: Can I move my data to another computer?
faq.a: Yes. Press "Download data" and you get a small resume-data.json file containing everything — every field, the photo, your chosen template, colour and paper size. Keep it as a backup, or copy it to another machine, open this page there and press "Load data". Your resume is a file you own, not a row in someone else's database.

faq.q: Can I print on US Letter?
faq.a: Yes. Flip the Paper toggle in the toolbar from A4 to US Letter and both the preview and the print dialog follow. A4 is the default because most of the world hires on it; switch to Letter if you are applying in the US or Canada, where it is the standard.

faq.q: Does it work offline?
faq.a: Yes. After your first visit the site's service worker keeps a copy of this page and its files in your browser, so it loads and prints with no connection at all. The tool never talked to a server in the first place, so once the page has arrived, nothing about it needs the internet.

faq.q: Can I use my own photo?
faq.a: Yes. Pick an image file and it is resized down in your browser — never uploaded — and placed into the templates that use one. Every template is also designed to look right without a photo, and for many corporate applications leaving it off is the safer choice.

faq.q: Will it pass ATS scanners?
faq.a: Use the Classic template for portals: it is a single-column layout with real selectable text and standard section names, which is exactly what parsers like. The fancier multi-column layouts — Sidebar, Banner, Compact — are for human readers, so send those as a PDF to a person, not to an upload portal.

faq.q: Is this real Ruby?
faq.a: Yes — CRuby, the reference implementation, compiled to WebAssembly by the Ruby core team. It is the same interpreter you would install locally.

faq.q: Can I use Rails or any gem?
faq.a: No. Gems need RubyGems and a network connection, neither of which exists here. The standard library that ships with Ruby is available.

faq.q: Why is the first run slow?
faq.a: The interpreter and its standard library are about 5 MB compressed, downloaded once and then cached by your browser; they unpack to roughly 17 MB in the cache.

faq.q: Can I read input with gets?
faq.a: Not currently. Ruby here runs as a script with no interactive stdin; put your data in the program itself.

faq.q: Is my Ruby code private?
faq.a: Entirely. It runs in your browser and is never transmitted anywhere.

faq.q: Which financial year are these slabs for?
faq.a: The year named in the banner at the top of the tool. That year lives in one place in the code, and the banner, the headings and the arithmetic are all rendered from it, so they cannot drift apart. Indian tax rules change with every Budget, so check the slabs, the standard deduction and the rebate against the current Finance Act before you rely on anything here. If they have moved, this page is out of date until I update it.
faq.t: CTC to in hand, with every step shown

faq.q: Is this tax advice?
faq.a: No. It is arithmetic, written out so you can check it rather than trust it. Your real liability depends on things this page never sees - other income, capital gains, a second employer in the same year, perquisites, an employer NPS contribution under 80CCD(2), arrears, or the declaration you gave payroll in April. For a number you are going to act on, talk to a chartered accountant.
faq.t: CTC to in hand, with every step shown

faq.q: Why does my payslip not match this exactly?
faq.a: Several small reasons that add up. Payroll usually posts the pension share of provident fund as a flat 1,250 rupees a month rather than 8.33 percent, applies professional tax on its own slab of monthly salary instead of the top rate, spreads TDS on a schedule of its own choosing, and may treat a reimbursement as taxable that this page assumes is not. The shape should match. The last few hundred rupees usually will not.
faq.t: CTC to in hand, with every step shown

faq.q: Does anything I type here get uploaded?
faq.a: No. There is no server, no account, and no analytics event that carries any figure you enter. A salary, a rent and a list of deductions together are close to identifying on their own, which is exactly why the whole calculation happens in this tab and why the page keeps working with the network switched off.
faq.t: CTC to in hand, with every step shown

faq.q: Should I ask for a lower basic so I take home more?
faq.a: Sometimes, and the sensitivity table shows you by exactly how much. A lower basic means less provident fund leaving your pay each month, but also a smaller employer contribution, a smaller gratuity accrual and a smaller HRA exemption if you are under the old regime. You are moving money between now and later, not creating any. Move the slider and decide which side you want it on.
faq.t: CTC to in hand, with every step shown

faq.q: Is my lockfile uploaded?
faq.a: No. It is read locally, parsed locally, and the SBOM is built locally and handed back through a blob URL. No network request is made at any point. That matters more than usual here: a lockfile for a private project names your internal packages, your registry hostnames and your whole dependency graph.

faq.q: Will it tell me if a package has a known vulnerability?
faq.a: No, and it never will. Matching a version against known advisories requires an advisory database, which requires a network request, which this page does not make. Export the CycloneDX file and feed it to a scanner that does. What this tool gives you is the inventory, produced without sending it anywhere first.

faq.q: Why does it say a check is “unavailable” instead of just zero?
faq.a: Because those are different answers and the difference matters. A v1 lockfile has no install-script flag and no licence field, so a report showing zero install scripts and no licence problems would be describing the file format rather than your project. Where the evidence cannot exist, the tool says so.

faq.q: Does it read yarn.lock or pnpm-lock.yaml?
faq.a: No. It recognises them and refuses them by name. Each format needs its own parser, and a half-parse would produce counts that look plausible and are wrong, which is worse than no answer. Handled: npm package-lock.json v1, v2 and v3, package.json, and requirements.txt including pip-compile output.

faq.q: A package came back flagged as a lookalike. Is it malicious?
faq.a: Unknown, and this page cannot find out. Plenty of legitimate packages sit one or two edits from a popular name — the tool proves it by running the same distance test across its own list of well-known packages and printing how many pairs it flags. Treat a flag as a prompt to open the registry page and look at the publisher, the repository and the publish dates.

faq.q: Is the exported CycloneDX file actually valid?
faq.a: It is written to the 1.5 schema: bomFormat, specVersion, a fresh random serial number, metadata with the producing tool, components typed as libraries with purls, and a dependencies graph where the lockfile made one derivable. Fields the input could not supply are omitted rather than filled with placeholders, because an SBOM that invents data is worse than a short one.

faq.q: Do I need WebGL support?
faq.a: Yes, which every current browser has. If the canvas stays black, your browser or GPU may have WebGL disabled or blocklisted.

faq.q: What uniforms are available?
faq.a: u_time (seconds since start), u_resolution (canvas size in pixels) and u_mouse (cursor position) - the same trio most shader toys provide, enough for animation and interaction.

faq.q: Is this like Shadertoy?
faq.a: The same idea - a live fragment-shader editor - running entirely in your browser with no account and nothing uploaded. The uniform names differ slightly, so a Shadertoy shader may need small tweaks.

faq.q: Why does my shader show an error?
faq.a: The GPU driver rejected it during compilation; the error text and line number are shown. Common causes are a missing semicolon, a type mismatch, or precision not being declared.

faq.q: Does it run on my machine?
faq.a: Yes, on your GPU, in your browser. Nothing is uploaded.

faq.q: Which SQL dialect is this?
faq.a: SQLite. It covers standard SQL closely for everyday querying, including window functions and CTEs, but MySQL- or PostgreSQL-specific syntax will not work.

faq.q: Does my data persist between runs?
faq.a: No. A fresh in-memory database is created for every run, which is why the starter script includes its own CREATE TABLE and INSERT statements. Keep them at the top.

faq.q: Can I upload a .db or .sql file?
faq.a: Not currently. Everything has to be written as statements in the editor.

faq.q: Is this good for practising SQL interview questions?
faq.a: Yes, particularly for joins, grouping, subqueries and window functions. Just be aware that if the interview targets MySQL or PostgreSQL specifically, a few functions will differ.

faq.q: Is my query data private?
faq.a: Entirely. The database lives in your browser's memory and is destroyed when the run ends. Nothing is sent anywhere.

faq.q: Is my database uploaded?
faq.a: No. It is loaded into sql.js - a real SQLite engine compiled to WebAssembly - entirely in your browser. There is no server and no network request.

faq.q: Can I open a Chrome or WhatsApp database?
faq.a: Yes. Point it at the file and it will recognise common forensic databases from their schema, offer a useful preset query, and decode their timestamps. WhatsApp message databases are often encrypted (.crypt14), which must be decrypted first with the key - this opens the decrypted .db.

faq.q: Will it change my file?
faq.a: No. The database is loaded into memory; any query, even a write, affects only that in-memory copy. The file on disk is untouched.

faq.q: Why does a query fail with "no such table"?
faq.a: Table names are case-sensitive and some contain characters that need quoting. Use the table dropdown to see exact names, or query sqlite_master to list them.

faq.q: What is the size limit?
faq.a: Up to 256 MB. Beyond that the browser tab struggles to hold the whole database in memory.

faq.q: What is steganography?
faq.a: Hiding the existence of a message rather than its contents. Encryption makes a message unreadable; steganography makes it unnoticed. They solve different problems and are strongest used together.

faq.q: Why must the output be a PNG?
faq.a: PNG is lossless, so the exact bit values survive. JPEG is lossy and recalculates pixel values during compression, which destroys the hidden data completely.

faq.q: Can this extract messages hidden by other tools?
faq.a: Only if they use the same scheme - last bit of each RGB channel, in order, with a 32-bit length header. Bit order and channel order vary between implementations. The low-bit view still helps you see whether anything is there.

faq.q: Is the image uploaded?
faq.a: No. The pixels are read and rewritten in your browser, and the result comes back as a download.

faq.q: How much can I hide in one image?
faq.a: Roughly three bits per pixel, so about 375 KB per megapixel. The exact capacity for your image is shown when you load it.

faq.q: What does /24 mean?
faq.a: The first 24 bits are the network portion, leaving 8 bits for hosts - 256 addresses, of which 254 are usable. It is equivalent to the subnet mask 255.255.255.0.

faq.q: Why does a /24 have 254 usable hosts and not 256?
faq.a: The first address identifies the network and the last is the broadcast address. Neither can be assigned to a host.

faq.q: Does this support IPv6?
faq.a: Not currently. IPv6 subnetting is simpler in practice - the prefix is almost always /64 for a LAN - and the address arithmetic needs 128-bit maths that this tool does not implement yet.

faq.q: Does it look up who owns the address?
faq.a: No. There are no WHOIS, geolocation or reputation lookups, because each of those tells a third party which address you are investigating. The classification shown comes from the reserved-range definitions in the RFCs, which are fixed.

faq.q: What is 169.254.x.x?
faq.a: A link-local address, assigned by the machine itself when DHCP failed. Seeing one usually means the device never got a lease.

faq.q: Are the sequence numbers real?
faq.a: Yes. The handshake tracks genuine seq/ack arithmetic - a SYN or FIN consumes one sequence number, data advances the sequence by its length, and each acknowledgement is the next byte expected. The test suite checks these against the worked examples in RFC 793.

faq.q: Which congestion-control algorithm is this?
faq.a: TCP Reno: slow start, congestion avoidance, fast retransmit and fast recovery. It is the classic textbook algorithm and the ancestor of what most systems still run. Modern variants like CUBIC and BBR change the growth curve, but the core idea - probe up, back off on loss - is the one shown here.

faq.q: Why does the window collapse to 1 on a timeout but only halve on duplicate ACKs?
faq.a: Because they signal different things. Duplicate ACKs mean packets are still arriving, so the path is working and a gentle cut is enough. A timeout means the sender has heard nothing back, so it must assume the pipe has drained and start probing from scratch. That asymmetry is deliberate and is the shape of the sawtooth.

faq.q: Is this a real network connection?
faq.a: No. It is a simulation of the protocol running as arithmetic in your browser. Nothing is sent, no socket is opened, and the only real TCP involved is the one that delivered this page. Change the inputs and the simulation recomputes; that is all it is doing.

faq.q: Is anything uploaded?
faq.a: No. Every segment and every round trip is computed locally, and there is no network request.

faq.q: Does a threat model like this prove anything?
faq.a: No. It is a thinking tool and a record of a conversation, not a certification, an audit or a test. It says what a group of people thought could go wrong on a particular day. It says nothing about whether the mitigations were built, whether they work, or whether somebody has already got in. Anyone who hands you a threat model as evidence of security has misunderstood what it is for.

faq.q: Why STRIDE and not something else?
faq.a: Because it is the easiest framework to start with and the hardest to argue with. Six categories, a fixed mapping from element types to categories, and no scoring to disagree about. It is one framework among several: LINDDUN handles privacy properly, PASTA is risk and attacker centred, and an attack tree suits one specific question better than a whole system. Any of them would find things STRIDE misses.

faq.q: Where is my work saved?
faq.a: In this browser, on this device, under the localStorage key lab.threat-model. It is not sent anywhere and it is not readable by any other site. A private window, cleared site data or a different browser will not have it, which is exactly why the JSON export exists. Export the file if the model matters.

faq.q: How does the tool decide which threats apply?
faq.a: It applies the classic STRIDE-per-element table and nothing more. External entities can be spoofed and can repudiate. Processes are exposed to all six. Data stores can be tampered with, read, destroyed, and repudiated against when they are a record of events. Data flows can be tampered with, read and blocked. That table is the whole of the automation here. The tool has not understood your architecture, and the proposals are prompts for you to answer, not findings.

faq.q: Why are likelihood and impact only three levels?
faq.a: Because more levels invite a precision nobody has. Low, medium and high are judgements a room can actually agree on, and their product gives six distinct risk values, which is enough to sort the list. If you want a calibrated severity number for a specific vulnerability, that is what CVSS is for, and there is a calculator for it in these labs.

faq.q: Can I bring last quarter's model back?
faq.a: Yes. Export JSON writes a plain file, and Import JSON reads it back with every decision, rating, mitigation and rejection reason intact. The file is readable text, so it belongs in version control next to the system it describes rather than in a folder somebody has to remember.

faq.q: Is anything I type uploaded?
faq.a: No. There is no server involved. A threat model is a list of a system's weak points and their owner's names, which is one of the least sensible things anyone could paste into a website, so this one makes no network request at all and works with the network switched off.

faq.q: What is a Unix timestamp?
faq.a: The number of seconds since 1 January 1970 UTC, ignoring leap seconds. It is the most common timestamp format in logs, APIs and JWT exp claims.

faq.q: What is Windows FILETIME?
faq.a: The number of 100-nanosecond intervals since 1 January 1601 UTC. It appears in the registry, NTFS metadata and Windows event logs, and the values are very large - around 133 quadrillion for a recent date.

faq.q: How do I know which epoch a number uses?
faq.a: Paste it here. Every epoch is applied at once and the ones producing a plausible date are highlighted. Usually only one does, and that is your answer.

faq.q: Why does my timestamp show a date in 1601 or 2185?
faq.a: You are reading it with the wrong epoch. A FILETIME read as Unix seconds lands far in the future; a Unix timestamp read as FILETIME lands in 1601.

faq.q: Does it handle time zones?
faq.a: Conversions are shown in UTC, with your local time alongside. Timestamps in these formats are stored in UTC by definition, so the zone only affects how it is displayed.

faq.q: Is anything uploaded?
faq.a: No. There is no server to upload to. The zones, the date and the working hours you set never leave the tab, and the .ics file is built here with a blob URL rather than fetched from anywhere. You can watch your Network tab stay empty while you drag the slot.

faq.q: Where do the time zone rules come from?
faq.a: From the IANA database inside your own browser, read through Intl.DateTimeFormat. That is deliberate: a copy baked into this page would be stale the moment a government moved a transition, and several do every year. The trade is that an old phone, or a machine with out-of-date system data, will draw out-of-date rules. If a date matters, confirm it with the other person rather than with this page.

faq.q: Why does it say there is no shared window?
faq.a: Because on the hours you gave it, there is not one. India and the US east coast have no overlap at all on a nine-to-five, which is a real fact about the planet rather than a fault in the drawing. When that happens the notes name the two zones that cannot meet, and show the closest the day gets: the stretch where the most people are working, and who would be outside their own hours for it.

faq.q: Does it know about holidays or my colleague’s calendar?
faq.a: No, to both, and it never will. It cannot see any calendar, it does not check free/busy, it does not know who works where, and it has no idea about public holidays, Friday half-days, Ramadan hours or the fact that nobody in Madrid answers anything at 14:00. Working hours are whatever you type into the two pickers on each row. That is a guess about people, not a fact about them.

faq.q: Why is India half an hour out of step with everything?
faq.a: India Standard Time is UTC+05:30, one offset for the whole country, and Nepal went further at +05:45. The Chatham Islands run +12:45. None of that is unusual enough to round away, so this page does not: the ticks on those rows sit on the half or the quarter, out of line with their neighbours. If you have ever had a call start thirty minutes late, you have met the reason.

faq.q: Will the .ics land at the right time in someone else’s calendar?
faq.a: The DTSTART is written as a UTC instant with a trailing Z, so a calendar application will render it in the correct local time for whoever opens it. That is the part this can get right. What it cannot do is send the file, add attendees, check whether anyone is free, or make the meeting exist — the .ics is a draft that lands in your downloads folder and nowhere else.

faq.q: The attack failed on my machine. Does that mean the bug is not real?
faq.a: No, and the tool is built to say so. What failed is the measurement. Your browser's clock is deliberately coarse, your machine is busy, and the signal being hunted is one loop iteration. Read the measured resolution the tool prints: if it is a tenth of a millisecond or worse, a failure there is a statement about the timer. A real attacker repeats orders of magnitude more, measures over a network where the repetitions are cheap, or sits on the same host with a cycle counter that none of these limits apply to.

faq.q: Why does it compare thousands of times for a single sample?
faq.a: Because one comparison of a short string takes a few nanoseconds and the clock cannot see anything that small. Running the comparison hundreds of thousands of times multiplies the one-iteration difference until it is larger than a clock tick. The tool calibrates that count from two things it measures on your machine: the cost of comparing one character, and how long a batch has to last before the scheduler's own jitter stops dominating it. It prints which of the two decided the number.

faq.q: Why the median rather than the average?
faq.a: Because one interruption is worth more than the entire signal. A garbage collection or a scheduler switch in the middle of one batch adds milliseconds to a measurement whose real difference is microseconds, and a mean will hand that candidate the win. A median throws it away. Some real attacks go further and take a low percentile or the fastest sample, on the argument that noise only ever makes a measurement slower and never faster; the median is used here because it is the choice that is hardest to get wrong.

faq.q: Is checking a password against a bcrypt hash vulnerable to this?
faq.a: Not in the way people expect. The comparison happens against the output of a deliberately slow hash, so the work is the same whatever you send and there is no prefix to walk. The real exposure is where a secret is compared as raw bytes: HMAC signatures on webhooks, API tokens, signed cookies, reset tokens, licence keys. Those are the comparisons worth auditing.

faq.q: What is the actual fix?
faq.a: Compare in constant time, with a function that already exists: hmac.compare_digest in Python, crypto.timingSafeEqual in Node, subtle.ConstantTimeCompare in Go. Better still, hash or HMAC both values and compare those, because then both inputs are the same fixed length whatever arrived and neither the length nor the content of the candidate changes the work done. Note what the constant-time function in this lab still leaks: its loop runs for the longer of the two lengths, so length is not fully hidden. Comparing digests is what fixes that too.

faq.q: Does the secret I type leave my browser?
faq.a: No. There is no server to send it to. The comparisons, the timing, the statistics and the plot all run in this tab, and nothing you type appears in your Network tab. The secret is not a real credential anyway — it is the thing the attack in front of you is trying to recover.

faq.q: Does this lab talk to a server or read my real TLS traffic?
faq.a: Neither. There is no TLS client in this page and it opens no connection of any kind. It is a model of the protocol built from the specification, so it can show you how a handshake is shaped and it can tell you nothing whatsoever about a real server. If you want to inspect an actual connection, that is what a packet capture and the PCAP analyzer are for.
faq.t: The TLS handshake, message by message

faq.q: Why is the certificate encrypted in TLS 1.3 but not in TLS 1.2?
faq.a: Because TLS 1.3 splits the server response in two. ServerHello carries only what is needed to derive keys, and the moment it lands both sides can compute the handshake traffic secrets from the key shares and the transcript. Everything after that point, the certificate chain included, travels under those keys. TLS 1.2 could not do this because the client had not sent any key material yet when the certificate went out, so there was nothing to encrypt it with.
faq.t: The TLS handshake, message by message

faq.q: If TLS 1.3 encrypts so much, why can my ISP still see which sites I visit?
faq.a: Because the server name extension in the ClientHello is plaintext, and it has to be: the server needs to know which certificate to present before there is any key to hide the question under. That single field is what domain-level blocking and logging are built on. Encrypted Client Hello fixes it by sealing the real ClientHello to a public key published in DNS, and it needs the server, the browser and a private DNS lookup all lined up, which is why it is not yet the default anywhere.
faq.t: The TLS handshake, message by message

faq.q: Are the keys on the key schedule tab real?
faq.a: The arithmetic is real and the inputs are not. Every value is HMAC-SHA-256 computed in your browser exactly as RFC 8446 section 7.1 specifies, and the transcript hashes are genuine SHA-256 digests of the sample handshake messages this lab builds. Two of the values, the Early Secret with no PSK and the derived secret that follows it, match the constants published in RFC 8448, which is the check that confirms the label encoding is right. What is invented is the ECDHE shared secret, the randoms and the stand-in certificate body, so nothing here will match a capture you own.
faq.t: The TLS handshake, message by message

faq.q: Is 0-RTT safe to turn on?
faq.a: It is a trade, and the honest answer is that it depends on what the first request does. Early data is replayable, because nothing fresh from the server covers it, and RFC 8446 says outright that the available defences are incomplete across a cluster of servers. It also has no forward secrecy, since it is keyed from the resumption secret rather than a fresh exchange. For an idempotent GET on a slow link it is a large win. For anything that changes state it is a bad idea, which is why browsers and servers both restrict it.
faq.t: The TLS handshake, message by message

faq.q: Why does TLS 1.3 still send a ChangeCipherSpec that does nothing?
faq.a: Middlebox compatibility. Enough deployed equipment had learned the exact shape of a TLS 1.2 handshake that a connection which did not look like one got dropped, so TLS 1.3 keeps a meaningless ChangeCipherSpec record and a random legacy session ID purely to look familiar on the wire. RFC 8446 requires receivers to ignore it. It is one of the more honest admissions in a modern protocol specification, and it is why reading a capture means knowing which records are decorative.
faq.t: The TLS handshake, message by message

faq.q: Is TLS 1.2 broken?
faq.a: No, and saying so would be the kind of overstatement this site tries to avoid. A TLS 1.2 connection with an ECDHE key exchange, an AEAD cipher suite and the extended master secret extension is sound today. What TLS 1.3 did was remove the option to configure it badly: static RSA, renegotiation, compression, CBC constructions and hundreds of weak suites are gone rather than merely discouraged. The privacy gain from encrypting the certificate and the alerts is real and separate from that.
faq.t: The TLS handshake, message by message

faq.q: Is my secret sent anywhere?
faq.a: No. The secret is decoded and the HMAC computed in this tab, and the QR is drawn on a canvas here rather than fetched from a chart service - which is how most online QR generators work, and the reason they end up holding your secret. There is no server in this tool and no request carrying anything you type is ever made. Open the Network tab and watch.

faq.q: Did you actually check this against the RFC test vectors?
faq.a: Yes, and the page runs them in front of you. The toolbar shows the result of the ten HOTP vectors in RFC 4226 Appendix D and all eighteen TOTP vectors in RFC 6238 Appendix B, across SHA-1, SHA-256 and SHA-512. If one failed the toolbar would say so in red rather than quietly showing you wrong numbers. You can re-run them yourself: open the browser console and call TotpEngine.selfTest().

faq.q: Should I use this instead of an authenticator app?
faq.a: No. Use an authenticator app or a hardware key for accounts that matter. This page holds a secret in a text field so you can watch what happens to it, which is the right trade for understanding the mechanism and the wrong one for protecting an account.

faq.q: Why does the code here not match my phone?
faq.a: Almost always the clock. TOTP has no channel to correct a drifting device, so a phone half a minute out shows the next window's code - drag the skew slider and you can watch that happen. If the clock is right, check the algorithm, the digit count and the step: a service using SHA-256, eight digits or a sixty-second period will not match the defaults.

faq.q: If TOTP can be phished, is it worth turning on?
faq.a: Yes. It removes the entire class of attacks that work on a password alone: credential stuffing, password reuse, and anything that falls out of a breach dump. What it does not remove is somebody being walked through a convincing login page in real time. Passkeys remove that, because the browser will not sign for the wrong origin.

faq.q: Is this the real TypeScript compiler?
faq.a: Yes. It is the official compiler bundle, running in a Web Worker in your browser. Type checking behaves the same way it does on your own machine.

faq.q: Why does the first run take a moment?
faq.a: The compiler is about 1.7 MB compressed and is downloaded the first time you run TypeScript. It unpacks to roughly 9 MB in the browser cache, so later runs start immediately.

faq.q: Can I use a tsconfig.json?
faq.a: Not currently. Compilation targets ES2020 with modules disabled, which suits the single-file programs this playground is built for.

faq.q: Can I import types from npm?
faq.a: No. There is no package registry wired up here, and the page's script-src policy refuses code fetched from a CDN, so only the built-in lib definitions are available.

faq.q: Does my TypeScript get uploaded anywhere?
faq.a: No. Compilation and execution both happen in your browser. Your source never crosses the network.

faq.q: Will this certificate mean anything to an employer?
faq.a: No, and it says so on its own face. Nobody watched you take the test, nothing checked who was typing, and every number on it was produced by your own browser. It is a practice record — good for pinning above a desk, good for showing yourself that last month was slower. Presented to an employer as a credential it would be a small forgery, which is why the sheet is worded so that nobody can be misled by it.
faq.t: Typing test with a printable certificate

faq.q: Why does the reference look nothing like the IDs on /verify?
faq.a: Because they are different things, and making them look alike would be the dishonest part. Certificates I actually issue carry an ID beginning KS- and exist as records that /verify answers for. This page mints references beginning PRACTICE- instead, and there is nothing behind them: the reference only lets you tell two of your own printouts apart. Typing a PRACTICE- reference into /verify will correctly find nothing.
faq.t: Typing test with a printable certificate

faq.q: How are gross and net WPM different?
faq.a: Gross WPM counts every character you typed, five characters to a word, over the elapsed minutes — the same convention every other typing test uses. Net WPM then subtracts one whole word for each character still wrong when the clock stopped. Gross is how fast your fingers moved; net is how much usable text you produced, and net is the number the certificate carries.
faq.t: Typing test with a printable certificate

faq.q: What is the consistency figure?
faq.a: Your speed is sampled once a second, and consistency is how little those samples varied. A hundred per cent would be a metronome, which no human is. A high number means you held an even rhythm; a low one usually means long pauses on particular keys, which is exactly what the table of costly keys underneath is pointing at.
faq.t: Typing test with a printable certificate

faq.q: Why can I not paste into the test?
faq.a: Because a pasted passage produces a number that means nothing, and this page then offers to print that number on something shaped like a certificate. Pasting is blocked outright. If text arrives in a large block anyway, the run is marked as not typed key by key, no certificate is offered for it, and it is kept out of your history.
faq.t: Typing test with a printable certificate

faq.q: Is anything I type, or my name, sent anywhere?
faq.a: No. The passage, your keystrokes, the name you print and your history all stay in this browser. There is no server behind this page to send them to, and the certificate is produced by your own browser's print dialog rather than rendered somewhere else. Your attempts are kept in this browser's local storage on this device, and Clear history deletes them.
faq.t: Typing test with a printable certificate

faq.q: Does it work on a phone?
faq.a: It runs, and the sheet prints. But a touch keyboard measures a different skill from a physical one, so compare a phone score with your other phone scores rather than with what you managed on a laptop. The certificate records the score, not the keyboard, and that is one more reason not to treat it as evidence of anything.
faq.t: Typing test with a printable certificate

faq.q: How is WPM calculated?
faq.a: By the standard convention: one word is five characters including spaces, so WPM is the total characters you typed divided by five, over the elapsed minutes. That is the same formula every other typing test uses, which means your number here is comparable with the ones you have seen elsewhere.

faq.q: Why is my code speed so much lower than my prose speed?
faq.a: Because it is a different skill. Prose is common words your fingers already know as units; code is punctuation, symbols and exact capitalisation, with far more use of the number row and the keys under your little fingers. A gap of 30-40% is completely normal, and closing it is the point of practising on real code.

faq.q: How is accuracy measured?
faq.a: Correct keystrokes divided by total keystrokes. Fixing a typo does not restore the accuracy you lost, because in real work the mistake still happened and still cost you time. Backspacing itself is not counted as a keystroke, so correcting is not penalised twice.

faq.q: Is my typing data sent anywhere?
faq.a: No. Everything runs in your browser, and your best score is kept in this browser's local storage on your own device. The Labs storage panel shows exactly what is stored and clears it in one click.

faq.q: Does it work on a phone?
faq.a: It runs, but a touch keyboard measures something quite different from a physical one. The scores are only meaningful against your own scores on the same kind of keyboard.

faq.q: Why does the passage show an arrow at the end of a line?
faq.a: That is a newline you need to type. In the code passages the line breaks are part of what you are practising, so they are shown rather than left invisible.

faq.q: Is my text sent anywhere?
faq.a: No. Every code point is examined in your browser, and the character data comes from the browser's own Unicode tables rather than a lookup service. There is no server behind this page and no network request when you press Inspect.

faq.q: What is a zero-width character?
faq.a: A code point that occupies a position in a string and paints nothing. Zero width space, the byte order mark, the soft hyphen and the two joiners are the common ones. They survive copy and paste, they count towards a length limit, and two strings that differ only by one of them are different strings to every computer and the same string to every person.

faq.q: What is Trojan Source?
faq.a: A 2021 result showing that bidirectional formatting characters let source code display in one order and compile in another. The reviewer approves what the screen shows and the compiler reads what the file stores. Every language with comments and string literals is affected, which makes it a review and CI problem rather than a bug in any one language.

faq.q: Why do two identical-looking usernames register as separate accounts?
faq.a: Because the uniqueness check compared the raw strings. Normalise to NFKC first and compare the normalised values, which folds fullwidth letters, ligatures and the mathematical alphabets down to plain ASCII. Cross-script lookalikes such as Cyrillic a survive NFKC untouched, so compare confusable skeletons as well if impersonation is part of your threat model.

faq.q: Why does a character sometimes have no name here?
faq.a: Because the full Unicode character database is megabytes and this page downloads nothing. Names are exact for ASCII, controls, formatting characters, bidi, tags, variation selectors and spaces, algorithmic for CJK, Hangul and private use, and absent for everything else. Category and script always come from the browser's own Unicode tables, so those two columns are exact for every character.

faq.q: How is a grapheme cluster different from a character?
faq.a: A grapheme cluster is what a person would call one character. A family emoji is one cluster, seven code points and twenty-five UTF-8 bytes. Truncating by code points or by bytes can cut a cluster in half, which is how a length limit produces half an emoji and how a substring produces a string no decoder will accept.

faq.q: Can someone take money out of my account just by knowing my UPI ID?
faq.a: No. A UPI ID is an address, like an email address. Somebody who has it can send you money, or raise a collect request asking you for money. The request cannot debit you on its own - it arrives as a prompt on your phone and dies there unless you approve it with your PIN. What people describe as being emptied by someone who knew their ID is nearly always an approval they were talked into giving.
faq.t: UPI and payment fraud, taken apart

faq.q: Do I ever need to enter my UPI PIN to receive money?
faq.a: No. Not in any app, not for any amount, not to verify anything, not once. The PIN is a signature on a debit and it does nothing else. Receiving needs no approval because there is nothing to approve - the money is simply there, and you find out afterwards. If a screen wants your PIN, money is leaving.
faq.t: UPI and payment fraud, taken apart

faq.q: Somebody sent me money by mistake and wants it back. What should I do?
faq.a: Do not return it through their link, their QR code or their request. Tell them to raise it with their own bank, which is how a genuine misdirected transfer is reversed - on the sender's written request, with a reference number. Leave the amount untouched, tell your own bank what happened, and keep the messages. If the money that reached you was itself stolen, passing it on by hand makes your account a link in the chain, and it is your account that gets frozen.
faq.t: UPI and payment fraud, taken apart

faq.q: Are the payment screens on this page real?
faq.a: No, and they are drawn so they could never be mistaken for one. Each carries a standing ribbon saying it is an illustration, no field on it accepts input, and the bar that looks like a confirm button is a paragraph of text with nothing behind it. There are no real UPI handles, no bank names and no logos anywhere on this page, and it makes no network request of any kind.
faq.t: UPI and payment fraud, taken apart

faq.q: Will I get my money back?
faq.a: Often not, and I would rather say that than imply otherwise. Your complaint triggers holds down the chain of accounts the money passed through, and only the portion still sitting somewhere in that chain can be held - anything withdrawn in cash, converted or moved abroad is out of reach. A hold is also not a refund: frozen money is evidence in a live case, and releasing it to you generally needs a court order and months of waiting. Partial recovery is the common good outcome, and nobody can promise you more in advance.
faq.t: UPI and payment fraud, taken apart

faq.q: What is the difference between calling 1930 and filing at cybercrime.gov.in?
faq.a: 1930 is the helpline, and it is what starts the hold - the complaint is pushed out to the banks and payment intermediaries in the transaction chain so funds still in transit can be stopped. cybercrime.gov.in is the formal complaint, and it gives you an acknowledgement number that every later conversation with a bank, an officer or a court will start from. Do both, in that order, and then call your bank's own fraud line separately.
faq.t: UPI and payment fraud, taken apart

faq.q: A buyer showed me a screenshot of the payment. Is that proof?
faq.a: No. A screenshot is an image, and images are trivially edited. The only thing that settles it is your own side: the message from your bank, or the entry in your own passbook or statement. Wait for that before handing anything over, however awkward the wait is, because the awkwardness of the wait is precisely what the script is built on.
faq.t: UPI and payment fraud, taken apart

faq.q: Is UPI itself insecure?
faq.a: Nearly everything on this page is social engineering rather than a technical failure. A UPI debit needs the payer's PIN, entered on the payer's own device, inside the payer's own app - which is a sound design, and it is why the fraud has to go through the person instead of around them. That is also the uncomfortable part: the system worked exactly as specified in every case here. Somebody was persuaded to authorise their own debit.
faq.t: UPI and payment fraud, taken apart

faq.q: Does this open or visit the link?
faq.a: No, never. It is parsed as text. No request is made, so the site owner has no idea you looked - which matters, because loading a phishing URL confirms to the sender that the target is live.

faq.q: Can it tell me where a shortened link goes?
faq.a: No, and that is deliberate. Resolving a bit.ly link means requesting it, which is the one thing this tool will not do. It will tell you that the link is shortened, which is itself worth knowing.

faq.q: What is a homograph attack?
faq.a: Registering a domain that uses characters from another script which look identical to Latin letters, so the name renders like a well-known site while being a completely different domain. This tool lists every non-ASCII character in the hostname with its codepoint.

faq.q: Is https enough to trust a link?
faq.a: No. HTTPS means the connection is encrypted, not that the site is honest. Most phishing sites use HTTPS, because certificates are free and take a minute to obtain.

faq.q: Is anything I paste logged?
faq.a: No. The analysis happens in your browser and nothing is stored or transmitted.

faq.q: Is the deep web the same as the dark web?
faq.a: No, and the difference is not a matter of degree. The deep web is everything a search engine cannot index - your webmail, your bank statements, a shared document, a database behind a form. The dark web is a much smaller thing: sites that live on a separate overlay network such as Tor and have addresses that ordinary DNS cannot resolve at all. Almost everything people call dark web is deep web, and almost all of the deep web is ordinary.
faq.t: Surface web, deep web, dark web

faq.q: Does this tool visit the URL I type?
faq.a: No. It reads the string on your own machine and makes no request of any kind. That is also its main limitation: a robots.txt rule, a noindex header and a login redirect are all things you can only learn by asking the server. Where the address cannot settle the question the tool says so rather than guessing.
faq.t: Surface web, deep web, dark web

faq.q: Are the .onion addresses on this page real?
faq.a: No, and they cannot be made real. A version 3 onion address is 56 base32 characters derived from a public key; the illustrative strings here contain hyphens and ordinary English words, which are not valid in that label, so none of them resolves anywhere. This lab explains the architecture. It is not a way in, and there are no addresses, directories or links off this site anywhere on it.
faq.t: Surface web, deep web, dark web

faq.q: Is the dark web really most of the internet?
faq.a: No. The claim people are half-remembering is about the deep web, which is genuinely far larger than the indexed surface web, and even there the famous figures are guesses. The dark web is a small fraction of that. By the Tor Project's own published metrics, onion service traffic has sat in the low single digits as a share of Tor's own traffic for years.
faq.t: Surface web, deep web, dark web

faq.q: Does Tor make you anonymous?
faq.a: It breaks the link between your address and the destination inside the network, which is a real and useful property. It does not defeat an adversary who can watch both ends and correlate timing, it does not stop a malicious exit relay reading plain HTTP, it does not change your browser's fingerprint, and it does nothing at all about signing into an account that identifies you. The caveat panel in the second tab lists these because they are the ways people are actually deanonymised.
faq.t: Surface web, deep web, dark web

faq.q: Why does the tool call a page on this very site deep web?
faq.a: Because this site's robots.txt disallows /partials/, /assets/data/ and /scripts/. Those paths have no login and no secret; they are served instantly to anyone who asks. They will simply never appear in a search result. That is the cleanest demonstration I have that deep does not mean sinister.
faq.t: Surface web, deep web, dark web

faq.q: Why do the percentages show ranges rather than numbers?
faq.a: Because the published studies disagree with each other by tens of percentage points, depending on how the crawl was seeded, how long it ran, whether dead addresses were counted and who did the categorising. A single figure would look better and tell you less. Anyone quoting you a precise percentage of the dark web is overstating what is measurable.
faq.t: Surface web, deep web, dark web

faq.q: Does this tool test my own wireless network?
faq.a: No. It cannot see your network, your adapter or any network at all - a web page has no access to the radio. This is an explanation of how the protocols work, drawn so you can step through them. To check your own network, open your router's wireless settings and read what the security mode says.
faq.t: Wi-Fi security, from WEP to WPA3

faq.q: Is WPA2 still safe to use?
faq.a: With a long random passphrase, yes, and AES-CCMP itself has no practical break. But the four-way handshake gives anyone who observes it an offline target: they can test passphrase guesses at their own pace with nothing further sent to the network. That makes the passphrase the entire defence, so it has to be worth something. WPA3 removes the target rather than relying on the passphrase to survive it.
faq.t: Wi-Fi security, from WEP to WPA3

faq.q: Why can a WPA3 handshake not be cracked offline?
faq.a: Because the password only enters the exchange blinded by random values that are never transmitted. A listener ends up with two scalars, two curve elements and two confirm hashes, and testing a single password guess against any of it would mean solving a discrete logarithm. So each guess has to be tried live against the access point, one at a time, where it can be rate-limited, refused and logged.
faq.t: Wi-Fi security, from WEP to WPA3

faq.q: Does hiding my network name make it harder to find?
faq.a: No. The beacon stops carrying the name, but every association and every probe from every client that knows the network still carries it in the clear. It is hidden from someone scrolling a list of networks and from nobody else. It is also slightly worse than doing nothing, because devices configured for a hidden network go looking for it by name wherever they are.
faq.t: Wi-Fi security, from WEP to WPA3

faq.q: Do I actually need a VPN on public wifi?
faq.a: Usually not for the reason it is sold. HTTPS already protects the contents, the integrity and the identity of nearly everything you do, and it closed the classic public-wifi scenario years ago. What still leaks is which hosts you connect to, through DNS, the TLS SNI field and the destination addresses. If hiding that from the local network is a specific concern of yours, a VPN genuinely helps - but it moves that trust to the provider rather than removing it, and it does nothing about tracking, phishing or malware.
faq.t: Wi-Fi security, from WEP to WPA3

faq.q: Are the keys and nonces on this page real?
faq.a: No, and the page says so on screen where they appear. It performs no cryptography. The hex strings are a deterministic placeholder that exists so that changing the network name visibly changes what depends on it, which is a real property worth seeing. The structure of the derivation, the sizes and the roles of each key are the real ones.
faq.t: Wi-Fi security, from WEP to WPA3

faq.q: How do I send a birthday wish link?
faq.a: Type the person's name, pick one of six looks, and copy the link. Anyone who opens it sees a full-screen animated card addressed to them. There is no sign-up and nothing to install.
faq.t: Make a birthday or festival wish someone will actually screenshot

faq.q: Which festivals are supported?
faq.a: 92 festivals, including Diwali, Holi, Navratri, Durga Puja, Ganesh Chaturthi, Raksha Bandhan, Pongal, Onam, Uttarayan, Bestu Varas, Eid al-Fitr, Eid al-Adha, Ramadan, Hanukkah, Rosh Hashanah, Christmas, Easter, Lunar New Year, Nowruz, Vesak and Songkran. Each one has its own greeting, colours and decoration.
faq.t: Make a birthday or festival wish someone will actually screenshot

faq.q: What if I spell the festival name differently?
faq.a: Spelling does not have to be exact. Transliterated names have no single correct spelling, so the tool matches approximately: bestu varsh, diwaly, crismas and gujarati new year all resolve correctly. Anything it does not recognise still produces a warm generic card rather than an error.
faq.t: Make a birthday or festival wish someone will actually screenshot

faq.q: Is the name I type stored anywhere?
faq.a: No. The link is assembled in your browser out of the text you type, and the name travels inside the link itself. There is no account, no database and no server request, so nobody including the site owner can see who you sent a wish to.
faq.t: Make a birthday or festival wish someone will actually screenshot

faq.q: Why does the link change after the card opens?
faq.a: Once the card has rendered, the query parameter is removed from the address bar so it reads as a page made for that person rather than a form somebody filled in. The card keeps a Copy link button, and that full link is the one to forward.
faq.t: Make a birthday or festival wish someone will actually screenshot

faq.q: Is it free?
faq.a: Yes, entirely. No sign-up, no watermark, no paywall and no limit on how many links you make.
faq.t: Make a birthday or festival wish someone will actually screenshot

faq.q: Is it really free, with no watermark?
faq.a: Yes. No account, no watermark, no export limit. The whole thing runs in your browser and the PNG downloads directly from the page.

faq.q: Is my text uploaded anywhere?
faq.a: No. The text is counted, laid out and drawn entirely in your browser, and the image is made locally. Nothing is sent to a server - which matters if the text is a draft, a private document or anything unpublished.

faq.q: Why are words like "the" and "and" missing?
faq.a: They are filler words that appear in every English text, so they would be the biggest words in every cloud while telling you nothing about this particular text. They are removed by default, but there is a switch to keep them, and you can add your own words to ignore.

faq.q: Some of my words did not appear - why?
faq.a: A tight shape can run out of room. The tool places the most frequent words first and tells you how many it placed; raise the "max words" limit, pick a rounder shape, or turn off "repeat words" so the space goes to new words rather than to repeats.

faq.q: Can I use the image commercially?
faq.a: The image is made entirely from your own text and downloaded to your machine - there is no licence attached and nothing is uploaded, so what you do with it is up to you.

faq.q: How do we start?
faq.a: With a free intro call — or just a message if you prefer. I listen to the problem first; if I am not the right person for it, I will say so and point you somewhere better.
faq.t: The work you can hire me for, in plain terms.

faq.q: How do you charge?
faq.a: Whichever way fits the work — hourly, project-based, full-time/retainer, or per session for corporate training. Either way you get a written scope with a quote before any work starts — deliverables, timeline, and price. No meters running quietly in the background. Ongoing 1:1 coaching is separate and billed monthly through the mentorship program.
faq.t: The work you can hire me for, in plain terms.

faq.q: Will you access any device or account I bring you?
faq.a: Only devices and accounts you own or are explicitly authorized to grant access to. I may ask for proof of ownership, and I decline or stop any work where that isn’t clear — no unlocking, bypassing, or monitoring of anyone else’s device, ever.
faq.t: The work you can hire me for, in plain terms.

faq.q: Do you work remotely?
faq.a: Yes — remote-first, with clients across the US, France, Taiwan, and India. Where the work allows it, delivery happens in the open on GitHub so you can verify progress yourself.
faq.t: The work you can hire me for, in plain terms.

faq.q: Do you train teams, not just individuals?
faq.a: Yes — corporate training is a separate service line. One team at a time, 10–40 people, remote or on site, in sessions from half a day to three days. It is quoted per session or per program rather than by the hour, and I build the material around the systems you already use after a short intro call — no stock deck. The mentorship program is the 1:1 version, billed monthly.
faq.t: The work you can hire me for, in plain terms.

faq.q: What topics can you train a team on?
faq.a: The list is above — security awareness, Linux and systems security, automation and AI workflows, engineering practice, technical writing, and professional skills like communication and remote collaboration. Topics combine into a longer program, and anything not listed is still worth asking about: you will get either a yes or an honest no.
faq.t: The work you can hire me for, in plain terms.

faq.q: Have you run corporate training before?
faq.a: Not under my own name — this is a new service line, and I would rather say so plainly. What it is built on: teaching engineers since 2021 through MountBlue, Springboard, Coding Ninjas, Correlation One, and Codementor, and six months as an Assistant Professor teaching operating systems and information security. I hold no instructor certification — none of the certificates I list is a teaching credential. If you need a vendor who has run this exact session two hundred times, that is a fair reason to hire someone else.
faq.t: The work you can hire me for, in plain terms.

faq.q: Can corporate training count as evidence for an audit?
faq.a: Partly, and I would rather be precise than convenient about it. ISO/IEC 27001:2022 Annex A 6.3 asks for information security awareness, education and training, and SOC 2 assessors usually map the same evidence to the common criteria. What they want in practice is a record of who attended, what was covered, and when — and that record comes with the session. India’s DPDP Act asks for reasonable security safeguards rather than naming training outright, so treat a session as support for that case, not a box it ticks. I am not an accredited training partner of any certification body, and I cannot promise an audit outcome.

faq.q: What do attendees get after a training session?
faq.a: The materials as delivered, a written summary of what was covered with the date and the hours, and a completion certificate for everyone who attended — each carrying a unique ID your auditor or HR team can check on the verification page without going through me. Company names are never published there, and any attendee who would rather not be listed gets their ID confirmed by email instead.

After the call you get a written outline and a fixed quote before any date is held. Invoices come from a business registered as a micro enterprise with the Ministry of MSME, Government of India, Udyam Reg. No. UDYAM-GJ-23-0050928. faq.a: Yes. Anything you share for an engagement — code, data, business details — is used only for that engagement and shared with no one. The formal version is in the Terms of Service and Privacy Policy.
