terms.d: Every point where an attacker could try to get in — open ports, input fields, file uploads, third-party scripts, people. Reducing it is usually cheaper than defending it.
Trying every possible password until one works. Speed depends entirely on the hashing algorithm: billions of guesses a second against MD5, a few thousand against bcrypt.
Writing more data into a fixed-size buffer than it can hold, so the excess spills into whatever sits next in memory — often the saved return address, which is what turns a bug into code execution.
Confidentiality, Integrity, Availability — the three properties security is meant to protect. Most attacks are easiest to classify by which one they break.
Taking username and password pairs leaked from one breach and replaying them against other sites, betting on password reuse. It needs no cracking at all.
Cross-Site Request Forgery. A page you did not intend to act on makes your browser send an authenticated request to a site you are already logged into, using your cookies.
Common Vulnerabilities and Exposures — the public catalogue giving one specific flaw one stable identifier, so everyone is talking about the same bug.
A formula turning a vulnerability's characteristics into a 0–10 severity score, so a backlog can be ordered by something other than who shouted loudest.
An incident where data leaves the control of the organisation holding it. Whether it becomes a crisis usually depends on what was stored and how it was hashed.
Layering controls so no single failure is fatal. The assumption is that any one layer will eventually be bypassed.
Exhausting a resource — CPU, memory, disk, bandwidth, process slots — until a system can no longer serve anyone. A fork bomb is the local version.
Brute force with a shortlist: real passwords from previous breaches, tried first. It beats exhaustive search because human password choice is not random.
A process that repeatedly forks copies of itself until the process table is full and the machine stops accepting new work.
Registering a domain that reads like a real one by substituting lookalike characters from another script — a Cyrillic a for a Latin a. The URL looks correct to a human.
An observable trace that something malicious happened — a file hash, a domain, a registry key. The unit of sharing between defenders.
Asking a question in a way that hides which answer you wanted, by making your query match many records at once. It is how a password can be checked against breach data without sending the password.
Giving an account, process, or person exactly the access the job needs and nothing more, so a compromise stays small.
An attacker sitting between two parties who each believe they are talking directly to the other, able to read and alter what passes through. TLS exists to make this detectable.
Making code or data hard to read without making it hard to run. It slows an analyst down; it is not a security control.
Open-source intelligence — what can be learned about a target from public sources alone: certificate logs, registration records, job ads, metadata in published files.
How much genuine unpredictability a password carries, measured in bits. Length buys more of it than substituting a 3 for an e.
Using ../ sequences in a filename to escape the directory an application meant to confine you to, and read or write somewhere else.
Authorised attack against a system to find what a real attacker could reach, with a written scope and a report at the end. The authorisation is what separates it from a crime.
Getting someone to hand over credentials or money by impersonating something they trust. Still the most common initial access route, because it targets people rather than software.
Turning limited access into greater access — a normal user becoming root, a read-only token gaining write. Usually the second step of an intrusion, not the first.
A precomputed lookup from hashes back to the passwords that made them, trading disk space for cracking time. Salting defeats it entirely.
Malware that encrypts a victim's files and sells back the key. Its leverage is availability, which is why backups are the actual countermeasure.
Regular-expression denial of service. A pattern with nested, overlapping repetition can take exponential time on a crafted input, hanging the process that ran it.
Stealing a session token and presenting it as your own. The password is never needed, which is why tokens deserve the same care as passwords.
Attacking the person rather than the system: urgency, authority, and familiarity used to get someone to open the door themselves.
Supplying input the application concatenates into a SQL statement, so your text becomes part of the query. Parameterised queries remove the class entirely.
Compromising something a target already trusts — a dependency, an update server, a vendor — so the malicious code arrives through a legitimate channel.
A written answer to who might attack this, what they want, and what they can do. Without one, security work is guessing.
Cross-Site Scripting. Injecting script into a page other people view, so it runs with their session and their origin. Reflected, stored, and DOM-based are the three shapes.
A vulnerability being exploited before a patch exists. The name is the number of days the defender has had to fix it.
A small archive that expands to something enormous, exhausting disk or memory on whatever unpacks it automatically.
An archive containing entries whose paths escape the extraction directory, so unpacking it overwrites files elsewhere on disk.
The Advanced Encryption Standard — the symmetric cipher most encrypted traffic and storage actually uses. One key encrypts and decrypts, applied over repeated rounds.
An encoding, not encryption. It rewrites arbitrary bytes using 64 safe characters so they survive text-only channels. Anyone can reverse it; it protects nothing.
A password hashing function designed to be slow, with a tunable cost factor. Slowness is the feature: it is what makes offline cracking expensive.
Shift every letter a fixed number of places along the alphabet. ROT13 is the shift-13 case. Broken by trying all 25 shifts.
An organisation browsers already trust, which vouches for the link between a public key and a domain name by signing its certificate.
Public append-only logs recording every certificate a CA issues, so a domain owner can discover certificates issued for their name without their knowledge.
Certificate Signing Request (PKCS#10) — a bundle containing your public key and the name you are claiming, signed by your private key and sent to a CA to be certified.
A way for two parties to agree on a shared secret over a channel anyone can read, without ever transmitting the secret itself.
A value only the private key could have produced, that anyone holding the public key can verify. It proves both origin and that nothing was altered.
Public-key cryptography built on elliptic curves, reaching the same security as RSA with far shorter keys — which is why modern TLS prefers it.
Breaking a substitution cipher by counting letters: in English, e and t dominate, and that shape survives the substitution.
A one-way function turning any input into a fixed-length digest. The same input always gives the same digest; the digest reveals nothing about the input.
A hash combined with a secret key, so the digest proves not only that data is unaltered but that it came from someone holding the key.

JSON Web Token — a signed, base64url-encoded set of claims. The common signed form (JWS) is not encrypted, so anyone holding the token can read every claim in it; an encrypted form (JWE) exists but is much rarer.
A 128-bit hash, comprehensively broken for security. Collisions can be produced on demand, so it survives only as a non-security checksum.
A number used once. It stops a captured message from being replayed later, and stops identical plaintexts from producing identical ciphertexts.
The text wrapper you see around keys and certificates — base64 between BEGIN and END lines. A container format, not a cryptographic one.
A keypair where one half encrypts or signs and the other decrypts or verifies. The public half can be published; the private half never leaves your hands.
The long-standing public-key algorithm, resting on the difficulty of factoring the product of two large primes.
Random data added to a password before hashing, unique per user, so identical passwords produce different hashes and precomputed tables become useless.
A 256-bit hash from the SHA-2 family, and the current sensible default for integrity checks and signatures.
Hiding the existence of a message rather than its contents — for example in the least significant bits of an image, where the change is invisible.
Transport Layer Security — the protocol behind the S in HTTPS. It authenticates the server, agrees a key, and encrypts everything after.
A Caesar cipher whose shift changes per letter according to a repeating keyword. Broken by finding the key length, then solving each position separately.
The browser's built-in cryptography API. It generates and uses real keys locally, which is what lets a page do genuine crypto without a server.
The standard structure of a TLS certificate: subject, issuer, validity dates, public key, extensions, and the CA's signature over all of it.
Combining plaintext with a key using exclusive-or. Unbreakable with a truly random key as long as the message; trivially broken when the key repeats.
Brand Indicators for Message Identification — a DNS record letting a mailbox show your logo beside authenticated mail. It requires DMARC enforcement first.
Classless Inter-Domain Routing notation — 192.168.1.0/24. The number after the slash counts the bits fixed as network, leaving the rest for hosts.
Cross-Origin Resource Sharing — the headers by which a server tells the browser which other origins may read its responses. It is enforced by the browser, not the server.
A cryptographic signature added to outgoing mail, verified against a public key in the sender's DNS. It proves the message was not altered in transit.
The policy tying SPF and DKIM together: what a receiver should do when a message fails, and where to send reports about it.
The Domain Name System — the distributed directory translating names people type into addresses machines route to.
DNS queries sent inside ordinary HTTPS, so they cannot be read or tampered with by whoever carries your traffic.
A and AAAA point at addresses, MX at mail servers, NS at nameservers, TXT at arbitrary text used for verification and policy, CAA at which CAs may issue for the name.
An HTTP Archive — a JSON export of everything a browser's network tab recorded. Useful for debugging, and dangerous to share: it captures headers and tokens verbatim.
The three-digit result of a request: 2xx succeeded, 3xx go elsewhere, 4xx you got it wrong, 5xx the server did. 418 is a joke that became permanent.
A policy telling sending mail servers to require TLS for your domain, closing the downgrade path where encryption is silently skipped.
A packet capture file — the raw frames a network interface saw, with timestamps. The primary evidence format for network forensics.
A number identifying which service on a host a connection is for. 443 is HTTPS, 22 is SSH, 25 is SMTP.
Registration Data Access Protocol — the structured JSON-over-HTTPS successor to WHOIS, returning parseable domain registration data.
A DNS record listing which servers may send mail for your domain. The oldest of the three email authentication checks, and the easiest to get subtly wrong.
The pattern separating the network part of an address from the host part, deciding which addresses are reachable directly rather than through a router.
How a sender discovers how fast the path can actually carry data — ramping up, backing off on loss, and settling near the limit without collapsing it.
SYN, SYN-ACK, ACK — the exchange establishing a connection and agreeing the starting sequence numbers for both directions.
Browser-to-browser audio, video, and data connections that carry media directly between peers rather than through a server.
The original domain registration lookup: plain text, inconsistently formatted, and largely redacted since GDPR. RDAP replaces it.
Any trace a system leaves behind that outlives the activity itself — a log line, a registry key, a thumbnail, a deleted-but-not-overwritten file.
The documented record of who held evidence, when, and what they did to it. Break it and the evidence may be worthless in court regardless of what it shows.
Metadata a camera writes into a photograph — model, serial number, exact timestamp, and often GPS coordinates. It survives copying and uploading unless deliberately stripped.
Windows' timestamp format: 100-nanosecond intervals since 1 January 1601. Mistaking it for a Unix timestamp puts your evidence in the wrong century.
A file shown as raw bytes in hexadecimal beside their printable characters — the view you need when a file is not what its extension claims.
The signature at the start of a file identifying its real type — PK for a ZIP, %PDF for a PDF. Extensions lie; magic bytes usually do not.
A capture of a machine's RAM. It holds what the disk never sees: decryption keys, plaintext passwords, running processes, network connections.
Data about data — who made a file, when, with what, and on which machine. Frequently more revealing than the content it describes.
A binary file holding part of the Windows registry — SYSTEM, SOFTWARE, SAM, NTUSER.DAT. A forensic goldmine of what ran, when, and for whom.
A measure of randomness in bytes. High entropy suggests encryption or compression; a sudden change of entropy inside a file suggests something is hidden in it.
Pulling readable text out of a binary. The oldest and still one of the most productive first moves in analysing an unknown file or memory image.
Seconds elapsed since 1 January 1970 UTC. The most common machine timestamp, and the baseline every other epoch gets converted to.
Human-readable names for a processor's actual instructions, one line per operation. The lowest level you can write without entering raw opcodes.
A deadlock-avoidance method that grants a resource request only if the system would still be in a safe state afterwards.
A single small binary providing hundreds of standard Unix commands, used where space is tight — embedded devices, rescue images, minimal containers.
Deciding which ready process runs next. First-come, shortest-job-first, round-robin and priority scheduling each optimise something different and starve something else.
Two or more processes each holding a resource the other needs, so none can proceed. Requires mutual exclusion, hold-and-wait, no preemption, and circular wait, all at once.
The vocabulary of operations a processor understands. x86 and ARM are different vocabularies, which is why a binary for one will not run on the other.
The part of an operating system that owns the hardware — memory, scheduling, devices, file systems. Everything else asks it for things through system calls.
The smallest unit of computation — AND, OR, NOT, XOR — built from a handful of transistors. Every operation a processor performs reduces to these.
Choosing which page of memory to evict when physical RAM is full. FIFO, LRU and optimal differ mainly in how badly they behave under real access patterns.
A running program with its own memory, file descriptors, and entry in the kernel's process table. That table is finite, which is what a fork bomb exploits.
A tiny, extremely fast storage slot inside the CPU. Instructions operate on registers; everything else has to be loaded into one first.
The program that reads your commands and asks the kernel to run them. bash, ksh and BusyBox ash are different shells with genuinely different syntax.
The slice of stack belonging to one function call — its local variables, the saved frame pointer, and the address to return to. Overflow a local buffer and you reach the last two.
The controlled doorway from a program into the kernel — open, read, write, fork. The only way user code can touch hardware.
The switch everything is built from. Billions of them on a modern die, combined into gates, then adders, then a processor.
An emulated computer running inside a real one, with its own kernel and its own memory ceiling. That ceiling is what makes destructive experiments safe.
A portable binary instruction format browsers execute at near-native speed. It is what lets a real compiler, database, or Linux kernel run inside a tab.
How an algorithm's cost grows as input grows, ignoring constants. O(n log n) beats O(n²) at scale even if it loses on ten items.
Halving a sorted range each step to find a value in O(log n). It requires the data to be sorted first, which is the cost people forget.
A program translating source code into machine code before it runs, reporting errors up front rather than at the moment of failure.
A function that can pause itself and resume later, keeping its state. Concurrency without threads, and without their locking problems.
Common Table Expression — a named subquery written with WITH, letting a complex SQL statement be read top to bottom instead of inside out.
Deterministic Finite Automaton — a state machine with exactly one transition per input, so matching runs in linear time with no backtracking.
A shape whose detail repeats at every scale. The Mandelbrot set is generated by iterating one short formula over each point in the plane.
Automatic reclamation of memory no longer reachable by the program. It removes a class of bugs and adds unpredictable pauses.
Nondeterministic Finite Automaton — a state machine that may have several possible transitions at once. Regex engines build one, then either simulate or determinise it.
A variable holding a memory address rather than a value. The source of C's power and of most of its security history.
Partition around a pivot, sort each side. O(n log n) on average, O(n²) when the pivot choice meets its worst case.
A pattern language for describing sets of strings. Compact, powerful, and easy to write in a form that takes exponential time.
A script the browser runs between a page and the network, able to answer requests from a cache. It is what makes a site work offline.
A small program run on the GPU for every pixel or vertex, in parallel. GLSL is the language WebGL uses for them.
The query language relational databases speak. You describe the result you want; the engine decides how to produce it.
The standard method for turning a regular expression into an NFA, one small machine per operator, wired together.
A compiler whose output is other source code rather than machine code — TypeScript to JavaScript being the common case.
A SQL function computing across a set of rows related to the current row, without collapsing them into one. Ranking and running totals are the usual uses.
India's DPDP Act term for whoever decides why and how personal data is processed — the party carrying the legal duties. Elsewhere called a controller.
India's Digital Personal Data Protection Act — consent requirements, purpose limitation, breach notification, and the rights individuals can exercise over their data.
The EU's General Data Protection Regulation. Applies by where the person is, not where the company is, which is why it reaches well outside Europe.
The US rules governing protected health information — who may hold it, how it must be secured, and what must happen when it leaks.
India's foundational technology law: electronic records, digital signatures, and the offences that make computer crime prosecutable.
The card industry's security standard for anyone storing, processing, or transmitting cardholder data. Contractual rather than statutory, and enforced by fines.
Personally Identifiable Information — anything that identifies a person alone or combined with something else. The combination is what people underestimate.
An audit report on how an organisation handles security, availability, confidentiality, processing integrity, and privacy. A report, not a certificate.
An automated sales development representative — software that researches prospects and drafts outreach, leaving a human to judge and send.
Applicant Tracking System — the software that reads a resume before a person does. It is why layout choices can cost you an interview.
Man, Machine, Material, Method — the four inputs every operation runs on, and a quick frame for locating where a process is actually failing.
A fair-code workflow automation tool — source-available under the Sustainable Use License, not OSI open source. Nodes for triggers, logic, and services, wired into pipelines you can self-host.
Work expanding past what was agreed without the timeline or price moving with it. Prevented by writing the scope down, not by working harder.

A control sequence in a stream of text that moves the cursor, sets a colour, or clears the screen. Because it can rewrite lines already printed, escapes in untrusted log output are a security problem rather than a formatting one.

A matching strategy that tries one possibility, fails, returns and tries the next. It is what lets a regular-expression engine support backreferences, and what makes it vulnerable to input crafted to force exponential retries.

Identifying a visitor from the combination of properties their browser exposes — screen size, fonts, timezone, graphics stack. No single value identifies anyone; together they usually do, and you cannot clear it the way you clear a cookie.

During a network partition a distributed system must choose between staying consistent and staying available. It says nothing about behaviour when there is no partition, which is most of the time — a detail the popular "pick two of three" phrasing loses.

Two machines disagreeing about the time, which turns a merged log into fiction. A suspiciously round offset — exactly five and a half hours — is usually a timezone set wrong rather than a clock that has drifted.

Comparing two secrets in a way that takes the same time whether they match at the first byte or the last. An ordinary comparison returns early, and that difference is measurable enough to recover the secret one byte at a time.

A response header listing where a page may load scripts, styles and other resources from. Its sharpest edge is that adding a nonce silently disables any "unsafe-inline" in the same directive, so a policy can be far stricter than it looks.
A small value a site asks the browser to store and send back on every subsequent request. That automatic sending is convenient, and it is also the entire mechanism CSRF depends on.

A seasonal offset change that makes one day 23 hours long and another 25. It moves the overlap between two timezones on the transition date, which is why a recurring meeting can quietly shift for half the participants.

A list of rules matched against each packet in order, with the first match deciding. Most firewall bugs are ordering bugs rather than syntax bugs — a broad rule early on quietly shadowing a specific one below it.
India's fifteen-character GST registration number, carrying a state code, an embedded PAN and a final check digit. A valid checksum proves the number is well formed, not that anyone is registered.

The standard describing how computers store fractional numbers as sign, exponent and mantissa. It is why 0.1 plus 0.2 is not 0.3: neither value is representable in binary, so both are stored as the nearest thing that is.

A number held as a fixed number of significant digits scaled by an exponent, trading exactness for range. Every value is really the nearest representable neighbour, and the errors accumulate as you add them up.

Text decoded with the wrong character set, so "café" arrives as "cafÃ©". Usually reversible by re-encoding and decoding correctly — unless a replacement character has already been substituted, at which point the bytes are gone.
The mapping between the bytes in a file and the characters they represent. Nothing in a plain text file records which one was used, which is why the wrong guess is so common and so recoverable.
A lock that permits exactly one thread inside a section of code at a time. It does not remove the interleaving between threads; it removes the interleavings that corrupt shared state.
The algorithm behind most diff tools, finding the shortest edit script between two files. It is what makes a diff read as a few changed lines rather than as a whole file rewritten.

The number of replicas that must acknowledge a read or a write. When reads plus writes exceed the replica count, every read is guaranteed to see the latest write — which is the whole arithmetic behind tunable consistency.

Two operations whose result depends on which happens first, when nothing guarantees an order. The classic is read-modify-write on a shared counter, where one thread's increment silently overwrites another's.
A firewall rule that can never match, because an earlier rule already covers everything it would have caught. It is invisible in the ruleset and only shows up when you walk a packet through in order.

A cookie attribute controlling whether the browser attaches it to cross-site requests. Setting it to None requires Secure, and getting that combination wrong means the cookie is rejected outright rather than stored with weaker settings.

A software bill of materials: the list of every component that went into a build, direct and transitive. Its value is answering "are we affected?" in minutes rather than days when a dependency turns out to be compromised.

A counter that permits up to N holders at once. A semaphore of one behaves like a mutex; anything above one still allows the concurrent access a mutex exists to prevent, which is the distinction people most often get wrong.

A firewall tracking established connections, so the reply to an allowed outbound request is permitted while an unsolicited inbound packet to the same port is not. It is why a home network works at all without per-service rules.
Combining two sets of changes using their common ancestor as a reference. The base is what lets a tool tell "deleted on one side" apart from "added on the other", which a two-way diff cannot do.

Recovering a secret from how long an operation takes rather than from what it returns. A comparison that stops at the first wrong byte leaks the position of that byte, and enough repeated measurements turn that into the whole value.

Information leaking through a system's physical behaviour rather than its output — time taken, power drawn, cache state, sound. The algorithm can be perfect and the implementation still gives the answer away.

Publishing a package or registering a domain whose name is one plausible typo away from a popular one, and waiting. In a dependency tree it is a supply chain attack that requires no compromise of anything.

The reference timezone every other offset is expressed against, and the only sane thing to store a timestamp in. Logs that record local time without an offset cannot be merged with anything, because nothing in the bytes says which local time it was.

A decimal checksum that catches every single-digit error and every adjacent transposition, which simpler schemes miss. It is the check digit on an Aadhaar number, and it proves only that the number is well formed.

An encrypted tunnel to a server that then makes requests on your behalf. It hides your traffic from the local network and your address from the destination, and it changes who can watch you rather than removing the need to trust anyone.

SPF permits ten DNS-costing lookups while evaluating a record, counted cumulatively through every include. Exceed it and the result is a PermError, which is not a pass — so a record somebody spent an afternoon on can protect nothing at all.

The daily XML summary receivers send back, listing who sent mail as your domain and whether it aligned. The pattern everyone misreads on their first one is the forwarder: SPF fails, DKIM passes, and nothing is wrong.

The contact-card format a scanned QR code can carry, so a phone offers to save a name and number rather than open a link. Its escaping rules for commas and semicolons are where most generators quietly get it wrong.

The schedule splitting each loan repayment between interest and principal. Early payments are almost entirely interest, which is why leaving a long loan after a few years returns far less equity than the amount paid suggests.
